questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 65-year-old patient with heart failure is being evaluated for therapy. Which medication, among the given options, has been shown to reduce mortality in patients with heart failure?
questions.explanation: For patients with Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF), the cornerstone of therapy involves drugs that provide a proven mortality benefit. Metoprolol succinate (a beta-blocker) is one of the few medications—along with ACE inhibitors/ARBs, MRAs like spironolactone, and SGLT2 inhibitors—that have been shown in large clinical trials to significantly increase survival. Beta-blockers work by countering the chronic harmful effects of sympathetic nervous system overactivation on the heart. Furosemide (Option B) and Torsemide (Option D) are loop diuretics that are essential for managing fluid overload and improving symptoms, but they have not been proven to reduce mortality. Prazosin (Option C) is an alpha-blocker used for hypertension but has no established survival benefit in heart failure. Metoprolol must be initiated at a very low dose in stable patients and gradually up-titrated. This evidence-based approach is fundamental for improving the long-term prognosis of elderly patients with chronic cardiac dysfunction
questions.learning: For patients with Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF), the cornerstone of therapy involves drugs that provide a proven mortality benefit.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is correct regarding the image given below:
options: It is called Argyl Robertson pupil
The vision is normal in right eye
Seen in optic neuritis, the pupil can paradoxically dilate in the both eyes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Seen in optic neuritis, the pupil can paradoxically dilate in the both eyes

The given image of "swinging flashlight test" shows both pupils constricting when the left eye is stimulated (normal response) followed by both pupils abnormally dilating when the right eye is stimulated (abnormal response).

This finding is suggestive of Marcus Gunn pupil which is also known as Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD).

In this patient the right eye is defective (Option A) and the left eye is normal (rules out option B).

Marcus Gunn pupil refers to the paradoxical response of the pupil to light and it is the earliest sign of optic nerve disease such as optic neuritis or optic nerve damage in glaucoma.It is caused due to a defect in the afferent pathway (optic nerve) of the pupillary light reflex in one eye.

Normal response to stimulation of the eye is constriction of the pupil of the stimulated eye (direct light reflex) and also of the contralateral eye (indirect or consensual light reflex).

Causes of RAPD:

• Optic nerve lesions (e.g.All types of optic neuritis, glaucoma)
• Optic tract lesions (e.g., infarction)
• Severe retinal disease (e.g., central retinal artery occlusion, extensive retinal detachment)
• Maculopathy (macular degeneration )

The below given image depicts the findings seen in Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD).

Option A:Argyl Robertson pupil is seen in neurosyphilis. In this condition,on light stimulation both the pupils will not constrict, but on accommodation (near target) both the pupils will constrict.

Argyll Robertson pupil is attributed to a dorsal midbrain lesion of neurosyphilis that affects the pupillary light pathway but spares the more ventrally placed pupillary near reflex pathway(Accomdation pathway), thereby causing a light-near dissociation.

Features of Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP) include:

• Bilateral small, irregular pupils in dim light
• Accommodation Reflex Present (ARP)- The eye accomdates by constricting the pupil for a near target.
• Light Reflex absent: pupils do not constrict when exposed to bright light.
• Cocaine eye drops(mydriatics) induced mydriasis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Leading questions can be asked in?
questions.explanation: A leading question is one that suggests the desired answer within the question itself, typically prompting a "yes" or "no" response. Under Section 146 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), leading questions are generally permitted during cross-examination. This stage allows the opposing party to challenge the witness's credibility and test the accuracy of their testimony. In contrast, leading questions are strictly prohibited during the examination-in-chief (Option D) and re-examination (Option B), except in special circumstances or if the witness is declared hostile. This rule ensures that the witness provides their own narrative without being coached by the party that called them. "Anytime" (Option (C) is incorrect because of these specific legal restrictions during different stages of the trial. Therefore, cross-examination is the standard and legal phase where leading questions are utilized to control the narrative and elicit favorable facts for the defense
questions.learning: A leading question is one that suggests the desired answer within the question itself, typically prompting a "yes" or "no" response. Under Section 146 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), leading questions are generally permitted during cross-examination.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Recommended HPV vaccination schedule for 9 to 14 year olds according to WHO SAGE guidelines is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 or 2 doses

The recommended HPV vaccination schedule for 9 to 14-year-olds according to WHO SAGE guidelines is 1 or 2 doses.

The recommendations for different age groups are as follows:

• 1 or 2 dose schedule for girls aged 9-14 years.
• 1 or 2 dose schedule for young women aged 15-20 years.
• 2 doses with a 6-month interval for women older than 21 years.
• 3 doses (or atleast 2 doses) for immunocompromised individuals.

As per WHO SAGE (Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization), a single-dose HPV vaccination schedule can provide comparable efficacy and durability of protection to a two-dose regimen. This can help in wider coverage of vaccination of all girls in low-middle income countries. Therefore, a 1 or 2-dose schedule is recommended for females aged between 9-20 years.

The available vaccinations for HPV are:

• Gardasil 9 (HPV 9) is a nonavalent vaccine active against HPV 6,11,16,18,31,33,45,52,58.
• Gardasil 4 (HPV 4) is a quadrivalent vaccine against 6,11,16,18. This is now replaced by HPV 9.
• Cervarix (HPV 2) is a bivalent vaccine active against 16, 18.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In Menke’s disease, which of the following enzymes would be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lysyl oxidase

Menke’s disease is due to defective lysyl oxidase.

It is an X‐linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in ATP7A, which encodes for a copper-transporting ATPase‐α polypeptide.
questions.learning: Lysyl oxidase Menke’s disease is due to defective lysyl oxidase. It is an X‐linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in ATP7A, which encodes for a copper-transporting ATPase‐α polypeptide.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man who has been employed in a shipyard for more than 30 years undergoes a routine medical examination. His occupational exposure places him at increased risk for pulmonary disease. Exposure to which of the following substances is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Asbestos

Asbestos exposure is classically associated with shipyard workers, construction workers, insulation workers, and plumbers. Inhaled asbestos fibers cause asbestosis, a diffuse interstitial pulmonary fibrosis, and significantly increase the risk of bronchogenic carcinoma and malignant mesothelioma. The latency period is typically 20–40 years after exposure.

Why not the other options?

• A. Cotton dust: Causes byssinosis, seen in textile workers.
• B. Coal dust: Causes coal workers’ pneumoconiosis (black lung disease), seen in coal miners.
• D. Silica: Causes silicosis, commonly seen in sandblasters, quarry workers, and miners.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Kinesin, Dyenin and Myosin proteins are examples of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Molecular motors

Kinesin, dynein, and myosin are examples of molecular motors.

The molecular motors are the force-generating proteins as they move proteins, organelles, and other cell parts (collectively referred to as “cargo”) to all parts of the cell.

Kinesin:

* The conventional form of kinesin is a double-headed molecule that moves its cargo toward the plus (“+”) ends of microtubules.

* Some kinesins are associated with mitosis and meiosis.

* Other kinesins perform different functions, and may also move cargo to the minus (“–”) end of microtubules.

Dyneins:

* They have two heads, with their neckpieces embedded in a complex of proteins.

* Cytoplasmic dyneins are similar to conventional kinesin, except they move particles and membranes to the minus (–) end of the microtubules.

* Axonemal dyneins are present with the axonemes of the cilia. An axoneme consists of a unique arrangement of nine outer microtubule doublets and two inner microtubules ("9+2" arrangement). The coordinated dynein–microtubule interactions within the axoneme are responsible for the ciliary and sperm movement.

Myosins:

* There are about 18 classes of myosins.

* The heads of some myosin molecules (myosin II) bind to actin and produce motion by bending their neck regions.

* Some myosin molecules (myosin V) may move the cargo, by walking along microfilaments, one head after the other.
questions.learning: Molecular motors Kinesin, dynein, and myosin are examples of molecular motors. The molecular motors are the force-generating proteins as they move proteins, organelles, and other cell parts (collectively referred to as “cargo”) to all parts of the cell.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: During psychotherapy, the therapist had mixed conscious and unconscious feelings towards his patient. This is known as_____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Countertransference

In the given clinical scenario, the therapist has mixed conscious and unconscious feelings towards his patient. This is known as counter-transference.

Counter-transference is the positive and negative feelings/emotions expressed by healthcare professionals towards their patients. It is the process of the physician unconsciously displacing onto the patient patterns of behaviors or emotional reactions as if he/she were a significant figure from earlier in the physician's life. Psychiatrists should be alert to signs of countertransference issues like missed appointments by the psychiatrist, boredom, or sleepiness during a session. Supervision and personal therapy can help the psychiatrist recognize and deal with these issues.

Transference is the positive and negative feelings expressed by the patients towards the healthcare professional. It is the process of the patient unconsciously displacing onto individuals patterns of behavior and emotional reactions that originated with significant figures from the past (generally in childhood). This displacement is onto the psychiatrist in a clinical scenario, who is a parent surrogate. The patient may be angry, hostile, demanding, or obedient to an extreme degree because of former relationships and patterns of behaviors. Failure to recognize this can make the psychiatrist react to the patient's behavior like a personal attack.

These are not defense mechanisms but are commonly encountered during clinical practice or while giving psychotherapy. In an interview, transference and counter-transference are very significant expressions of unconscious processes.

Option C: Dissociation is an immature defense mechanism. In this, involuntary splitting/suppression of mental functions occurs from the rest of the personality in a way that allows the expression of forbidden unconscious impulses without having a sense of responsibility for actions.
questions.learning: Countertransference — In the given clinical scenario, the therapist has mixed conscious and unconscious feelings towards his patient. This is known as counter-transference.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the desirable Total Fertility Rate in India at present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2.1

The desirable Total Fertility Rate is at 2.1 which is considered the replacement rate for a population , resulting in relative stability of total population numbers.

The current fertility rate for India in 2023 is 2.139 births per woman, a 0.93% decline from 2022. The fertility rate for India in 2022 was 2.159 births per woman, a 0.92% decline from 2021.

Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is defined as the average number of children a woman would have if she were to pass through her reproductive years bearing children at the same rates as the women now in each age group.

Pearl PF0245: Fertility Indicators

* Crude birth rate

* It is the simplest measure of fertility although its usage is unsatisfactory.

* It is the number of live births per 1000 estimated mid-year population in a given year.

* Birth rate = No. of live births during the year x 1000/Estimated mid-year population

* India, as per SRS bulletin 2018, had a birth rate of 20.0 per 1000 population

* General Fertility Rate

* It is the number of live births per 1000 women in the reproductive age group (15 - 49 years) in a given year.

* GFR = Number of live births in an area in a year x 1000/Mid-year population of women in the reproductive age in the same area in the same year.

* It is a better indicator of fertility than crude birth rate

* The demerit of this indicator is that not all women in the denominator are exposed to childbirth

* Age-specific fertility rates

* It is the number of live births in a year to 1000 women in any specified age group.

* It is a more precise measure of fertility and is also a sensitive indicator of family planning achievement.

* ASFR = Number of live births in a particular age group x 1000/Mid-year female population of the same age group.

* Total Fertility Rate

* It represents the average number of children a woman would have if she were to pass through her reproductive years bearing children at the same rates as the women in each age group now.

* It is the sum of all age specific fertility rates multiplied by 5.

* This measure gives the approximate magnitude of completed family size.

* Gross Reproductive Rate

* It is the average number of girls that would be born to a woman if she experiences the current fertility pattern throughout her reproductive span, assuming no mortality.

* Net Reproduction Rate

* It is the number of daughters a newborn girl will bear during her lifetime assuming age-specific fertility and mortality rates.

* NRR is a demographic indicator.

* NRR of 1 is equivalent of approximately the 2 child norm.

* If the NRR is less than 1, then the reproductive performance of the population is said to be inadequate.
questions.learning: 2.1 The desirable Total Fertility Rate is at 2.1 which is considered the replacement rate for a population , resulting in relative stability of total population numbers.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: On examination, a person has distended neck veins, absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, and a shift of the trachea. What is the management?
options: Bedside CXR in casualty followed by chest tube insertion
questions.explanation: The clinical signs of respiratory distress, distended neck veins (due to decreased venous return), absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, and contralateral tracheal deviation are diagnostic of a tension pneumothorax. This is a surgical emergency where air under pressure collapses the lung and shifts the mediastinum, potentially leading to obstructive shock. Immediate needle decompression using a wide-bore cannula in the 2nd intercostal space (midclavicular line) or the 4th/5th intercostal space (anterior axillary line) is life-saving and must be performed before obtaining imaging. Waiting for a chest X-ray (Option A) is dangerous as it delays critical treatment. Pericardiocentesis (Option C) is the treatment for cardiac tamponade. Pleurodesis (Option D) is used to prevent recurrence in stable patients but has no role in acute emergency stabilization. Definitive chest tube thoracostomy should follow the initial needle decompression
questions.learning: The clinical signs of respiratory distress, distended neck veins (due to decreased venous return), absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, and contralateral tracheal deviation are diagnostic of a tension pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 18 year old girl with primary amenorrhea, no breast development and Prader 3 genitalia was found to have raised FSH. Her karyotype revealed 45 XO/46 XY and USG revealed Mullerian structures with poorly visualized gonads. What would be the next line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bilateral gonadectomy

In Turner's syndrome, most affected individuals have a 45,X karyotype, while others have mosaic karyotypes (45,X/46,XX; 45,X/46,XY).The presence of Y chromosome material is associated with a 12% risk of a gonadoblastoma. If a Y chromosome is identified, laparoscopic prophylactic gonadectomy is recommended at the time of diagnosis to eliminate the risk of malignancy.

• Gonadoblastomas can be precursors to germ cell malignancies, such as dysgerminomas (most commonly), teratomas, embryonal carcinomas, or endodermal sinus tumors.
• The karyotype should be determined in any individual with delayed puberty and increased basal FSH concentrations.
• Regardless of the karyotype, the individual with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism has some form of ovarian “failure”

Note:Prader staging system is used for the degree of virilisation of the external genitalia

Prader 0: Classical / typical female external genitalia

Prader 1: Female external genitalia with clitoromegaly

Prader 2: Clitoromegaly with partial labial fusion forming a funnel-shaped urogenital sinus

Prader 3: Increased phallic enlargement. Complete labioscrotal fusion forming a urogenital sinus with a single opening

Prader 4: Complete scrotal fusion with urogenital opening at the base or on the shaft of the phallus.

Prader 5: Classical / typical male external genitalia
questions.learning: Bilateral gonadectomy — In Turner's syndrome, most affected individuals have a 45,X karyotype, while others have mosaic karyotypes (45,X/46,XX; 45,X/46,XY).The presence of Y chromosome material is associated with a 12% risk of a gonadoblastoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 44-year-old man is referred to your center for management of severe hyperglycemia. During examination, you note that the patient has enlarged feet, coarse facial features and prognathism. You suspect acromegaly. Which of the following tests can you use as a screening method for this condition?
options: Oral glucose challenge test with GH level
Insulin-like growth factor-1 binding protein-3 (IGFBP-3) level
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Insulin like growth factor-1 levels

The best screening test for acromegaly is the measurement of serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) level.

Other options:

Options A and B: Oral glucose challenge test with growth hormone (GH) levels is used for further confirmation of the diagnosis. Increased insulin-like growth factor-1 binding protein-3 (IGFBP-3) levels can also be seen in patients with acromegaly. But they are not typically used as initial screening methods.

Option D: IGF-1 levels are more reliable than random GH levels because GH secretion is pulsatile. IGF-1 levels reflect long-term exposure to GH and provide a more stable indicator of excessive GH production.

Acromegaly is characterized by excessive GH secretion, usually caused by a somatotrope adenoma in the pituitary gland. It can also be due to ectopic GH secretion or hypothalamic tumors.

The clinical presentation of acromegaly includes frontal bossing, increased hand and foot size, coarse facial features, mandibular prognathism, widened space between lower incisors and other manifestations such as soft tissue swelling, deepening voice, carpal tunnel syndrome, arthropathy, and acanthosis nigricans.

It can also lead to cardiovascular complications (cardiomyopathy, left ventricular hypertrophy, and hypertension), obstructive sleep apnea, diabetes mellitus, an increased risk of colon polyps, and colonic malignancy.

The primary treatment for acromegaly is surgical resection of GH-secreting adenomas. Somatostatin receptor ligands like octreotide and lanreotide, which suppress GH and IGF-1 levels, are used as adjuvant treatment or when surgery is not possible or unsuccessful. Radiation therapy may be considered for patients who cannot tolerate or do not respond to medical therapy. Other treatment options include GH receptor antagonists like pegvisomant and dopamine agonists like cabergoline.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In a 1-year-old male child presenting with fever and neck stiffness, which pathogen is the most common cause of meningitis in this age group?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of fever and neck stiffness in a 1-year-old child is diagnostic of acute bacterial meningitis. In children over one month of age, Streptococcus pneumoniae (the pneumococcus) is the most common and leading cause of bacterial meningitis globally. Other frequent pathogens in this age group include Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). Klebsiella (Option A) is more commonly associated with neonatal sepsis or hospital-acquired infections. Staphylococcus aureus (Option C) is a rare cause of meningitis, usually occurring after trauma or neurosurgery. Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Option D) causes chronic meningitis, which typically has a more subacute onset over weeks rather than an acute presentation. Immediate treatment with intravenous Ceftriaxone and Vancomycin is required after lumbar puncture. Due to its high prevalence as the primary cause of acute community-acquired meningitis in toddlers, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the correct answer

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is true about chromic catgut?
options: It is made from cat gut
It is made from rabbit gut
It is absorbed by enzymatic degradation and macrophage phagocytosis
It is tanned with nickel salts to improve handling and to resist degradation in tissue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is absorbed by enzymatic degradation and macrophage phagocytosis

Chromic catgut is absorbed through macrophage phagocytosis and enzymatic degradation within 90 days.

It is made from collagen derived from healthy sheep or cattle. It is then tanned with chromium salts to improve handling and resist degradation in tissue.

The tensile strength lasts for 21-28 days. It has a moderate tissue reaction as compared to plain catgut, which has a high tissue reactivity.

It is used to ligate superficial vessels, suture subcutaneous tissues, and is used for stomas and other tissues that heal rapidly. It is not used in tissues that heal slowly and require prolonged support.
questions.learning: It is absorbed by enzymatic degradation and macrophage phagocytosis Chromic catgut is absorbed through macrophage phagocytosis and enzymatic degradation within 90 days.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the adjuvant therapy in fungal corneal ulcer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Atropine Sulfate eye ointment

Atropine sulfate (1%) eye ointment or eye drops is used as the nonspecific supportive treatment in both bacterial as well as a fungal corneal ulcer.

Atropine sulphate (1%) is a cycloplegic drug that is used as an adjunct in the treatment of corneal ulcers to

• reduce pain from ciliary spasm
• Prevent posterior synechiae formation that can develop from secondary iridocyclitis
• Increase blood supply to the anterior chamber that gets more antibodies into aqueous humor
• Reduce exudation by decreasing hyperpermeability of the vessels

Another cycloplegic that can be used as an adjunct is homatropine 2%.

Topical steroids such as Dexamethasone(option C) will increase fungal replication and corneal invasion and hence are contraindicated in the treatment of fungal corneal ulcers.

Management of fungal corneal ulcer includes

Definitive treatment:

• Topical antifungal eye drops: used for 6-8 weeks

• Filamentous fungi such as Aspergillus and Fusarium- Drug of choice (DOC) is natamycin (5%). Others include amphotericin B (0.1-0.3%), fluconazole (0.2%) or voriconazole 10%.
• Yeast such as Candida- Drug of choice (DOC) is Amphotericin B. Others include Nystatin 3.5%.

• Intracameral or intracorneal administration of Voriconazole in cases with intraocular extension or anterior chamber involvement.
• Systemic antifungals such as tablet fluconazole are given in severe cases of deeper fungal keratitis.
• Therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty for unresponsive cases.

Adjunct therapy:

1. Cycloplegics : Atropine sulphate 1% or homatropine 2%
2. Systemic analgesics and anti-inflammatory drugs such as paracetamol, ibuprofen to decrease pain and edema.
3. Vitamins A,B-complex,C- to aid healing of the ulcer.
4. Hot fomentation, dark goggles, rest, good diet.
questions.learning: Atropine Sulfate eye ointment Atropine sulfate (1%) eye ointment or eye drops is used as the nonspecific supportive treatment in both bacterial as well as a fungal corneal ulcer.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Identify the condition as shown below in the X-ray radiograph of a neonate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia

This rare anterior defect of the diaphragm is commonly referred to as Morgagni, retrosternal, or parasternal hernia. The above X-ray radiograph shows congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Note the presence of bowel loops in the chest and absence of bowel loops in the abdomen.

* Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a birth defect of the diaphragm.

* The most common type of CDH is a Bochdalek hernia; other types include Morgagni hernia, diaphragm eventration and central tendon defects of the diaphragm.

* Malformation of the diaphragm allows the abdominal organs to push into the chest cavity, hindering proper lung formation.

* CDH is a life-threatening pathology in infants and a major cause of death due to two complications: pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension.

Bochdalek hernia:

* The Bochdalek hernia, also known as a postero-lateral diaphragmatic hernia, is the most common manifestation of CDH, accounting for more than 95% of cases.

* In this instance the diaphragm abnormality is characterized by a hole in the postero-lateral corner of the diaphragm which allows passage of the abdominal viscera into the chest cavity.

Morgagni hernia:

* This rare anterior defect of the diaphragm is commonly referred to as Morgagni, retrosternal, or parasternal hernia.

* It accounts for approximately 2% of all CDH cases, and is characterized by herniation through the foramina of Morgagni which are located immediately adjacent and posterior to the xiphoid process of the sternum.

Diaphragm eventration:

* Diaphragmatic eventration refers to an abnormal contour of the diaphragmatic dome.

* Elevation of the affected portion of the diaphragm is usually seen as a smooth hump, while the remainder of the hemidiaphragm contour is normal.

* This rare type of CDH occurs because in the region of eventration the diaphragm is thinner, allowing the abdominal viscera to protrude upwards.

Treatment:

* The first step in management is orogastric tube placement and securing the airway (intubation).

* The baby will usually be immediately placed on a ventilator.

* Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has been used as part of the treatment strategy in some cases.
questions.learning: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia — This rare anterior defect of the diaphragm is commonly referred to as Morgagni, retrosternal, or parasternal hernia. The above X-ray radiograph shows congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements correctly describes Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA)?
options: It can be used for screening for hearing loss
It can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss
questions.explanation: BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) is an objective, non-invasive electrophysiological test that measures electrical activity generated in the cochlea and auditory brainstem pathways in response to click stimuli. It is widely used as a screening tool for hearing loss, particularly in neonates, infants, and uncooperative patients who cannot participate in conventional audiometry. Why other options are wrong: (B) It is an invasive procedure is incorrect because BERA is completely non-invasive. It involves only placing surface electrodes on the scalp and earlobes — no surgical intervention or penetration of any body structure is required. (C) It can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss is incorrect as a standalone best answer because while BERA can detect sensorineural hearing loss, its primary and most characteristic use is screening — making option A more specific and complete as the correct answer. (D) It is a subjective investigation is incorrect because BERA is a purely objective test — it does not require any behavioral response from the patient. Results are based entirely on recorded electrical waveforms, making it ideal for testing infants and unconscious patients
questions.learning: BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) is an objective, non-invasive electrophysiological test that measures electrical activity generated in the cochlea and auditory brainstem pathways in response to click stimuli.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 60-year-old female patient presented with purplish, itchy, flat-topped lesions on his shins for the past 3 months. The patient also gives a history of chewing tobacco for 20 years. She occasionally drinks alcohol and smokes. On examination, the lesions are seen as in the image below. Which of the following is the first line of management for the condition seen in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Topical corticosteroids

The clinical features and characteristic lesions showing fine white lacework in buccal mucosa called Wickham's striae shown in the image are diagnostic of lichen planus. The first line of management is potent topical corticosteroids like clobetasol propionate ointment 0.05%.

Lichen planus is a type of lichenoid disorder affecting the papillary dermis. It is a T-cell mediated autoimmune disease against the basal keratinocytes. The primary lesions of lichen planus are described by the characteristic "6 Ps": planar (flat-topped), purple, polygonal, pruritic, papules, and plaques. These well-defined areas of purple-coloured, itchy, flat-topped papules may be with interspersed lacy white lines known as Wickham's striae(shown below). It may present with mucous membrane lesions in the absence of skin lesions, commonly involving the tongue and buccal mucosa.

Various factors that can precipitate the disease are:

* Viruses like Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, Human herpesviruses (HHV-6, HHV-8), Varicella zoster

* Betel quid which contains areca nut and tobacco leaf

* Environmental factors like:

* Drugs like antimicrobials, antihypertensives, antimalarials, antidepressants, anticonvulsants

* Radiotherapy

* Anxiety, depression, stress

Histology: Most useful investigation to confirm the diagnosis. Basal epidermal cell degeneration/destruction by dermal CD8+ T lymphocytes is characteristically seen in lichen planus. Other findings are:

* Hyperkeratosis

* The degeneration leads to the formation of spaces in the epidermis known as Max-Joseph spaces.

* Saw-toothed appearance of the Rete ridges

* Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate is present at the dermo-epidermal junction.

Other options:

Options A and C: Ciclosporin, and methotrexate are used in third-line management and not first-line management of the disease.

Option D: Oral corticosteroids are used in the second-line management of the disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A patient following a road traffic accident presented with subcutaneous emphysema. On auscultation, there was no air entry on the right side. Vitals were unstable. What will be your immediate management?

e-FAST- Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma
options: Insertion of wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space (ICS)
Wide bore needle decompression and IV fluids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Insertion of wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space (ICS)

The given clinical scenario of a patient with h/o road traffic accident (RTA) with no air entry on the right side and hemodynamic instability suggests a diagnosis of tension pneumothorax. This is managed by immediate decompression by insertion of a needle in the appropriate place.

Pneumothorax refers to the presence of excess air in the pleural space. Entrapment of air occurs by:

1. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax - due to the spontaneous rupture of apical pleural blebs or cystic spaces immediately below the visceral pleura.
2. Secondary pneumothorax - due to the rupture of dilated cystic spaces in lung diseases like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
3. Tension pneumothorax -  a one-way valve mechanism that directs airflow into the pleural space leading to a higher than atmospheric pressure environment, and prevents expansion of the lung.

Tension pneumothorax is characterized by chest pain, tachypnoea, tachycardia, and hypotension. On examination, the trachea is deviated away from the side of the injury, and breath sounds are absent on the affected lung. A patient can develop subcutaneous emphysema as a complication, secondary to the pneumothorax.

Tension pneumothorax is a surgical emergency and the excessive pressure has to be immediately relieved. Tension pneumothorax is managed by immediate needle decompression in the 5th intercostal space (ICS), followed by definitive management with a chest tube inserted in the same space.

Other options:

Option B: While IV fluids are a part of the resuscitation protocol, hypotension in a tension pneumothorax is due to an obstructive type of shock, increasing circulating volume will have minimal effect on improving blood pressure. The management of the primary cause, tension pneumothorax, takes higher precedence as the next immediate step.

Option C: Intubation is performed when the patient is unresponsive post chest tube insertion.

Option D: Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma (eFAST) is not required before emergency decompression as tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, but it can be performed following chest tube insertion.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with fever, weakness, hypotension, and tachycardia. Peripheral blood smear examination confirms infection with Plasmodium falciparum. In this clinical scenario, which drug is considered the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with signs of "Severe (or Complicated) Malaria," as evidenced by systemic instability (hypotension/shock, tachycardia) and a smear positive for Plasmodium falciparum. Plasmodium falciparum (Option B) is the species most frequently associated with multi-organ failure and death. Vivax (Option A) and Ovale (Option C) can cause severe malaria but are more classically known for relapses due to liver hypnozoites. Malariae (Option D) is usually a chronic, milder infection. In falciparum infections, "sequestration" of infected erythrocytes in capillaries leads to cerebral malaria, pulmonary edema, and acute renal failure. According to WHO guidelines, the immediate treatment for severe malaria is intravenous Artesunate. Falciparum malaria is a true medical emergency, especially when systemic symptoms like hypotension are present, requiring rapid parasite clearance and intensive supportive care to prevent mortality

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: During which phase of the cardiac cycle does the first heart sound occur?
questions.explanation: The first heart sound (S1), the "lub" of the "lub-dub," is produced primarily by the closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves. This occurs at the very beginning of ventricular systole, specifically during the phase of isovolumetric contraction. In this phase, the ventricles begin to contract, raising the internal pressure. As soon as the ventricular pressure exceeds the atrial pressure, the AV valves snap shut, producing S1. This sound signals the start of systole. Aortic ejection (Option B) follows this phase once the semilunar valves open. Isovolumetric relaxation (Option D) is when the second heart sound (S2) occurs due to the closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves. Rapid atrial filling (Option A) occurs during diastole. Understanding the correlation between heart sounds and the phases of the cardiac cycle is fundamental for cardiac auscultation and diagnosing valvular disorders. Therefore, S1 is definitively associated with the initiation of isovolumetric contraction

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the histological image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Transitional epithelium

The above image shows transitional epithelium.

The deepest layer has columnar cells, the middle layers are made up of polyhedral cells and the surface layer has cells that are large and shaped like an umbrella.

Transitional epithelium is found in the renal pelvis and calyces, the ureter, the urinary bladder, and part of the urethra. Because of this distribution, it is also called urothelium. In the urinary bladder, it is usually observed that transitional epithelium can be stretched considerably without being damaged. When stretched it appears to be thinner and the cells become flattened or rounded.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT considered a component of the urban health care delivery system?
questions.explanation: The Subcenter is the peripheral-most unit of the rural health care delivery system in India, serving a population of 3,000 to 5,000. It is not a standard structural component of the Urban health care delivery system. Under the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM), the primary tier in cities is the Urban Primary Health Centre (U-PHC) (Option A), which serves approximately 50,000 people. Secondary care is provided by Urban Community Health Centres (U-CHC) (Option B) or small hospitals. District Hospitals (Option C) serve as the tertiary referral centers for both urban and rural populations within the district. Urban health systems also rely on community-level workers like ASHAs and Mahila Arogya Samitis, but they lack the physical "Subcenter" building found in the rural three-tier model. Recognizing these structural differences is essential for public health administration and ensuring that healthcare services are tailored to the specific demographic needs of urban dwellers

questions.text: Bleeding as shown in the image is due to which of the following vessels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bridging veins

The image showing a bleed over the arachnoid layer but under the dura is suggestive of a subdural hemorrhage. Most commonly, it results from the shearing of cortical bridging veins.

Subdural hemorrhage (SDH) is a collection of blood between the dura and the arachnoid layers of the meninges. The causes of SDH include

• trauma
• anticoagulants, antiplatelets
• alcohol abuse
• battered baby syndrome.

Non-contrast CT is the investigation of choice.

Other options:

Middle meningeal artery rupture would result in an extradural hemorrhage.

Lenticulostriate artery would lead to an intraparenchymal hemorrhage.

Vertebral artery dissection leads to subarachnoid hemorrhage or sometimes intraparenchymal hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: When choosing the power of an intraocular lens (IOL) for a child younger than one year, which factors should be taken into account?
questions.explanation: Pediatric cataract surgery requires careful IOL power calculation due to the rapid growth of the eye. A child's eye undergoes significant elongation of the axial length and flattening of the cornea during the first few years of life. This physiological growth results in a predictable myopic shift over time. If a child is corrected to emmetropia (zero power) at infancy, they will become severely myopic (nearsighted) as they grow. Therefore, when selecting an IOL for a child under 1 year old, surgeons typically "under-correct" the eye, leaving the infant with a significant amount of hypermetropia initially to account for the future myopic shift. Option B is the result of the desired under-correction, but Option A is the underlying biological phenomenon that necessitates it. Options C and D relate to the capsule rather than the refractive shift. Thus, myopic shift is the primary factor driving IOL power choice

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A person holds a fixed false belief that he owns a large amount of property and that someone he knows is attempting to take it away from him. Which type of delusion best describes this belief?
questions.explanation: This patient is experiencing two distinct delusions. The belief that he owns extensive property is a delusion of grandeur, which is a false and exaggerated belief in one’s own importance or wealth. The belief that someone is trying to take it away from him is a delusion of persecution, characterized by the false belief that one is being targeted, harassed, or conspired against. Delusions of reference (Option B) involve believing that neutral events (like news reports) are directed personally at oneself. Nihilistic delusions (Options C and D) involve the false belief that the self or the world does not exist. Since the patient's beliefs are focused on self-importance and being harmed by others, "grandeur and persecution" is the correct clinical description

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is an inhibitor of RNA synthesis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rifampicin

Rifampicin is an inhibitor of RNA synthesis. It binds to the beta subunit of DNA dependent RNA-polymerase (rpoB) to form a stable drug-enzyme complex. The binding suppresses the chain formation in RNA synthesis.

Option A: 5-Fluorouracil inhibits thymidylate synthesis.

Option C: Nitrofurantoin produces highly reactive intermediates that cause DNA damage

Option D: Novobiocin is a potent inhibitor of bacterial DNA gyrase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In cases of paracetamol poisoning, N-acetylcysteine is used as an antidote. What is its mechanism of action in preventing toxicity?
questions.explanation: Paracetamol is metabolized into a toxic intermediate called NAPQI, which is normally detoxified by glutathione. In an overdose, glutathione stores are depleted, allowing NAPQI to accumulate and cause hepatic necrosis. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) prevents this by acting as a glutathione precursor, effectively replenishing glutathione levels to facilitate detoxification. NAC does not inhibit the formation of the toxin (Option A), nor does it directly remove paracetamol from the system (Option B). It also does not neutralize liver enzymes (Option D). NAC therapy is most effective when initiated within 8 hours of ingestion but may still provide benefit up to 36 hours post-overdose. Additionally, NAC directly binds to NAPQI and enhances the non-toxic sulfation metabolic pathway. This life-saving intervention is the cornerstone of managing paracetamol-induced acute liver failure

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the primary use of the given imaging modality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Staging of esophageal cancer

The provided imaging modality is an endoscopic ultrasound of the oesophagus, primarily utilized for staging oesophagal carcinoma.

Esophageal carcinoma is more commonly seen in men. Tobacco use and alcohol are strong risk factors. Adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus are the two most common types. The squamous cell variant usually affects the upper two-thirds and the adenocarcinoma variant usually affects the lower third. The incidence of adenocarcinoma is increasing.

Clinical features include:

* Dysphagia (most common)

* Regurgitation

* Vomiting

* Odynophagia

* Weight loss

In the advanced stage, there can be hoarseness of voice due to recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, horner’s syndrome, chronic spinal pain, and diaphragmatic paralysis.

Flexible endoscopy with biopsy is preferred for confirmation of diagnosis. Other investigations include barium swallow, which shows a rat-tail appearance due to irregular narrowing or ulceration. Contrast-enhanced CT and PET can be used to assess distant metastasis. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) is the investigation of choice to assess tumour invasion and lymph node metastasis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person is found dead in a swimming pool. Autopsy reveals water in the stomach and lungs, along with fine mucoid froth at the nose and mouth. What is the most likely mode of death?
questions.explanation: Wet drowning is the mode of death in approximately 90% of drowning cases and occurs when water is actively inhaled into the respiratory tract. This aspiration leads to the washout of pulmonary surfactant, alveolar collapse, and terminal asphyxia. The pathognomonic autopsy findings for wet drowning include copious, persistent mucoid froth at the nostrils and mouth, as well as overdistended, water-logged lungs and water in the stomach from swallowing. Dry drowning (Option A) occurs due to severe reflex laryngospasm that prevents water from entering the lungs; in these cases, the lungs remain dry. Near drowning (Option C) refers to a scenario where the individual survives for at least 24 hours after the event. Cardiac arrest (Option D) is a non-specific terminal event. Thus, the presence of lung water and froth confirms wet drowning

Copper T-380A (Paragard):

It is named so for the 380 mm2 of copper surface area. A higher surface area of copper results in higher contraceptive efficacy.

It has a plastic T-shaped core with copper placed around the vertical stem and horizontal arms. A silver core within the copper sheath is included to prevent fragmentation of the copper, extending the lifespan of the Copper T-380A.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During the assessment of a 3-year-old child with short stature, the measured height is 90 cm and the lower segment length is 45 cm. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In this case, the child’s total height is 90 cm with a lower segment (LS) of 45 cm, making the upper segment (US) also 45 cm. This gives a US:LS ratio of 1:1. Since the normal US:LS ratio for a 3-year-old is 1.3:1, the finding indicates a shortened upper segment (short-trunk dwarfism). Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia is a condition that specifically involves vertebrae and proximal epiphyses, resulting in this 1:1 ratio. Achondroplasia (Option A) and congenital hypothyroidism (Option B) both cause disproportionate short stature where the upper segment is longer than the lower segment (US > LS). Rickets (Option C) typically presents with skeletal deformities like bowing and can cause a US > LS ratio. Therefore, the specific 1:1 ratio accurately points toward spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia as the most likely underlying genetic condition for this child’s short stature

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A mother is concerned that her child is not eating well. Her 15-month-old son is found to have a length that is 2 standard deviations below the median for his age. Based on this finding, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In pediatric anthropometry, stunting is defined as a deficit in height (or length)-for-age. According to WHO growth standards, a child whose length is between -2 and -3 standard deviations (SD) below the median is classified as having moderate stunting (Option D). Stunting is typically a marker of chronic, long-term undernutrition or recurrent infections. Acute malnutrition (Option A) and wasting (Option B) are defined by a low weight-for-height ratio, representing recent or sudden weight loss. Being underweight (Option C) refers to a low weight-for-age, which can be a composite of both stunting and wasting. Because the mother's concern specifically relates to a deficit in "length" rather than "weight," stunting is the correct descriptive term for this child's nutritional deficit. Managing this involves ensuring adequate nutrient-dense complementary feeding

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 53-year-old female was diagnosed with breast cancer. She was managed appropriately and was advised to start chemotherapy. Further investigations were done that revealed she had heart failure as well. Which of the following drugs would you avoid in this patent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epirubicin

In this patient with heart failure, epirubicin is avoided as it is cardiotoxic.

Epirubicin, an anthracycline antibiotic is an anti-neoplastic drug that is produced from the fungus Streptomyces peucetius.

It works by interacting with DNA directly and affecting transcription and replication. It has the potential to create free radicals which cause irreversible cardiotoxicity and cardiomyopathy which is dose-dependent.

The dose of the drug commonly used is 100–120 mg/m2 every 3–4 weeks. A total dose of greater than 900 mg/m2 increases the risk of cardiotoxicity.

Adverse effects:

* Cardiomyopathy is the most common adverse effect and it can be either acute, in the form of myocardial damage("pericarditis-myocarditis syndrome"), or a chronic form of dose-dependent cardiomyopathy leading to heart failure.

* Alopecia, anemia, amenorrhea, leukopenia, nausea, vomiting.

* Mucositis, diarrhea, thrombocytopenia.

* Less common: acute lymphoid leukemia,acute myelogenous leukemia,atrioventricular block,esophagitis,hyperpigmentation,myelodysplastic syndrome

Note :

The toxicity profile of epirubicin is similar to doxorubicin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A diagnosis of pheochromocytoma is suspected. Which imaging modality is considered the most appropriate for localizing this tumor?
options: Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT) of the Chest and Abdomen
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor arising from chromaffin cells. The most specific imaging modality for localization is the MIBG scan, because metaiodobenzylguanidine is structurally similar to norepinephrine and is selectively taken up by adrenergic tissue. This allows precise detection of both adrenal and extra-adrenal tumors (paragangliomas), as well as metastases. Why other options are wrong: (A) Sestamibi Scan: Primarily used for parathyroid adenomas and cardiac imaging, not for pheochromocytoma. (C) Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT): Although commonly used as an initial imaging modality and has good sensitivity, it is not as specific as MIBG for confirming catecholamine-secreting tumors. (D Ultrasound (USG): Limited utility due to poor sensitivity and difficulty visualizing adrenal lesions, especially small or extra-adrenal tumors. Thus, MIBG scan is the most appropriate and specific modality for localizing pheochromocytoma

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct with regard to clubbing? 1. It usually affects the fingers symmetrically. 2. It does not involve the toes. 3. It may be associated with malignant lung conditions. 4. It may recede following lung transplantation in cystic fibrosis. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 and 4

Clubbing is a bulbous enlargement of the distal phalanges caused by proliferation of connective tissue beneath the nail bed. It is commonly associated with chronic pulmonary, cardiac, gastrointestinal, and hepatobiliary diseases.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. It usually affects the fingers symmetrically: Correct. Clubbing usually affects the fingers symmetrically and often involves both hands.
• Statement 2. It does not involve the toes: Incorrect. Clubbing commonly involves both the fingers and toes, not just the fingers.
• Statement 3. It may be associated with malignant lung conditions: Correct. Clubbing is associated with malignant lung diseases, especially bronchogenic carcinoma, as well as chronic suppurative lung diseases.
• Statement 4. It may recede following lung transplantation in cystic fibrosis: Correct. Clubbing may regress after successful treatment of the underlying disease, including lung transplantation in patients with cystic fibrosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What are the rays used in linear accelerator (LINAC) therapy for curing cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. X-ray

X-rays are the most common form of radiation used in radiotherapy. They are produced from a LINAC (linear accelerator).

It is used in radiation therapy to deliver high-energy X-rays or electrons to target specific areas of the body, typically to treat cancerous tissues. It uses microwave technology to accelerate charged particles (such as electrons) at a high speed and then directs them into a target (usually a heavy metal) to produce X-rays. These X-rays are then carefully directed at the patient's body to deliver therapeutic radiation doses to the tumor while minimising damage to surrounding healthy tissues. For precise therapy, this LINAC is referred to as a CyberKnife when it is mounted on an electronic robotic arm. It is used in inoperable cranial lesions as stereotactic radiotherapy.

Other options:

Option A: Proton beams offer a therapeutic advantage of having a steep dose falloff at the end of their path. Advantages are mostly physical, not biological; however, new data suggest different genes may be induced after proton versus X-ray treatment

Option B: Neutron beams are used in visualizing soft tissue and can even provide better contrast than X-rays in some cases, but are rarely used clinically due to complex setup and limited availability.

Option D: Cobalt 60 undergoes beta-decay and emits 1.25 MeV (average) gamma rays, which penetrate deeper tissues while sparing skin, used in the Gamma Knife. The gamma knife is mainly used to treat inoperable intracranial lesions.
questions.learning: X-ray X-rays are the most common form of radiation used in radiotherapy. They are produced from a LINAC (linear accelerator).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A diabetic patient presents to the outpatient department with fatigue and polyuria. On examination, vital signs are stable, and an HbA1c test is performed. What is the HbA1c cut-off percentage used to define well-controlled diabetes?
questions.explanation: As established in Question 35, Glycosylated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) is the standard for monitoring long-term glycemic control. For the majority of non-pregnant adults with diabetes, the American Diabetes Association (ADA) and other global guidelines recommend an HbA1c cut-off of less than 7.0% to define controlled diabetes. Maintaining this level significantly reduces the risk of long-term microvascular complications like retinopathy and nephropathy. A cut-off of 6.5% (Option B) is used as a diagnostic threshold to define the presence of diabetes, rather than the target for control. 6.0% (Option A) is near the normal range and may be too strict for many patients, increasing the risk of hypoglycemia. 7.5% (Option D) is considered suboptimal control. These targets must be individualized; for example, elderly patients or those with short life expectancy may have a more relaxed target (e.g.,). However, "7.0%" is the standard "general" goal for effective diabetes management

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient develops profuse uterine bleeding following a lower segment cesarean section (LSCS). Despite administration of oxytocin, the bleeding persists. What should be the next immediate step in management?
questions.explanation: In cases of persistent atonic postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) where first-line uterotonics like oxytocin fail, the next recommended step is mechanical intervention. Uterine balloon tamponade (e.g., using a Bakri balloon) is the preferred first-line mechanical measure. It is a minimally invasive, fertility-preserving procedure that applies hydrostatic pressure to the uterine walls to control bleeding and allow for patient stabilization. Uterine artery embolization (Option B) is an alternative for stable patients but requires interventional radiology. Internal iliac artery ligation (Option C) is a more complex surgical procedure reserved for refractory cases. Hysterectomy (Option D) is the definitive last resort for life-threatening hemorrhage after conservative measures have failed. Thus, balloon tamponade is the appropriate immediate next step
questions.learning: In cases of persistent atonic postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) where first-line uterotonics like oxytocin fail, the next recommended step is mechanical intervention.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with pruritic hypopigmented macules and confluent patches over the chest. Skin scraping and KOH preparation show an abundance of yeast-like cells and short branched filaments like a 'Spaghetti and meatball appearance'. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malassezia

The clinical scenario is suggestive of  Pityriasis Versicolor and the causative agent is the lipophilic, yeast-like fungus Malassezia furfur (Pityrosporum orbiculare).

Pityriasis Versicolor is a chronic, usually asymptomatic, involvement of the stratum corneum, characterized by discrete or confluent macular areas of discoloration or de-pigmentation of the skin.

The areas involved are mainly the chest, abdomen, upper limbs, and back.

Skin scraping and KOH preparation show an abundance of yeast-like cells and short branched filaments (Spaghetti and meatball appearance).

Treatment includes topical azoles or terbinafine for 2 weeks.

The image below shows the hypopigmented lesions of P. versicolour over the chest.

Electron microscopic image of Malassezia furfur

Other options:

* Tinea corporis/ ringworm infection is caused by the dermatophyte Trichophyton rubrum. It results from invasion and proliferation of the causal fungi in the stratum corneum with lesions on the trunk and limbs.

* Candida, the causative agent for candidiasis, appear as budding gram-positive cells on wet films and smears. Mycelial forms suggest colonization. Culture colonies are creamy-white and have a yeasty odor. Candida albicans, the most commonly implicated pathogenic species, form chlamydospores on corn meal agar.
questions.learning: Malassezia — The clinical scenario is suggestive of Pityriasis Versicolor and the causative agent is the lipophilic, yeast-like fungus Malassezia furfur (Pityrosporum orbiculare).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department two hours after a road traffic accident with altered consciousness and a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 10. A CT scan of the brain is shown below. Based on the clinical presentation and imaging findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The CT scan demonstrates a "biconvex" (lenticular), sharply demarcated, hyperdense mass in the peripheral space, which is the pathognomonic radiological appearance of an Extradural Hematoma (EDH). EDH occurs between the skull and the dura mater and is most commonly caused by an arterial bleed from the middle meningeal artery following a temporal bone fracture. A Subdural Hematoma (SDH, Option A) appears as a "crescent-shaped" mass that crosses suture lines. Intracerebral hemorrhage (Option B) and hemorrhagic contusions (Option D) occur within the brain parenchyma itself rather than the extra-axial spaces. Clinically, EDH patients may exhibit a "lucid interval" followed by rapid neurological deterioration as the hematoma expands and causes midline shift or herniation. This is a neurosurgical emergency requiring prompt evacuation of the clot. The hyperdense (white) appearance indicates acute bleeding, consistent with the history of an accident occurring only two hours prior
questions.learning: The CT scan demonstrates a "biconvex" (lenticular), sharply demarcated, hyperdense mass in the peripheral space, which is the pathognomonic radiological appearance of an Extradural Hematoma (EDH).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A schoolboy presented with the following finding. He has a history of trauma to his upper arm in the past. Which nerve is most likely to be injured in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radial nerve

The image shows wrist drop and the radial nerve is commonly damaged in this condition.

It occurs because the radial nerve supplies the dorsiflexors of the wrist and digits and an injury to it lends them paralyzed. Other findings include numbness on the dorsoradial aspect of the hand , the dorsal aspect of the radial 3 1/2 digits and  over the anatomical stuff box. When there is compression in the axilla, radial nerve palsy is called Saturday night palsy. There is paralysis of the triceps, and weakness of the wrist and hand.

Shaft of humerus fracture is one of the most common causes of radial nerve injury because of how its closely related to the nerve. Given below is the course of radial nerve

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is used to prevent cardiotoxicity induced by daunorubicin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dexrazoxane

Anthracycline (daunorubicin)

Oxidative damage

Daunorubicin causes dose-dependent anthracycline cardiotoxicity via free radical–mediated myocardial injury. Dexrazoxane is an iron-chelating agent that reduces reactive oxygen species formation in cardiac tissue. It is used prophylactically to protect against anthracycline-induced cardiomyopathy. Cardiac protection is its key clinical role.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: From the given image, which option corresponds to type III choledochal cyst?
questions.explanation: The Todani classification is used to categorize bile duct cysts. According to the provided diagram , the Type III choledochal cyst, also known as a choledochocele, is represented by the image labeled D. A Type III cyst is characterized by a focal dilation specifically of the intraduodenal segment of the common bile duct. Type I (Option B/A) involves fusiform dilation of the extrahepatic duct. Type II (Option A/B) is a saccular diverticulum. Type IV (Option D/C) involves multiple cysts in both the intrahepatic and extrahepatic systems. Because the image marked "D" specifically illustrates the cystic dilation within the wall of the duodenum at the Ampulla of Vater, it corresponds exactly to the definition of a Type III cyst. Accurate classification is essential because the surgical management (ranging from endoscopic sphincterotomy to duct excision) varies significantly depending on the cyst's anatomical type
questions.learning: The Todani classification is used to categorize bile duct cysts. According to the provided diagram , the Type III choledochal cyst, also known as a choledochocele, is represented by the image labeled D.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The following is due to the deficiency of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin A

The given image depicts Bitot's spots characteristically seen in deficiency of vitamin A. Bitot's spots are seen as white patches of keratinized epithelium on the sclera. It is more commonly bilateral and on the temporal side.

Vitamin A deficiency arises mostly due to the inadequate amounts of vitamin A in diet. It can present as night blindness, conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, and keratomalacia. In later stages, it can lead to xerophthalmia. It also increases the risk of developing measles, diarrhea, and dysentery. Skin manifestations include xerosis, scaling, and dermomalacia. Phrynoderma may also be seen as keratotic follicular papules affecting the thighs and upper arms. It is shown in the image below.

In patients above the age of 1 year, vitamin A deficiency is treated with 200,000 IU of vitamin A orally or 100,000 IU by intramuscular route. It should be repeated the next day and two weeks later.

Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin that plays an essential role in vision, reproduction, and maintenance of epithelial integrity. The various forms of vitamin A include retinol (storage form), retinal, retinoic acid, and beta-carotene. It is stored in the liver perisinusoidal stellate (Ito) cells as retinyl ester (retinyl palmitate).

Other options:

Option A - Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin that aids in iron absorption and collagen maturation. It cannot be synthesized in humans because of the absence of L-gulonolactone oxidase. Vitamin C deficiency results in scurvy.

Option C - Vitamin B deficiency has clinical manifestations pertaining to each type.

Option D - Vitamin E deficiency can present as posterior column and spinocerebellar symptoms. Peripheral neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia, and pigmented retinopathy are other features seen.
questions.learning: Vitamin — A The given image depicts Bitot's spots characteristically seen in deficiency of vitamin A. Bitot's spots are seen as white patches of keratinized epithelium on the sclera.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with chronic kidney disease presents with severe anemia, and laboratory evaluation shows a normocytic, normochromic anemia. What is the most appropriate treatment to manage this condition?
questions.explanation: Anemia in Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is primarily caused by a deficiency in erythropoietin, as the damaged kidneys can no longer produce sufficient amounts of this hormone to stimulate red blood cell production. The resulting anemia is typically normocytic and normochromic. The standard treatment is the administration of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs), such as darbepoetin alfa or epoetin alfa. Folic acid (Option A) and Vitamin B12 (Option B) are used for megaloblastic (macrocytic) anemias and would not correct the underlying hormonal deficit in CKD. Iron chelation therapy (Option D) is used for iron overload, not for treating anemia. While ensuring adequate iron stores is an important supportive step, the core therapeutic intervention for correcting the hormonal lack and associated normocytic anemia in CKD patients is the use of ESAs like darbepoetin alfa
questions.learning: Anemia in Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is primarily caused by a deficiency in erythropoietin, as the damaged kidneys can no longer produce sufficient amounts of this hormone to stimulate red blood cell production.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following condition leads to the development of wing beating tremor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wilson's disease

Wing beating tremor is seen in Wilson's disease.

In Huntington's chorea, rapid jerky movements are seen and Sydenham's chorea is seen in Rheumatic disease. In Parkinsonism, the type of tremor is called resting tremor because they disappear on movement.

Wilsons disease:

The autosomal-recessive disease is caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, which encodes a membrane-bound, copper-transporting ATPase.

Clinical symptoms:

* Hepatitis and cirrhosis

* Behavioral disturbances

* Wing beating tremor( shown in the image below)

* Ophthalmic characteristics:

* Deposition of copper in the posterior capsule of the lens resulting in sunflower cataract

* KF ring

Diagnosis:

* Presence of KF rings

* Decreased serum ceruloplasmin (copper-containing enzyme/ferroxidase) levels

* Measured hepatic copper levels in liver biopsy

* Increased 24-hour urine copper excretion

The gold standard for diagnosis: Liver biopsy with quantitative copper assays

Treatment: Trientine and Zinc is the first choice of a drug regimen to be used for treating mild hepatic decompensation in Wilson’s disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child suffering from phenylketonuria was started on necessary dietary modifications but the neurological symptoms persisted. Phenylalanine hydroxylase levels in the serum are normal. Which of the following enzymes is likely to be deficient in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tetrahydrobiopterin synthase

This child with phenylketonuria with neurological symptoms not improving despite dietary modifications and normal serum phenylalanine hydroxylase level is suggestive of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthase deficiency.

A diet low in phenylalanine (eg: tapioca) is the mainstay of treatment for classic phenylketonuria but may not be sufficient in BH4 deficiency where supplementation with BH4 and deficient neurotransmitter precursors (L-dopa) is required to overcome the block.

Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inborn error of metabolism seen due to a defect in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (classic phenylketonuria) and less commonly, due to a defect in BH4 synthase (non-classical). These defects result in the impaired conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine. The patient develops clinical features due to elevated levels of phenylalanine metabolites and decreased levels of tyrosine. The excess phenylalanine in the blood is metabolized to phenylpyruvate (positive ferric chloride) and phenylacetate (mousy odour) which are excreted in the urine. Infants appear normal at birth and gradually develop symptoms of hyperreflexia, seizures, hypopigmentation, low IQ, hyperactivity, and tremors.

Tandem mass spectroscopy is the investigation of choice. Guthrie test is a screening test that shows with absence of growth of Bacillus subtilis. The ferric chloride test is positive with the development of a transient blue-green colour.

Other options -

Option A: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme in the synthesis of epinephrine, converts tyrosine to DOPA, its deficiency does not cause phenylketonuria

Option B:  Homogentisic acid oxidase converts homogentisic acid to maleylacetoacetic acid in the tyrosine degradation pathway and its deficiency causes alkaptonuria with a dark colour of urine on standing, bluish-black pigmentation in connective tissue (ochronosis) and arthritis.

Option D: Dopa decarboxylase is another enzyme involved in the synthesis of epinephrine. It converts DOPA to dopamine in the presence of vitamin B6. While enzymes involved in epinephrine synthesis cause neurological dysfunction, they do not cause phenylketonuria as such.
questions.learning: Tetrahydrobiopterin synthase — This child with phenylketonuria with neurological symptoms not improving despite dietary modifications and normal serum phenylalanine hydroxylase level is suggestive of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthase deficiency.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What type of visual field defect is most likely seen when a tumor of the anterior pituitary compresses the optic chiasma?
questions.explanation: The optic chiasma is the site where the nasal fibers of both optic nerves cross to the opposite side. These nasal fibers carry visual information from the temporal (outer) halves of the visual field. An anterior pituitary tumor (such as a macroadenoma) typically compresses the central part of the chiasma from below. This selective compression of the decussating nasal fibers results in a loss of the outer half of the visual field in both eyes, a condition known as bitemporal hemianopia. Homonymous hemianopia (Option A) occurs with lesions posterior to the chiasma in the optic tract. Quadrantic hemianopias (Options B and D) result from lesions in the optic radiations in the temporal or parietal lobes. Bitemporal hemianopia is a classic neurological localizing sign that often provides the first clinical evidence of a pituitary lesion. Thus, it is the most likely defect in this anatomical scenario
questions.learning: The optic chiasma is the site where the nasal fibers of both optic nerves cross to the opposite side. These nasal fibers carry visual information from the temporal (outer) halves of the visual field.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following laryngeal cartilages is least likely to be calcified?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Epiglottis

Epiglottis is unlikely to be calcified as it is made up of elastic cartilage.

Only hyaline cartilages can undergo ossification (calcifications on x-ray). It between the ages of 25-65y. These calcifications may be confused with foreign bodies of esophagus or larynx on x-rays.

The hyaline laryngeal cartilages are:

* Thyroid

* Cricoid

* Most of arytenoid.

The elastic laryngeal cartilages are:

* Epiglottis

* Corniculate

* Cuneiform

* Tip of arytenoid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the type of joint present at the marked region.
questions.explanation: The arrow in the X-ray identifies the first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint, which is the articulation between the trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal. This joint is functionally classified as a saddle (sellar) joint. Saddle joints feature reciprocal concave-convex surfaces that allow for a wide range of motion, including flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and uniquely, opposition. Ellipsoid joints (Option A), such as the wrist (radiocarpal) joint, allow for biaxial movement but lack the axial rotation seen in saddle joints. Condylar joints (Option B), like the knee, allow primarily for flexion and extension with limited rotation. Plane joints (Option C), found between the other carpal bones, permit only limited gliding movements. The saddle configuration of the first CMC joint is what gives the human thumb its exceptional mobility and ability to grasp objects, making it a common site for osteoarthritis due to the high mechanical loads it bears during daily activities
questions.learning: The arrow in the X-ray identifies the first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint, which is the articulation between the trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman from a tropical region presents with a brown, macular lesion on the palm of her hand. There is no itching or scaling. Microscopic examination of skin scrapings reveals brownish, branched, septate hyphae along with budding cells. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Exophiala werneckii

Tinea nigra is a superficial fungal infection characterized by brown-to-black macular patches, usually on the palms or soles, without itching or scaling.

Causative organism: Exophiala (Hortaea) werneckii, a dematiaceous (pigmented) fungus.

• Brown, septate, branched hyphae
• Budding yeast-like cells
• Pigmentation due to melanin in the fungal cell wall
• Infection is superficial and benign.
• Treated effectively with topical antifungals or keratolytic agents.

Why not other options:

A. Malassezia furfur: Causes pityriasis versicolor → hypopigmented/hyperpigmented scaly patches on trunk, not palm macules.

C. Trichophyton rubrum: Dermatophyte causing tinea corporis/pedis, with itching and scaling, not pigmented macules.

D. Candida albicans: Causes moist intertrigo or oral thrush with erythema and satellite lesions, not brown palm lesions.
questions.learning: Exophiala werneckii Tinea nigra is a superficial fungal infection characterized by brown-to-black macular patches, usually on the palms or soles, without itching or scaling.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Peutz–Jeghers syndrome are true 1. Heterogeneous loss of function of the STK11 gene 2. Presents as multiple hamartomatous polyps in the GIT 3. Histology shows arborising smooth muscle bundles 4. It is an autosomal recessive condition 5. Extra-intestinal manifestations of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome include hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, and 3

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is due to loss-of-function mutation of the STK11 tumor suppressor gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. It presents with multiple hamartomatous GI polyps showing classic arborizing smooth muscle bundles on histology. Retinal pigment hypertrophy is seen in familial adenomatous polyposis, not Peutz–Jeghers.
