questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with blunt trauma to the abdomen. On evaluation, liver injury was noted for which primary repair was done. Coagulation function was monitored intraoperatively, using the method shown below. What is the method used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thromboelastography

In the case of liver injury, intraoperative monitoring of coagulation function is done by thromboelastography which is shown in the given image.

Thromboelastography (TEG) is a non-invasive test that quantifies the ability of whole blood to form a clot. It is useful in intraoperative coagulation status assessment. The dynamic changes in the viscoelastic properties of a blood sample during the clotting can be detected and quantified by thromboelastography. Underlying coagulation deficiencies show different shapes in the TEG. They are shown in the image as follows

Advantages of thromboelastography:

•

Blood coagulability, including coagulation cascade, platelet function, and fibrinolysis can be assessed.

•

It is a simple bedside test

•

Can diagnose coagulopathic bleeding

•

Can be used as a guide in transfusion therapy and decrease the use of blood products

•

Can detect dynamic changes in blood coagulation during resuscitation

•

Predict the clinical efficacy of therapeutic agents affecting blood coagulability

Other options:

Option B: Plethysmography is a semiquantitative method to measure segmental blood flow and velocity in the carotid and peripheral vascular systems. It is safe, inexpensive and easy to use. It is useful in the diagnosis of vascular disease.

Option C: Sonography or ultrasound is a cheap and easily available imaging method. It is used as a first-line imaging method to assess liver, biliary, renal tract, obstetric, and gynecological disease. It is also useful in guiding needle placement during interventional procedures. Ligaments, tendon and muscle injuries can also be studied by an ultrasound.

Option D: Elastography is a newer imaging modality, which detects the changes in elasticity of tissues. It is based on the concept that the pathological process alters the elastic properties of tissue. It is useful in differentiating malignant and benign breast neoplasms, identifying traumatic changes in the muscles and tendons, helping to decide the biopsy site accurately, assess liver fibrosis and steatosis.
questions.learning: Thromboelastography — In the case of liver injury, intraoperative monitoring of coagulation function is done by thromboelastography which is shown in the given image.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A worried mother brought her 6-year-old unimmunized child to the ER with complaints of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Examination reveals a bull-neck appearance and a pseudomembrane over the tonsils that bleeds when removed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diphtheria

The given clinical scenario of a 6-year-old suffering from fever, cough, and shortness of breath with a pseudomembrane and bull neck appearance on examination is suggestive of diphtheria.

Diphtheria is caused by the bacteria Corynebacterium diphtheriae which spreads via droplets through the respiratory tract (most important), cutaneous lesions, and fomites.

Respiratory tract diphtheria is characterized by a thick, adherent pseudomembrane (grey or white) on one/both tonsils and adjacent pharynx. Underlying soft tissue oedema and enlarged lymph nodes can cause a bull-neck appearance.

Patients with laryngeal diphtheria are at risk for suffocation because of local soft-tissue oedema and airway obstruction by the diphtheritic membrane.

Management includes antitoxin therapy as a single empirical dose of 20,000-100,000 units and antibiotics. Penicillin G/ Benzylpenicillin is the drug of choice for diphtheria. However, in case of an allergy to the same, Erythromycin is used. Other antibiotics used are clindamycin, rifampin, and tetracycline.

A greyish-white membrane forms over the tonsils in the oropharynx and spreads to the soft palate and posterior pharyngeal wall. The membrane in diphtheria extends beyond the tonsils onto the soft palate and is dirty grey. It is adherent, and its removal leaves a bleeding surface. In the larynx, the diphtheritic membrane may cause airway obstruction.

Cervical lymph nodes, particularly the jugulodigastric, become enlarged and tender, sometimes presenting a bull-neck appearance. The patient is ill and toxaemic, but fever seldom rises above 38°C.

D/D for membrane over tonsil:

* Streptococcus & other pyogenic organisms

* Diphtheria

* Infectious mononucleosis

* Vincent’s angina

* Leukaemia

* Candida

* Agranulocytosis

* Malignancy

* Aphthous ulcer

* Traumatic ulcer

Other options :

Option A: Infectious mononucleosis most commonly presents in adolescents with initial symptoms of fever, sore throat, fatigue, myalgia, and malaise. Pharyngitis is often the most prominent sign, with the enlargement of the tonsils and an exudate resembling that of streptococcal pharyngitis. It can be associated with tender, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.

Option B: In acute membranous tonsillitis, exudates from the crypts coalesce to form a membrane on the surface of the tonsil that is easily wiped away without any bleeding.

Option D: Oral candidiasis/Oral thrush associated with candida albicans presents as white plaque-like lesions with cheesy exudate on an erythematous mucosa. They are typically painful and can be easily brushed off.
questions.learning: Diphtheria — The given clinical scenario of a 6-year-old suffering from fever, cough, and shortness of breath with a pseudomembrane and bull neck appearance on examination is suggestive of diphtheria.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In an HIV-positive patient who presents with multiple dog bites, what is the appropriate management?
questions.explanation: HIV-positive patients are considered immunocompromised, and multiple dog bites are classified as Category III exposure. This requires a comprehensive approach: immediate wound management (washing with soap and running water for 15-20 minutes), the full rabies vaccine course, and the administration of Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG). Option A is insufficient because immunocompromised individuals may not mount a timely immune response, making RIG essential for immediate passive protection. RIG alone (Option B) does not provide the long-term protection afforded by the vaccine. Simple wound care (Option C) cannot prevent the virus from reaching the central nervous system. Because rabies is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms appear, the combined use of active and passive immunization is the mandatory standard of care for Category III bites

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with confusion, vomiting, and abdominal pain, and is diagnosed with diabetic ketoacidosis. What is the primary treatment to control her elevated blood glucose levels?
questions.explanation: In the acute management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), the primary goal of insulin therapy is to stop ketogenesis and gradually normalize blood sugar. Regular (Short-acting) insulin is the only correct choice for initial management in an emergency setting. It is typically administered as a continuous intravenous drip because of its rapid onset and short half-life, allowing for precise titration based on hourly glucose monitoring. Lente insulin (Option B) is an intermediate-acting insulin used for chronic basal control, not for emergencies. Glyburide (Option C) is an oral sulfonylurea that is ineffective in Type 1 diabetes (where there is absolute insulin deficiency) and never used for DKA. insulin (Option D) is a pre-mixed combination used for daily maintenance. Therefore, regular insulin remains the global standard of care for stabilizing patients with DKA to effectively resolve acidosis and hyperglycemia
questions.learning: In the acute management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), the primary goal of insulin therapy is to stop ketogenesis and gradually normalize blood sugar.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As per NCEP- ATP III, which of the following is not a criterion for metabolic syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High LDL

As per NCEP- ATP III, high LDL is not included in the definition criteria of metabolic syndrome.

Metabolic syndrome is present if three or more of the following five criteria are met, which is given by NCEP-ATP III (National Cholesterol Education Program and Adult Treatment Panel III). It includes:

• Central obesity: waist circumference >102 cm (M), >88 cm (F)
• Hypertriglyceridemia: triglyceride level ≥ 150 mg/dL
• Low HDL cholesterol: <40 mg/dL and <50 mg/dL for men and women, respectively.
• Hypertension: blood pressure ≥130 mmHg systolic or ≥ 85 mmHg diastolic.
• Fasting plasma glucose level: ≥100 mg/dL or previously diagnosed type 2 diabetes.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with sudden, severe scrotal pain. Examination reveals scrotal swelling and erythema, a high-riding right testis, absence of the cremasteric reflex on the right side, and a negative Prehn’s sign. Based on these clinical findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Testicular torsion is a urological emergency, most common in adolescents. The "high-riding" position of the testis (due to twisting of the cord) and the "absence of the cremasteric reflex" are highly specific clinical indicators of torsion. A negative Prehn's sign (where lifting the scrotum does not relieve the pain) further supports torsion over inflammatory causes. Epididymo-orchitis (Option D) typically features a positive Prehn's sign and a preserved cremasteric reflex. Hydrocele (Option A) is usually painless and transilluminates. A strangulated hernia (Option B) presents with bowel obstruction symptoms and a mass that cannot be separated from the inguinal canal. Testicular torsion requires immediate surgical exploration and orchidopexy (of both sides, due to the "bell-clapper" deformity being bilateral). The "golden period" for salvage of the testis is within 6 hours of pain onset. Delay in diagnosis and treatment lead to irreversible ischemia and testicular necrosis
questions.learning: Testicular torsion is a urological emergency, most common in adolescents. The "high-riding" position of the testis (due to twisting of the cord) and the "absence of the cremasteric reflex" are highly specific clinical indicators of torsion.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The image given below shows neuromuscular monitoring of the patient after anesthesia. What is the most commonly used nerve for monitoring?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ulnar nerve

The following image shows neuromuscular monitoring and the most commonly used nerve for monitoring is the ulnar nerve.

The mechanosensor with electrodes is placed over the region of the ulnar nerve. This assesses the contraction of the adductor pollicis muscle to monitor neuromuscular activity.

Monitoring of neuromuscular blockade is required to monitor the blockade intraoperatively, ensure its complete reversal postoperatively, and prevent residual blockade. To monitor the neuromuscular function, a peripheral motor nerve is supramaximally stimulated and the response of the muscle is assessed.

The most commonly assessed nerve-muscle unit is the ulnar nerve-adductor pollicis muscle. This is because it is easily accessible, has the lowest risk of direct muscle stimulation, and the response can be evaluated visually, by tactile methods, or by objective methods. To stimulate the ulnar nerve, the electrodes are best applied to the volar aspect of the wrist.

Other nerve-muscle units that can be assessed include:

• Posterior tibial nerve- flexor hallucis brevis muscle
• Facial nerve- orbicularis oculi muscle
• Facial nerve- corrugator supercilii muscle

Many methods can be used for objective monitoring of neuromuscular function:

• Mechanomyography (MMG)
• Electromyography (EMG)
• Acceleration of the muscle response (AMG)
• Kinemyography (KMG)
• Cuff pressure modality (CPM)
• Compressomyography (CMG)
• Phonomyography (PMG)

Zone1
Central
Always explored, after proximo-distal vascular control

Zone2
Lateral
Only explored if the hematoma is pulsatile or expanding, else conservative/ angioembolization

Zone3
Pelvic
Only explored if the hematoma is pulsatile or expanding, else conservative/ angioembolization

If there is a penetrative injury in any of the zones, surgical management is done.

Mattox maneuver is left medial visceral rotation to expose the aorta.

Cattell-Braasch maneuver is done by right medial visceral rotation to expose IVC.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Gall stone chemistry most commonly seen amongst the following is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Crystalline cholesterol monohydrate

The most common gallstone chemistry seen is crystalline cholesterol monohydrate.

Types of gallstones:

1. Cholesterol stones (75% of gallstones) have >70% cholesterol by weight and are composed of crystalline cholesterol monohydrate. The majority of cholesterol stones have a mixed composition with bile pigments and calcium, in addition to the cholesterol. They are the most common type of gall stones worldwide and in India.
2. Pigment stones have <20% cholesterol and are dark due to the presence of calcium bilirubinate as the major constituent.

1. Black pigment stones (20% of gallstones) - are formed due to supersaturation of unconjugated bilirubin (seen in hereditary hemolytic anemia (like sickle cell and hereditary spherocytosis)
2. Brown pigment stones (5% of gallstones) - formed secondary to infections (like E. coli, and Ascaris lumbricoides)

Note: Pure cholesterol stones are uncommon and account for <10% of all stones.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16 year old girl presents to the OPD with a history of primary amenorrhoea and cyclical pain. Perineal examination reveals a bulge protruding from the vagina. Identify the cause of this presentation:
options: Transverse septum in the proximal vagina
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Imperforate hymen

A history of cyclical abdominal pain, primary amenorrhea and a bulging vaginal membrane suggest cryptomenorrhoea caused by an imperforate hymen.

Imperforate hymen is a urogenital anomaly which occurs due to failure of canalization of the inferior end of the vaginal plate. It usually remains unrecognized until puberty. It can lead to mucocolpos in early infancy.

Patients present with amenorrhea, cyclic abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, and a hypogastric lump on abdominal examination. A bluish bulging membrane at the vaginal opening is noted on genital examination and the Valsalva maneuver.

Ultrasound of the pelvis reveals normal internal genitalia and hematocolpos. Laparoscopy should be performed along with hymenectomy to exclude endometriosis.

Most common causes of cryptomenorrhea:

• Intact/imperforate hymen - a bluish convex bulge is seen
• Transverse vaginal septum - a pinkish concave covering is seen

Ultrasound pelvis confirms the diagnosis. A simple cruciate incision of the hymen allows the free drainage of the collected menstrual blood and restores the reproductive capacity in most cases.
questions.learning: Imperforate hymen — A history of cyclical abdominal pain, primary amenorrhea and a bulging vaginal membrane suggest cryptomenorrhoea caused by an imperforate hymen.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 58-year-old man presents with chronic cough, weight loss, and progressive dyspnea. On evaluation, he is found to have a primary liver malignancy. A whole-body imaging study demonstrates multiple hypermetabolic lesions in both lungs, consistent with pulmonary metastases. What is the principle of the imaging investigation shown?
options: Increased glucose metabolism in tissues using ¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased glucose metabolism in tissues using ¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)

The imaging shown is an ¹⁸F-FDG PET-CT scan, which detects increased glucose metabolism in tissues. ¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is a radioactive glucose analog that is taken up by metabolically active cells through glucose transporters and phosphorylated by hexokinase. Because malignant cells have increased glycolytic activity (Warburg effect), they accumulate FDG and appear as hypermetabolic (“hot”) lesions on PET imaging.

Why not the other options?

• A. Tissue perfusion using iodine contrast – Principle of contrast-enhanced CT, not PET.
• B. Decreased glucose metabolism in tissues – PET identifies areas of increased, not decreased, glucose uptake in most malignancies.
• D. Water diffusion in brain tissue – Principle of diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI), mainly used in acute stroke and certain brain lesions.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the term used to denote the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births?
questions.explanation: It is a common error to use the terms "rate" and "ratio" interchangeably in maternal health. The Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) specifically measures the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. This measure reflects the obstetric risk associated with pregnancy. The Maternal Mortality Rate (Option A), in contrast, measures deaths per 1,000 women of reproductive age, reflecting the risk of death in the general female population. The Infant Mortality Rate (Option C) measures deaths of infants under 1 year per 1,000 live births. The Perinatal Mortality Rate (Option D) includes late fetal deaths and early neonatal deaths. Because the denominator "live births" is used to define the obstetric risk, the "ratio" is the correct statistical term. Understanding this distinction is vital for accurate public health reporting and international comparisons
questions.learning: It is a common error to use the terms "rate" and "ratio" interchangeably in maternal health. The Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) specifically measures the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with sarcoidosis shows Koeppe's nodules on ophthalmologic examination. Where are these seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Iris

Koeppe's nodules and Bussaca's nodules develop on the iris in granulomatous uveitis.

Koeppe's nodules are seen at the pupillary margin. Bussaca's nodules are seen on the peripheral part of the anterior surface of iris.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common cause of death in case of esophageal varices in a patient with liver cirrhosis:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypovolemic shock

The most common cause of death in esophageal varices in a patient with liver cirrhosis is hypovolemic shock due to variceal bleed/hemorrhage. Hypovolemic shock is the most common type of shock and to some degree is a component of all other types of shock.

Hypovolemic shock occurs due to massive hemorrhage or fluid loss from vomiting, diarrhea, and severe burns. This results in low blood volume and cardiac output. Patients present with hypotension, a weak rapid pulse, tachycardia, and cool, clammy, cyanotic skin (due to cutaneous vasoconstriction, which shunts the blood away to vital organs like the heart and brain). More than 90% of otherwise healthy individuals recover with appropriate fluid resuscitation.

Shock is defined as a systemic state of low tissue perfusion which is inadequate for normal cellular respiration. Shock can be classified as follows:

Shock
Inciting mechanism

Hypovolemic shock

Reduced circulating blood volume

(eg., hemorrhage, dehydration)

Cardiogenic shock

Failure of the cardiac pump

(eg., myocardial infarction, cardiac dysrhythmias)

Obstructive shock

Mechanical obstruction of cardiac filling

(eg., cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax)

Distributive shock

Systemic vasodilation leading to organ hypoperfusion

(eg., anaphylaxis due to histamine release, sepsis due to the release of bacterial products, spinal cord injury due to sympathetic failure)

Endocrine shock

Combination of hypovolemic, cardiogenic or distributive shock.

(eg., hypo and hyperthyroidism, adrenal insufficiency)

* Baroreceptor reflex

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An intubated patient in the ICU had a chest X-ray taken to evaluate for fever spikes over the last 24-48 hours. The radiograph is shown below. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
options: Start antibiotics and send samples for culture
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ultrasound-guided aspiration

The given clinical history of an intubated ICU patient and the X-ray features point toward a diagnosis of pleural effusion. Ultrasound-guided aspiration is the next step in the management of the patient. Antibiotics should be started once the pleural tap has been done and infective etiology is suspected.

Options A and B: ET tube suctioning and chest physiotherapy are done to remove thick secretions out of the upper and lower respiratory tract. It wouldn't help in removing the fluid of a pleural effusion.

Pleural effusion is a common finding in the ICU setting and in intubated patients. Many factors contribute to the impairment of pleural fluid turnover in such cases as prolonged recumbency, ventilator-produced positive pressure, and reduced plasma oncotic pressure.

The diagnosis of pleural effusion may be made by clinical examination (dull note on percussion) or by imaging. A pleural tap for confirmation of diagnosis and to relieve breathing difficulty is now done under ultrasound guidance.

The CXR features of pleural effusion include:

• Obliteration of costophrenic angle on the side of pleural effusion
• Air-fluid interface (meniscus sign)
• Large effusions show: Complete opacification of the lung, mediastinal shift, and tracheal deviation away from the effusion

Differential diagnosis in an intubated patient with opacities on CXR might be pneumonitis secondary to gastric acid or food aspiration. But the X-ray would show patchy infiltration unlike the homogenous density seen in pleural effusion.
questions.learning: Ultrasound-guided aspiration — The given clinical history of an intubated ICU patient and the X-ray features point toward a diagnosis of pleural effusion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old medical student has been preparing for exams for several nights with inadequate sleep and irregular meals. Laboratory tests reveal mild hypoglycemia. Which of the following hormones is most likely to show an increase in secretion during this period of fasting, stress, and deep sleep recovery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Growth hormone

Growth hormone increases during fasting, stress, and deep sleep.

Growth hormone is secreted from the somatotropes located in the anterior pituitary. Its main role is the growth of the human body. The growth hormone levels show diurnal variation and variation across different age groups. Adolescents have the highest circulating levels of growth hormone, followed by children and adults. The levels are relatively low during the day and the pulsatile release of this hormone occurs during sleep.

Stimuli that increase GH secretion:

* Hypoglycemia, deoxyglucose, fasting, starvation

* Exercise

* Protein meal, infusion of arginine

* Glucagon

* Deep sleep

* Estrogens and androgens

* Stressful stimuli

Important regulators of growth hormone:

* Growth hormone-releasing hormone- stimulates the production of the hormone

* Somatostatin- inhibits the release of GH

* Ghrelin- increases the GH release

Actions of growth hormone:

* Growth of cartilage, bones, and organs.

* Increases amino acid uptake and protein synthesis in the cells and decreases protein breakdown.

* Diabetogenic action: Increases the hepatic glucose release and decreases the glucose uptake by muscles and fat.

* Increases fat utilization. It is ketogenic and increases circulating free fatty acid levels.

• Somatostatin (GHIH)
• Exogenous GH

questions.text:
BCYE medium is used to culture:

BCYE - Buffered charcoal yeast extract
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Legionella

BCYE medium (buffered charcoal yeast extract agar) is used to culture Legionella pneumophila.

Legionella pneumophila has fastidious growth requirements and grows on complex media such as  BCYE medium with L-cysteine and antibiotic supplements (e.g., polymyxin B, cefazolin, vancomycin). The charcoal acts as a detoxifying agent. It grows slowly, and the colonies may take 3–6 days to appear.

questions.text: What is the incidence of breech presentation in singleton deliveries at term? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3%

Breech presentation refers to a longitudinal lie in which the fetal buttocks or lower extremities present first.

Incidence: Approximately 3% of singleton pregnancies at term

Breech presentation is more common earlier in pregnancy, but most fetuses spontaneously convert to cephalic presentation before term.

Types of breech presentation:

• Frank breech → hips flexed, knees extended (most common)
• Complete breech → hips and knees flexed
• Footling breech → one or both feet presenting

Risk factors:

• Prematurity
• Multiple pregnancy
• Placenta previa
• Uterine anomalies
• Polyhydramnios or oligohydramnios

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
The drug 'X' is a GHRH analogue that is FDA-approved for the treatment of HIV-associated lipodystrophy and not used for Growth hormone deficiency. Identify the drug 'X'.

GHRH- Growth Hormone Releasing Hormone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tesamorelin

Tesamorelin is approved for use in HIV-associated lipodystrophy but not for GH deficiency. It is a synthetic N-terminal modified form of human GHRH. It does not get degraded by dipeptidyl peptidase 4 and therefore has a longer duration of action.

It increases the levels of growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) but reduces visceral fat accumulation.

Tesamorelin is approved for use in HIV-associated lipodystrophy but not for GH deficiency.

Other options:

Option A: Octreotide is a somatostatin analogue that decreases growth hormone levels. It is used in the treatment of acromegaly, variceal bleeding, diarrhoea due to adenomas secreting VIP (vasoactive intestinal peptide), and sulfonylurea toxicity. One of its adverse effects is gallstone formation.

Option B: Somatropin is a growth hormone analogue. It is used in growth hormone deficiency and other short-stature conditions like Turner's syndrome, Noonan syndrome, and Prader-Willi syndrome. Their use is contraindicated in acute critical illness, active malignancy, and proliferative retinopathy.

Option D: Mecasermin is a recombinant human IGF-1. It is used in IGF-1 deficiency, growth hormone receptor defects, and antibodies against growth hormone receptors. Adverse effects include hypoglycemia and lipohypertrophy. Another recombinant human IGF-1 with its IGFBP-3, mecasermin rinfabate has been FDA-approved for HIV-associated adipose redistribution syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the suturing technique shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Simple interrupted sutures

Simple interrupted sutures involve inserting the needle at right angles to the incision so that it passes through both sides of the wound and exits again at right angles. The needle should be rotated through the tissue to prevent enlargement of the needle hole.

The distance from the needle point to the wound edge should approximately equal the tissue depth, and subsequent sutures should be spaced at twice this distance. Each suture must extend into the wound depth and be placed at right angles to its axis. The suture is then tied using a surgeon's knot in case of nonabsorbable suture or a square knot for absorbable sutures.

Option A and C: Mattress sutures can either be vertical or horizontal. The initial suture is inserted as in an interrupted suture. The needle can then be moved either horizontally or vertically, traversing both edges of the wound once again. Such sutures are very useful in producing an accurate approximation of irregular wound edges. They can produce either eversion or inversion of a wound edge.

The images below show horizontal and vertical mattress sutures respectively:

Option D:  In subcuticular suturing, the suture is anchored at one end of the wound. Small bites of subcuticular tissue are taken on alternate sides of the wound and then pulled together gently at the apex. This approximates the wound edges together. The final bite leaves a trailing loop of the suture, and a knot can be tied. The knots can be tied loosely or secured by means of a collar and bead when non-absorbable sutures are used. If the suture is absorbable, a buried knot is used.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Mutism and akinesis in a person who is aware of his surroundings and somewhat alert is best described as a feature of:
questions.explanation:

Akinetic mutism is a feature of Stupor.

• In this condition , the patient is unable to initiate action and speech but appears awake and alert.
• There is severe reduction of relational function – speech and action.

Akinetic mutism is also seen in Schizophrenia with affective psychosis and dissociative states.

• Basal ganglia

Option B, Twilight state

• Abrupt onset of abnormal violent behavior
• Occurs in

• Epilepsy
• Alcoholism
• Brain trauma

Option D, Delirium

• Global impairment of consciousness and cognition.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During surgery for patent ductus arteriosus, which anatomical structure is most susceptible to injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Left recurrent laryngeal nerve

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is most susceptible to injury during surgery for patent ductus arteriosus.

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the 6th arch artery while the right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the 4th arch artery. This occurs because the distal portion of the 6th arch disappears on the right side along with the 5th arch artery. Thus the nerve on the right side loops under the 4th arch artery.

The patent ductus arteriosus is due to a defect in the 6th aortic arch, also known as the pulmonary arch, as it gives off a branch to the growing lung bud. On the right side, this arch forms the right pulmonary artery proximally and disappears distally. On the left side, the distal part remains patent to form the ductus arteriosus that shunts blood from the right ventricle to the dorsal aorta. This is obliterated after birth forming the ligamentum arteriosum. If the ductus arteriosus remains patent after birth, it is referred to as patent ductus arteriosus.

Pearl PF0428: Derivatives of Various Aortic Arches

The aortic arches or pharyngeal arch arteries are a series of six paired embryological vascular structures which give rise to the great arteries of the neck and head. They are ventral to the dorsal aorta and arise from the aortic sac.

The following table shows various arterial structures derived from the aortic arches:

Aortic arches

Arterial Structures

Second aortic arches

Third aortic arches

Fourth aortic arches

Left: aortic arch

Regress completely

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A gym owner noticed that people who come to the gym also drink iced tea. He concluded that drinking iced tea is the sole reason to lose weight. What is this relationship called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spurious

In the gym owner's case, concluding that iced tea alone causes weight loss is a spurious relationship because it ignores other key factors like exercise and overall diet.

A spurious relationship is when two variables appear to be connected but are actually linked by another factor or are coincidental. In this scenario, the gym owner observed that gym-goers also drink iced tea and concluded that iced tea is the sole cause of weight loss. However, this conclusion is just coincidental because it ignores other important factors, such as exercise, diet, and lifestyle changes, which likely contribute to weight loss.

An association can be broadly grouped under three headings:

* Spurious association

* Indirect association

* Direct (causal) association: One-to-one causal association and Multifactorial causation

Option B: Direct (causal) association: Two variables are stated to be causally related (AB) if a change in A is followed by a change in B. When factor A is present, disease B must result. Measles is one such disease in which such a relation exists.

Option C: Indirect association: The indirect association is an association between a variable and disease due to the presence of another factor, known or unknown, that is also known as the "confounding" variable. For example, endemic goitre is generally found in high altitudes, thereby showing an association between altitude and endemic goitre. But, endemic goitre is not due to altitude but due to an environmental deficiency of iodine. Thus, a common factor (i.e., iodine deficiency) can result in an apparent association between two variables, when no association exists.

Option D: Multifactorial causation is seen in non-communicable diseases or conditions (e.g., Coronary heart disease) where the etiology is multifactorial.
questions.learning: Spurious — In the gym owner's case, concluding that iced tea alone causes weight loss is a spurious relationship because it ignores other key factors like exercise and overall diet.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The parameter which provides an estimate of the amount by which the disease under study can be reduced in a population, if the suspected factor is eliminated from that population, is called:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Population attributable risk

Population attributable risk (PAR) estimates the amount of disease occurrence in the entire population that could be prevented if the suspected risk factor were completely eliminated.

• A. Relative risk: Measures the risk of disease in exposed compared with unexposed.
• B. Attributable risk: Measures the excess risk among the exposed population due to the exposure.
• C. Population attributable risk — Correct: Estimates the disease burden in the total population attributable to the exposure.
• D. Risk difference: Difference in risk between exposed and unexposed; essentially the same concept as attributable risk in many contexts.
questions.learning: Population attributable risk Population attributable risk (PAR) estimates the amount of disease occurrence in the entire population that could be prevented if the suspected risk factor were completely eliminated. • A.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A barium swallow study of a woman with dysphagia is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The barium swallow image shows the pathognomonic "bird’s beak sign"—a massive dilation of the proximal esophagus ending in a smooth, symmetric, tapering narrowing at the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). This is the classic radiological finding for Achalasia, a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the failure of the LES to relax and the absence of peristalsis. Distal esophageal spasm (Option B) typically shows a "corkscrew" appearance on barium swallow. Jackhammer esophagus (Option C) is a hypercontractile disorder that may show high-pressure segments but not the specific bird's beak narrowing. Clinically, achalasia presents with progressive dysphagia for both solids and liquids from the onset, often accompanied by regurgitation and weight loss. Diagnosis is confirmed by esophageal manometry, which is the gold standard. Management includes pneumatic dilation, botulinum toxin injection, or definitive surgical Heller’s myotomy. The bird's beak sign is one of the most reliable and high-yield radiological identifiers in gastroenterology
questions.learning: The barium swallow image shows the pathognomonic "bird’s beak sign"—a massive dilation of the proximal esophagus ending in a smooth, symmetric, tapering narrowing at the lower esophageal sphincter (LES).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which condition is characterized by a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio and FEV1 as a percentage of the predicted value, along with morning wheezing and shortness of breath?
questions.explanation: The spirometric finding of an FEV1/FVC ratio is the hallmark of an obstructive lung disease. Among the options, Asthma (Option A) is the only obstructive condition. Asthma characteristically presents with episodic shortness of breath and wheezing, which is often worse in the morning or at night. Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD) (Option B), Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) (Option C), and Silicosis (Option D) are all restrictive lung diseases. Restrictive diseases are characterized by a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio and reduced lung volumes (Total Lung Capacity). COPD also shows an obstructive ratio, but the reversible nature and morning symptoms in a potentially younger patient favor asthma. Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating bronchodilator reversibility (an increase in FEV1 by ). Identifying the "obstructive" vs. "restrictive" patterns is the first and most vital step in interpreting pulmonary function tests
questions.learning: The spirometric finding of an FEV1/FVC ratio is the hallmark of an obstructive lung disease. Among the options, Asthma (Option A) is the only obstructive condition.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a given population, 4050 births were recorded over a period of 1 year. Among these, 50 were stillbirths, 50 died in the 1st week of life and 150 died within 8-28 days of life. What is the neonatal mortality rate of this population?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 50

The neonatal mortality rate (NMR) refers to the rate of deaths within the first 28 days of life. It is calculated using the following parameters:

* Early neonatal deaths- death in the first 7 days of life

* Late neonatal deaths - after 7th day but before 28th completed day of life

The neonatal mortality rate (NMR) of the given population is 50 per 1000 live births.

Neonatal mortality rate = No. of deaths of neonates < 28 days within a year x 1000 / Total live births in the same year

In this population, there were 4000 live births (no. of total births - no. of stillbirths).

NMR = (50+150) x 1000/4000 = 100/2 = 50

Pearl PF0989: Neonatal Mortality Rate

* Neonatal deaths are those that occur during the neonatal period, commencing at birth and ending at 28 completed days after birth.

* NMR = Number of deaths of children under 28 days of age in a year x 1000/Total live births in the same year

* Main causes of neonatal death are birth asphyxia (leading cause), preterm complications, intrapartum related complications, sepsis, pneumonia, congenital anomalies, tetanus, diarrhea, etc.

* India’s NMR  is about 25 per 1000 live births.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the hormones 1 and 2 in the following image
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1: Inhibin, 2: Testosterone

The image shows the Hypothalamic pituitary axis and the hormones 1 is Inhibin and 2 is testosterone.

Hypothalamus stimulates the Anterior pituitary via GnRh to release FSH and LH.

LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone, which in turn inhibits LH by a negative feedback mechanism. FSH stimulates Sertoli cells to secrete inhibin, which in turn inhibits FSH by a negative feedback mechanism.

Testosterone inhibits LH secretion by acting directly on the anterior pituitary and by inhibiting the secretion of GnRH from the hypothalamus. Inhibin acts directly on the anterior pituitary to inhibit FSH secretion.

FSH also stimulates the secretion of ABP (androgen-binding protein). FSH and androgens maintain the gametogenic function of the testes. Hypothalamic lesions in animals and hypothalamic disease in humans lead to atrophy of the testes and loss of their function.
questions.learning: 1: Inhibin, 2: Testosterone The image shows the Hypothalamic pituitary axis and the hormones 1 is Inhibin and 2 is testosterone. Hypothalamus stimulates the Anterior pituitary via GnRh to release FSH and LH.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A doctor tells a 31-year-old woman, who is 20 weeks pregnant, that her baby has a developmental defect. She has come to you for a second opinion. The following USG finding is seen. Identify the defect.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anencephaly

The given ultrasound image shows an open defect in the calvaria and skin leading to the exposure of the cranial neural tube. This is consistent with the diagnosis of anencephaly.

Anencephaly results from incomplete closure of the neural tube. It is one of the earliest detectable congenital defects that can be detected as early as 10 to 11 weeks of gestation.  Screening can also be done by serum estimation of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP). The following are the radiological signs seen in anencephaly.

• Frog eye sign - Absence of cranial calvaria, prominent orbits thereby resembling the face of a frog.
• Shower cap sign - The absence of the cranium could lead to the protrusion of a disorganized mass of brain tissue. This resembles a shower cap giving rise to a characteristic triangular facial appearance.

Many neural-tube defects can be prevented with preconceptional supplementation of folic acid. A dose of 4 mg daily is recommended in subsequent pregnancies.

Other options:

Option B: Omphalocele is a midline anterior abdominal wall defect through which the solid abdominal viscera and/or bowel may herniate. The extruded abdominal contents are covered in a sac. These are due to the persistence of physiological herniation of the gut or as a part of the OEIS complex (omphalocele, exstrophy, imperforate anus, and spinal abnormality) and cloacal exstrophy. The ‘elephant’s trunk’ sign on ultrasound, due to the prolapsed terminal ileum is said to be pathognomonic for cloacal exstrophy of the OEIS complex.

The first image below shows a patient with cloacal exstrophy showing the elephant trunk sign representing the intussuscepted ileum. The second image shows omphalocele while the third image shows gastroschisis (a close differential diagnosis for omphalocele). The fourth image demonstrates an ultrasound image of the fetus suggestive of an omphalocele (asterix)

Option C: Cystic hygroma is a congenital multiloculated lymphatic lesion that is classically found in the left posterior triangle of the neck. It occurs as a result of sequestration or obstruction of developing lymph vessels. It must be carefully differentiated from nuchal translucency (NT) as both may appear similar. This defect can be picked up in a first-trimester ultrasound.

The image below shows a newborn with cystic Hygroma on the right side of the neck and cystic hygroma of the neck in the fetus.

Option D: Encephalocele is caused due to defects in the skull through which the meninges and/or neural tissue herniate. The squamous part of the occipital bone is the most frequently affected bone. In meningoencephalocele or occult spina bifida with Chiari malformations, the scalloping of the frontal bones is observed in the ultrasound as the lemon sign while anterior curvature of the cerebellum with effacement of the cisterna magna in the posterior fossa forms the banana sign.

The image shows a newborn with encephalocele. The second and third images below show the banana and the lemon sign respectively.
questions.learning: Anencephaly — The given ultrasound image shows an open defect in the calvaria and skin leading to the exposure of the cranial neural tube. This is consistent with the diagnosis of anencephaly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the level of lymph nodes indicated in the marked region of the neck in the given anatomical image.
questions.explanation: The marked lymph nodes are located along the upper part of the internal jugular vein, extending from the skull base to the hyoid bone, which corresponds to Level II (Upper Jugular Nodes). This level includes the clinically significant jugulodigastric node, which is frequently involved in malignancies of the oropharynx and nasopharynx. Regarding the distractors, Level Ia (Option B) refers to submental nodes in the midline under the chin, and Level Ib (Option C) refers to submandibular nodes lateral to them. Level IV (Option D) consists of lower jugular nodes located between the cricoid cartilage and the clavicle. The vertical position of the nodes along the superior third of the sternocleidomastoid muscle as shown in the image confirms they belong to Level II. Identifying these levels is crucial for staging and planning neck dissections in head and neck cancer patients
questions.learning: The marked lymph nodes are located along the upper part of the internal jugular vein, extending from the skull base to the hyoid bone, which corresponds to Level II (Upper Jugular Nodes).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man seeks treatment for erectile dysfunction and prefers a medication that does not require precise timing before sexual activity because of an unpredictable schedule. Which phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitor would be most suitable due to its longer duration of action?
questions.explanation: Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors are the first-line pharmacological treatment for erectile dysfunction. Among the commonly prescribed agents, Tadalafil is distinct due to its exceptionally long half-life of approximately 17.5 hours. This provides a "window of opportunity" that lasts up to 36 hours, earning it the nickname "the weekend pill." This prolonged duration allows for greater spontaneity, as the patient does not need to time the dose immediately before sexual activity. In contrast, Sildenafil (Option A) and Vardenafil (Option C) have much shorter durations of action, typically lasting 4–6 hours. Avanafil (Option D) is characterized by a very rapid onset of action (15 minutes) but has a shorter duration compared to Tadalafil. All PDE-5 inhibitors require sexual stimulation to be effective and are contraindicated in patients taking nitrates due to the risk of severe hypotension. Tadalafil’s unique pharmacokinetic profile makes it the preferred choice for patients seeking flexibility and long-lasting efficacy
questions.learning: Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors are the first-line pharmacological treatment for erectile dysfunction. Among the commonly prescribed agents, Tadalafil is distinct due to its exceptionally long half-life of approximately 17.5 hours.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old G2P1 at 8 weeks diagnosed to have hyperthyroidism. What is the drug of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Propylthiouracil

PTU is preferred in the 1st trimester because methimazole/carbimazole are linked to congenital anomalies (e.g., aplasia cutis). Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated. After 1st trimester, therapy is usually switched to methimazole. This switch reduces PTU-related hepatotoxicity later in pregnancy.
questions.learning: Propylthiouracil PTU is preferred in the 1st trimester because methimazole/carbimazole are linked to congenital anomalies (e.g., aplasia cutis). Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
Arrange the steps of the  experimental study :

A. Blinding

B. Randomization

C. Defining inclusion and exclusion criteria

D. Statistical analysis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. C - B - A - D

C - B - A - D is the correct order of steps in an experimental study.

Defining inclusion and exclusion criteria → Randomization → Blinding → Statistical analysis

Phases of experimental study:

1. Planning phase

• Literature review
• Trial design
• Protocol
• Budget, funding
• Approvals - ethics, collaborating institutes, funding agencies, sponsors

2. Preparatory phase

• Organization, staffing
• Delegation, responsibility, and accountability
• Standardization of protocols, training, data management, privacy
• Pilot testing, quality control

3. Operational phase

• Selection of target population
• Choosing a sample study population
• Eligibility screen: Exclusion and inclusion criteria
• Informed consent
• Subject registration, baseline evaluations
• Randomization
• Blinding
• Conduct a study on the groups allocated
• Follow-ups, evaluation protocol
• Exit plan, termination point
• Trial monitoring

4. Analysis phase

• Preliminary clarifications
• Initial Data Analysis, definitive analysis
• Statistical inference

5. Conclusion

• Validity, interpretation
• Writing reports, manuscripts, dissemination

Randomization is the random allocation of the participants into the study and control groups in the experimental studies.

Blinding is done after randomization to reduce the possibility of bias, such as subject variation bias (due to participants), observer bias, and evaluation bias (by the investigator).
questions.learning: C - B - — A - D C - B - A - D is the correct order of steps in an experimental study. Defining inclusion and exclusion criteria → Randomization → Blinding → Statistical analysis Phases of experimental study: 1.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following types of pulse is generated in accordance with the Frank-Starling law?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pulsus alternans

The Frank–Starling law states: The force of ventricular contraction increases with increasing ventricular filling (preload).

In simple terms: More end-diastolic volume → stronger contraction → greater stroke volume. This mechanism allows the heart to adjust cardiac output automatically.

Pulsus alternans shows alternating strong and weak beats due to beat-to-beat variation in stroke volume. It reflects impaired myocardial contractility where ventricular filling influences force of contraction via the Frank–Starling mechanism.

Seen classically in left ventricular systolic dysfunction.

A) Pulsus bisferiens

Pulse with two systolic peaks.

Seen in:

• Aortic regurgitation
• Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

B) Pulsus paradoxus

Fall in systolic BP >10 mmHg during inspiration.

Seen in:

• Cardiac tamponade
• Severe asthma
• Constrictive pericarditis

Respiratory phenomenon, not Frank-Starling related.

Not related to Frank-Starling mechanism.

D) Pulsus parvus

Weak, small pulse.

Seen in:

• Severe aortic stenosis

Due to reduced stroke volume, not alternating contractility.
questions.learning: Pulsus alternans — The Frank–Starling law states: The force of ventricular contraction increases with increasing ventricular filling (preload). In simple terms: More end-diastolic volume → stronger contraction → greater stroke volume.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with sudden chest pain and dyspnea, and pulmonary embolism is suspected. Which imaging modality is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: For a patient with suspected acute Pulmonary Embolism (PE), CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is currently the gold-standard and most definitive imaging modality (Option B). CTPA allows for the direct visualization of emboli within the pulmonary arterial system with high sensitivity and specificity. Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scans (Option C) are used primarily when CT is contraindicated (e.g., in severe renal failure), but they are less definitive. Doppler echocardiography (Option A) can show signs of right heart strain but cannot confirm the presence of a clot itself. MR pulmonary angiography (Option D) is less validated and more time-consuming than CTPA. Therefore, because of its rapid availability, high accuracy, and ability to provide alternative diagnoses, CTPA remains the definitive diagnostic tool of choice in modern emergency departments. Finding a filling defect on CTPA is sufficient to initiate therapeutic anticoagulation
questions.learning: For a patient with suspected acute Pulmonary Embolism (PE), CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is currently the gold-standard and most definitive imaging modality (Option B).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female patient presented with a 4 x 3 cm lump over the right breast. On examination, Peau d'orange appearance can be noted. What is the tumor staging in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. T4b

Skin involvement over the breast- peau d'orange appearance classifies this as stage T4b.

Peau d'orange appearance is due to the blockage of subcuticular lymphatics. The resultant edema deepens the mouth of the sweat glands and hair follicles giving rise to the typical orange peel appearance.

This given clinical scenario in this woman with peau d’orange of the breast suggests her staging is T4b. Tumor of any size with overlying skin involvement (Peau d'orange appearance) classifies it as stage T4b.

The term peau d’orange describes the orange-peel appearance of the skin. The dermal lymphatic blockade gives rise to edema in the breast. The sweat glands and hair follicles get buried due to the edema resulting in a typical orange peel appearance. Infiltration of the ligaments of Cooper results in dimpling of the skin. Infiltration of the lactiferous glands gives rise to retraction of the nipple. Spread into the chest wall results in fixation of the breast into the chest wall. This leads to restricted mobility of the breast

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: During subclavian vein catheterization, a patient develops a sudden drop in oxygen saturation. Chest examination reveals increased resonance in the upper right lung. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Subclavian venous catheterization is a high-risk procedure due to the proximity of the lung apex (pleura). A sudden drop in oxygen saturation during the procedure is a major warning sign. The clinical finding of "increased resonance" (hyperresonance) on percussion in the upper right lung indicates an air-filled space where lung tissue should be. This is pathognomonic for an iatrogenic pneumothorax (Option B) caused by the needle accidentally puncturing the lung. Arterial puncture (Option A) would cause local hematoma but not immediate hyperresonance or oxygen drops. Cardiac tamponade (Option C) presents with distant heart sounds and low BP (Beck's triad). Chylothorax (Option D), or lymph leakage, would cause dullness on percussion due to fluid accumulation rather than hyperresonance. Therefore, the combination of acute respiratory distress and hyperresonance identifies pneumothorax as the definitive procedural complication. Immediate management includes stopping the procedure and considering a chest tube or needle decompression
questions.learning: Subclavian venous catheterization is a high-risk procedure due to the proximity of the lung apex (pleura). A sudden drop in oxygen saturation during the procedure is a major warning sign.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs interferes with the action of interleukin-2 (IL-2) without inhibiting calcineurin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sirolimus

Sirolimus (rapamycin) suppresses T-cell proliferation by inhibiting the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), thereby blocking the cellular response to interleukin-2 (IL-2). Unlike calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine and tacrolimus), sirolimus does not inhibit IL-2 synthesis; instead, it prevents IL-2-mediated signal transduction, thereby inhibiting T-cell activation and proliferation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Tacrolimus: Calcineurin inhibitor; prevents transcription and production of IL-2 by inhibiting T-cell activation.
• B. Mycophenolate mofetil: Inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), blocking de novo purine synthesis and selectively suppressing T- and B-lymphocyte proliferation; does not act on the IL-2 pathway.
• D. Azathioprine: Purine analog that inhibits DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells, including lymphocytes; no direct effect on IL-2 signaling.
questions.learning: Sirolimus Sirolimus (rapamycin) suppresses T-cell proliferation by inhibiting the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), thereby blocking the cellular response to interleukin-2 (IL-2).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The image given is of the eustachian tube. Identify the muscle marked with the arrow.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tensor veli palatini

The muscle marked is the tensor veli palatini, the primary muscle responsible for opening the pharyngotympanic (Eustachian) tube during swallowing and yawning. By opening the tube, it equalizes pressure between the middle ear and the nasopharynx, maintaining normal hearing and middle ear ventilation.

• Tensor veli palatini inserts into the cartilaginous part of the Eustachian tube and actively opens it during swallowing.

Why not the other options?

• A. Stylopharyngeus: Elevates the pharynx during swallowing; does not open the Eustachian tube.
• B. Superior constrictor: Constricts the pharyngeal wall during swallowing.
• D. Levator veli palatini: Elevates the soft palate and assists in opening the tube but is not the primary dilator.
questions.learning: Tensor veli palatini — The muscle marked is the tensor veli palatini, the primary muscle responsible for opening the pharyngotympanic (Eustachian) tube during swallowing and yawning.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A 30-year-old woman on oral contraceptives for the past 6 months presents with 6 weeks of amenorrhea. What would be the best method of assessing the gestational age of this patient?

LMP- Last menstrual period

USG- Ultrasonography
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Crown rump length by USG

The best method of assessing the gestational age of a patient on oral contraceptives with 6 weeks of amenorrhea is by measuring the crown-rump length (CRL) using ultrasonography.

Gestational age refers to the duration of pregnancy calculated from the first day of the LMP. It is usually expressed in weeks. Following the use of oral contraceptives, ovulation may have been later than 2 weeks after the LMP. Therefore, gestational age calculated with the help of LMP will be inaccurate.

First-trimester ultrasound measurement of CRL is the best method to assess gestational age. It is measured from the vertex to the coccyx.

• CRL (in mm) + 6.5 = gestational age in weeks (or)
• CRL (in mm) + 42 days = gestational age in days.

CRL measurement is shown in the image below:

Ultrasonographic parameters for estimation of the gestational age according to the trimester are as follows:

Trimester

Parameter

1st

Crown-rump length (CRL)

2nd and 3rd

• Biparietal diameter (BPD)
• Abdominal Circumference (AC)
• Head Circumference (HC)
• Femur Length. (FL)

Other options:

Option B: Adding 280 days to the LMP will provide the expected delivery date (EDD). Adding 9 months + 7 days to the LMP or 280 days to the LMP is Naegele’s formula for calculating the EDD.

Option C: Measurement of fundal height in cm (with a variation of 1-2cm) is roughly equal to the gestational age in weeks, after 24 weeks of pregnancy. This is measured from the superior border of the symphysis pubis to the top of the uterine fundus when the bladder is empty.
questions.learning: Crown rump length by USG — The best method of assessing the gestational age of a patient on oral contraceptives with 6 weeks of amenorrhea is by measuring the crown-rump length (CRL) using ultrasonography.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the maximum number of occupants allowed in a two-room house to prevent overcrowding?
questions.explanation: The public health standards for housing define overcrowding based on the number of rooms and the floor area relative to the number of occupants. According to standard Indian health guidelines (based on the Model Building Bye-laws), the accepted occupancy limit to prevent overcrowding in a two-room house is 3 people (Option B). Option A (2 people) is the limit for a one-room house. Option C (4 people) would typically require 2.5 to 3 rooms depending on the specific age of the occupants (children count as half). Option D (5 people) is excessive for two standard rooms. Overcrowding is a significant risk factor for the transmission of infectious diseases, particularly respiratory infections like TB and meningitis. Therefore, for the purpose of housing and health standards, 3 people is the definitive maximum capacity for a two-room dwelling
questions.learning: The public health standards for housing define overcrowding based on the number of rooms and the floor area relative to the number of occupants. According to standard Indian health guidelines (based on the Model Building Bye-laws), the accepted occupancy…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10 year old boy was brought for psychiatric evaluation for intellectual disability. On examination, his IQ was 45. He has a long face, large ear ,large testis and a cardiac murmur and A history of poor intellectual function is present in the paternal family.What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fragile X syndrome

The given clinical vignette along with the family history is suggestive of fragile X syndrome.

* Fragile X syndrome is the second most common genetic cause of mental retardation (Down syndrome being the most common).

* It is caused by a trinucleotide mutation in the familial mental retardation-1 (FMR1) gene.

* When the cells were cultured in a folate-deficient medium, the cytogenetic alteration was discovered as a break in the staining in the long arm of the X chromosome. As it appeared that the chromosome was “broken” at this locale, it was named as a fragile site.

* In fragile X syndrome, the affected males are mentally retarded, with an IQ in the range of 20 to 60.

* The characteristic phenotypic features includes:

* Long face with a large mandible

* Large everted ears

* Large testicles (macro-orchidism)

* In some cases, hyperextensible joints, a high arched palate, and mitral valve prolapse may also be noted.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes has the highest catalytic efficiency?
options: Km of an enzyme = 10 micromole and Kcat = 20 per sec
Km of an enzyme = 2000 nanomole and Kcat = 50 per sec
Km of an enzyme = 2 micromole and Kcat = 200 per sec
Km of an enzyme = 4 micromole and Kcat = 200 per sec
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Km of an enzyme = 2 micromole and Kcat = 200 per sec

The highest catalytic efficiency is seen when Km= 2 micromole and Kcat = 200 per sec.

Catalytic efficiency is calculated as Kcat/Km, where Km is inversely proportional to the binding affinity of the enzyme and Kcat is the catalytic constant (Vmax divided by the total number of active sites of the enzyme present). Higher values of Kcat and lower values of Km gives better catalytic efficiency. Catalytic efficiency can be used to compare the performance of 2 different enzymes in catalyzing a reaction.

Step 1: Km of each option after converting respective units to moles will be 10, 2, 2 and 4 (each multiplied by 10-6) moles.

Step 2: The catalytic efficiency is calculated as Kcat/Km. On substituting the values in various options after converting to moles, the values come out to be 2, 25, 100 and 50 (each multiplied by 106) M-1 s-1.

Some enzymes can be so efficient that they convert the substrate to product instantaneously. They are limited only by the rate at which substrate diffuses towards the enzyme in a solution. These are called diffusion-limited enzymes and their catalytic efficiency is as high as 108 M-1 s-1.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 68-year-old man presents with chronic back pain, frequent fatigue, and a history of recurrent urinary tract infections over the past three months. Laboratory tests show elevated ESR, and skull X-ray reveals abnormalities. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate to further evaluate his condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation—elderly male with back pain, anemia (suggested by fatigue), and the provided skull radiograph showing multiple "punched-out" lytic lesions—is pathognomonic for Multiple Myeloma . Once this diagnosis is suspected, the most appropriate and essential next diagnostic test is Serum Protein Electrophoresis (SPEP) (Option D). This test will identify the presence of a monoclonal "M-spike," confirming the production of monoclonal proteins by malignant plasma cells. MRI of the brain (Option A) and CT scan (Option C) would show the structural lesions but do not provide the definitive biochemical evidence required for diagnosis. A PET scan (Option B) is useful for staging but is not the primary diagnostic investigation. Therefore, because SPEP (along with UPEP) is the gold standard for confirming the underlying plasma cell dyscrasia, it is the definitive next step. Early diagnosis is critical for managing potential renal failure and hypercalcemia

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following dosage regimens for the adult leprosy treatment kit is incorrect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rifampicin 450 mg weekly

According to the WHO-recommended Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) for leprosy, the incorrect dosage for adults is Rifampicin 450 mg weekly, as the correct dose is 600 mg once a month.

Leprosy, caused by Mycobacterium leprae, is treated using Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT), recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). The treatment regimen depends on the classification of the disease.

Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy, which involves fewer skin lesions and a lower bacterial load, is treated with rifampicin (600 mg once a month) and dapsone (100 mg daily) for six months.

Multibacillary (MB) leprosy, which has widespread lesions and a higher bacterial load, is treated with rifampicin (600 mg once a month), clofazimine, 300 mg once a month (Option D)+ 50 mg daily(Option B), and dapsone (100 mg daily) for 12 months. These drugs help kill the bacteria, prevent resistance, and reduce transmission.

Early diagnosis and treatment adherence are crucial to preventing complications, disability, and further transmission of the disease. MDT is provided free of cost through national leprosy programs worldwide, ensuring patient accessibility. Along with antibiotics, supportive care such as wound care, physiotherapy, and management of nerve damage are essential in preventing deformities and disability. Corticosteroids may be used in cases of lepra reactions to manage inflammation and nerve damage. With proper treatment and early intervention, leprosy is completely curable, reducing the risk of long-term complications.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In a case where an Rh-negative mother delivers an Rh-positive infant and the newborn has a positive Coombs test, what is the underlying mechanism responsible for this hypersensitivity reaction?:
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario describes Erythroblastosis Fetalis (Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn), which is a classic Type II hypersensitivity reaction. In this condition, maternal IgG antibodies against the Rh antigen cross the placenta and bind to the baby's Rh-positive red blood cells. These antibody-coated cells are then recognized and destroyed by the fetal splenic macrophages through the process of Antibody-Dependent Cellular Cytotoxicity (ADCC). Option A is a non-standard term. Option C refers to Type III hypersensitivity (immune complex diseases like SLE). Option D refers to Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity (like the TB skin test). The positive Coombs test confirms that antibodies are already bound to the fetal RBC surface. Therefore, the direct destruction of cells mediated by specific antibodies identifies ADCC as the definitive immunological mechanism in Rh incompatibility

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: On centrifugation of a cell, LDH will get deposited in the __? LDH- Lactate Dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cytoplasm

On centrifugation of a cell , the cell organelles can be seperated and then detected by specific marker enzymes. LDH is a marker enzyme of cytoplasm and hence will get deposited in the cytoplasm itself. LDH levels in cytoplasm are clinically significant as they leak into plasma whenever there is cell damage or necrosis, making it a useful diagnostic marker.

Other options:

Option A) Mitochondria are organelles responsible for cellular respiration and energy production. They contain enzymes involved in the citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle) and the electron transport chain. LDH is primarily found in the cytoplasm, not within mitochondria. While some LDH isoforms have been reported in the mitochondria of certain cell types, the bulk of LDH activity is in the cytoplasm.

Option B) Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing various hydrolytic enzymes involved in cellular digestion and waste processing. LDH is not typically found in lysosomes.

Option D) Proteins and fats are sorted, altered, and packaged for transportation by the Golgi complex, also known as the Golgi apparatus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, regular hand washing is advised to prevent disease transmission. Which level of prevention does this measure represent?
questions.explanation: Primary prevention aims to prevent the onset of a disease in a person who is currently healthy. Hand washing is a classic example of this level of prevention; it is a specific protective measure designed to interrupt the transmission of pathogens (like the SARS-CoV-2 virus) to a susceptible individual, thereby preventing the initial infection. Primordial prevention (Option A) would involve broad social policies like establishing a national sanitation infrastructure. Secondary prevention (Option C) involves the early detection of the virus through testing in an asymptomatic person. Tertiary prevention (Option D) involves the treatment and rehabilitation of a patient with severe COVID-19 pneumonia to prevent long-term disability. Hand washing, along with wearing masks and vaccination, constitutes the core of primary preventive strategies used to control the spread of communicable diseases during a pandemic. These actions empower the individual to reduce their own risk of illness through simple, effective, and evidence-based behavioral interventions

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A farmer was brought to the emergency department with diarrhea, sweating, excessive lacrimation,salivation and garlicky odour. His pulse rate is 55/min and his plasma cholinesterase level was 50U/mL. Which of the following can be used to treat this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atropine

The clinical features are suggestive of organophosphate poisoning and IV atropine is the treatment of choice.

The organophosphates commonly used as pesticides are anticholinesterases. Toxicity occurs by excessive inhalation of vapors, ingestion, or percutaneous absorption. It inhibits the cholinesterase activity which results in an increase of acetylcholine, leading to cholinergic symptoms.

The predominant initial signs are of muscarinic excess which includes: (DUMBBELSS)

* Diarrhea

* Urination

* Miosis

* Bronchospasm

* Bradycardia

* Emesis

* Lacrimation

* Salivation

* Sweating

This may be followed by cognitive disturbances, convulsions, and neuromuscular blockade.

Treatment:

* Maintenance of vital signs particularly respiration

* Removal of clothing and washing of the skin

* IV atropine 2- 5 mg. If IV administration is not possible, then 2 mg IM every 5-10 minutes (till muscarinic symptoms disappear)

* Pralidoxime, a cholinesterase reactivator can also be used for treatment

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A man presents with high VLDL and chylomicrons, with eruptive xanthomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presentation of elevated VLDL and chylomicrons signifies extremely high triglyceride levels. This profile is characteristic of Familial Hypertriglyceridemia (Type IV Hyperlipoproteinemia). The massive triglyceride elevation results in "eruptive xanthomas," which are small, yellowish skin papules appearing suddenly on the skin. This condition also carries a significant risk of acute pancreatitis. Familial hypercholesterolemia (Option D) involves isolated high LDL and total cholesterol, typically presenting with tendon xanthomas rather than eruptive ones. Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (Option B) involves high IDL and would show palmar xanthomas. Familial hyperlipidemia (Option A) is a general term rather than the specific biochemical entity described. Because the eruptive xanthomas and the specific elevation of triglyceride-rich VLDL and chylomicrons are described, Familial Hypertriglyceridemia is the most accurate clinical diagnosis. Management focuses on fibrates and lifestyle changes
questions.learning: The presentation of elevated VLDL and chylomicrons signifies extremely high triglyceride levels. This profile is characteristic of Familial Hypertriglyceridemia (Type IV Hyperlipoproteinemia).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic cholelithiasis. While dissecting Calot's triangle, a lateral injury to the common bile duct occurred, leading to significant bile leakage into the operative field. The surgeon has limited experience in laparoscopy. What is the most appropriate intraoperative management step at this stage?
options: Continuing laparoscopic repair of the common bile duct
Placing a drainage tube in subhepatic space
Closing the abdomen and taking the patient for ERCP and biliary stenting
Converting the laparoscopic surgery to open surgery and placing a T-tube through the injured common bile duct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Converting the laparoscopic surgery to open surgery and placing a T-tube through the injured common bile duct

Bile duct injury is one of the most serious complications of laparoscopic cholecystectomy, most commonly occurring during dissection of Calot’s triangle due to misidentification of biliary anatomy. In this case:

• Lateral injury to the common bile duct (CBD)
• Significant bile leak
• Surgeon has limited laparoscopic experience

The safest management is to convert to open surgery and repair the injury over a T-tube, which decompresses the biliary tree and allows postoperative cholangiography.

Why not the other options?

• A. Continue laparoscopic repair of common bile duct: Not advisable in an inexperienced surgeon; increases the risk of further injury and stricture.
• B. Place only a drainage tube in subhepatic space: Inadequate for a recognized CBD injury.
• C. Close abdomen and perform ERCP and biliary stenting later: ERCP is useful for postoperative leaks but recognized major intraoperative bile duct injuries should be addressed immediately.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person sustains a stab injury, as shown in the image. The wound is longer than its width, deep with clean-cut margins, and has one acute angle and one blunt angle. Which of the following is the most likely weapon responsible for this injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Single-edged knife

The shape of a stab wound provides important clues about the type of weapon used. A single-edged knife typically produces a stab wound with:

• One acute (sharp) angle – produced by the cutting edge
• One blunt or squared-off angle – produced by the blunt back of the blade
• Clean-cut margins
• Depth greater than the surface length of the wound

The wound described and shown in the image is characteristic of a single-edged knife injury.

Why not the other options?

• B. Screwdriver: Produces a puncture wound, usually circular, slit-like, or cruciate depending on the tip, not a clean incised stab wound with characteristic angles.
• C. Broken glass piece: Produces irregular lacerated/incised wounds with uneven margins and variable wound shapes.
• D. Double-edged dagger: Produces a stab wound with both ends acute and symmetrical, as both edges are sharp.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the pathology in the given radiograph of a newborn.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Imperforate anus

The given radiograph of a newborn shows imperforate anus/anal atresia.

Anorectal atresia, also known as imperforate anus, refers to a spectrum of abnormalities of the rectum and anus. There are many possible abnormalities as follows:

* The absence of an anal opening.

* The anal opening is in the wrong place.

* A connection, or fistula, joining the intestine and urinary system.

* A connection joining the intestine and vagina.

* In females, the intestine can join with the urinary system and vagina in a single opening, known as a cloaca.

Incidence is one in every 5,000 live births.

The newborn presents with an inability to pass meconium, abdominal distension, anal dimple, and sometimes passing meconium per urethra. It is divided into low intermediate and high lyings according to the Wingspread classification. Diagnosis is done using Wangenstein invertogram . Treatment is surgical.

questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with abnormal uterine bleeding. Pelvic examination reveals an ovarian mass. Histopathology confirms a sex cord–stromal tumor with Call-Exner bodies. Which of the following is the most useful tumor marker for diagnosis and follow-up of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibin-B

Granulosa cell tumor belongs to sex cord-stromal tumors of the ovary.

Key features

• Usually unilateral
• Yellowish solid tumor (due to lipid content)
• Produces estrogen

Hormonal effect

Excess estrogen causes:

• Precocious puberty in children
• Menorrhagia / irregular bleeding in reproductive age
• Postmenopausal bleeding in elderly women

Call-Exner bodies are small follicle-like structures filled with eosinophilic material.

They resemble immature ovarian follicles and are considered the histologic hallmark of granulosa cell tumors.

Granulosa cell tumor = Coffee-bean nuclei + Call-Exner bodies
