questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: An HPE image of the endometrium is shown. The hormone responsible is secreted by?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Corpus luteum

Secretory endometrium (corkscrew glands seen in the image) is due to progesterone from the corpus luteum in luteal phase. Granulosa/theca produce estrogen; primary follicles do not produce luteal progesterone.

Follicular epithelium shows tall glands with pseudostratification and telescoping.

In the secretory phase, progesterone causes characteristic histological changes:

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Tortuous (saw-tooth) glands | Glands become coiled and irregular

| Glycogen secretion | Nutrient supply for implantation

| Stromal edema | Progesterone effect on endometrial stroma

| Predecidual changes | Preparation for pregnancy

B) Primary follicle

Primary follicles mainly contribute to early estrogen production, not progesterone.

C) Granulosa cells

Granulosa cells produce estrogen (via aromatization of androgens).

D) Theca interna

Theca interna cells produce androgens, which are converted to estrogen by granulosa cells.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A barber aged 42 years presented with a healed ulcer as below, over the lower medial aspect of the right leg. On examination, he has varicose veins on both his legs. What is the most likely type of ulcer he had?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Venous ulcer

The history of varicose veins and the presence of an ulcer at the lower 1/3rd of the leg with eczema and pigmentation is characteristic of a venous ulcer.

Venous ulcers are due to chronic venous insufficiency and are particularly seen in the area between the muscles of the calf and ankle. They are accompanied by lipodermatosclerosis and hemosiderosis(If these features are not present then the ulcer is probably not of venous origin). Ambulatory venous hypertension is the most acceptable theory in the pathophysiology of venous ulcers. It has a sloping edge and the floor contains granulation tissue covered by slough and exudate. Marjolin’s ulcer is a type of squamous cell carcinoma seen in chronic long-standing venous ulcers.

Management of venous ulcers:

* Bisgaard's regimen

* Education

* Elevation of the affected limb to reduce the edema

* Elastic compression stockings - The ideal interface pressure in venous ulceration is 35-40 mmHg.

* Evaluation

* 4 layer bandaging system comprising of:

* Orthopedic wool

* Cotton crepe

* Elastic bandage - first compressive layer

* Cohesive bandage - second compressive layer

* Antibiotics are given only if the wound is infected.

* Regular dressing.

* Medical management by oral pentoxifylline is considered which helps in reducing the viscosity and improving circulation.

* Surgery- ulcer excision with pinch mesh grafting has a good outcome and helps in preventing recurrence.

The lower limb, commonly on the medial side of the ankle, is never above the middle third of the leg

Deep, penetrating the fascia exposes the tendons, muscles, and underlying bone.

The ulcer is painful, with irregular margin tenderness, and hyperesthetic.

Vertically oval, and painless, the floor may have pale to no granulation tissue, induration, and tenderness at the base.
painless, punched-out with regular calloused margins.

Bony deformities may be present.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department with severe maxillofacial trauma from a road traffic accident, resulting in airway compromise. What is the most appropriate immediate airway management?
questions.explanation: In the setting of severe maxillofacial trauma where the airway is acutely compromised, standard methods such as orotracheal intubation (Option B) may be impossible due to massive bleeding, edema, or anatomical disruption. In such an emergency "can't intubate, can't oxygenate" scenario, Cricothyroidotomy is the most appropriate immediate surgical airway intervention. It is faster and easier to perform than a formal tracheostomy (Option A) and provides a secure airway below the site of the trauma. Bag-mask ventilation (Option D) is often ineffective when there is structural damage to the face or upper airway obstruction. Cricothyroidotomy involves an incision through the cricothyroid membrane, allowing for rapid cannulation. While it is a temporary life-saving measure, it must eventually be converted to a formal tracheostomy if long-term airway support is needed. Clinicians must be trained in this procedure as part of advanced trauma life support (ATLS) to prevent hypoxic brain injury or death in patients with complex head and neck injuries
questions.learning: In the setting of severe maxillofacial trauma where the airway is acutely compromised, standard methods such as orotracheal intubation (Option B) may be impossible due to massive bleeding, edema, or anatomical disruption.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient presents with clinical features including non-caseating granulomas and a characteristic saddle nose deformity. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Wegener's granulomatosis (now known as Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis) is a small-vessel vasculitis that characteristically affects the upper and lower respiratory tracts and the kidneys. The combination of non-caseating granulomas on biopsy and a saddle nose deformity (resulting from the destruction of the nasal septal cartilage) is a classic clinical presentation. While Syphilis (Option D) and Leprosy (Option B) can also cause saddle nose deformity through bone and cartilage destruction, their pathology involves endarteritis obliterans or specific neuro-cutaneous features rather than non-caseating granulomatous vasculitis. Tuberculosis (TB) (Option A) is characterized by caseating granulomas and primarily affects the lungs or bones, rarely presenting with primary saddle nose deformity in this manner. Diagnosis of Wegener's is supported by the presence of c-ANCA antibodies. Management requires aggressive immunosuppression with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide. Early recognition is vital to prevent permanent facial disfigurement and life-threatening pulmonary or renal failure. This specific anatomical-histological pairing is a favorite topic in both ENT and pathology exams
questions.learning: Wegener's granulomatosis (now known as Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis) is a small-vessel vasculitis that characteristically affects the upper and lower respiratory tracts and the kidneys.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the nerve supply of the structure marked in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trochlear nerve

The structure marked in the image is the superior oblique muscle. It is innervated by the trochlear nerve.

There are seven extraocular muscles present in the eye. They are:

• Levator palpebrae superioris - Which elevates the upper eyelids
• Four recti muscles - Superior, inferior, medial, and lateral recti
• Two obliques - Superior and inferior oblique

The muscles originate from the back of the orbit in a common tendinous ring called the annulus of Zinn and are inserted into the sclera.

All the extraocular muscles are innervated by the oculomotor (III) nerve except:

• Lateral rectus which is supplied by abducens (VI) nerve
• Superior oblique which is supplied by trochlear (IV) nerve
questions.learning: Trochlear nerve — The structure marked in the image is the superior oblique muscle. It is innervated by the trochlear nerve.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: In a pregnant woman presenting with an anal wart, as shown in the image, what is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: The image shows condyloma acuminata (anal warts) caused by human papillomavirus (HPV). In this scenario, the treatment of choice is cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen. Cryotherapy works by freezing and destroying wart tissue, leading to necrosis and eventual shedding. It is preferred because it is minimally invasive, relatively painless, bloodless, and allows precise control over the depth of tissue destruction, making it highly effective for genital and anal warts—even in pregnancy. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Trichloroacetic acid (TCA): Although it can be used, it is not the treatment of choice for anal warts compared to cryotherapy. (B) Excision: Surgical removal is effective but more invasive, with risks like bleeding and possible anal stricture formation, so not first-line. (D) Oral acyclovir: This is used for herpes simplex virus, not HPV, so it has no role in treating condyloma acuminata
questions.learning: The image shows condyloma acuminata (anal warts) caused by human papillomavirus (HPV). In this scenario, the treatment of choice is cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Function of utricle and saccule?
questions.explanation: The utricle and saccule are the two otolith organs located within the vestibule of the inner ear. Their primary physiological function is the detection of linear acceleration and deceleration, as well as the position of the head relative to gravity (static equilibrium). The utricle primarily detects horizontal movement, while the saccule is more sensitive to vertical movement. Angular acceleration (Option C) is the function of the semicircular canals, which detect rotational movements of the head. Hearing (Options A and D) is exclusively the function of the cochlea. Inside the utricle and saccule, specialized sensory areas called maculae contain hair cells embedded in a gelatinous membrane covered with calcium carbonate crystals (otoliths). When the head moves linearly, the inertia of these crystals bends the hair cells, sending signals to the brain via the vestibular nerve. Understanding these distinct vestibular roles is essential for diagnosing different types of vertigo and balance disorders in clinical practice

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 62-year-old diabetic patient presents with severe ocular pain, lid edema, proptosis, chemosis, and complete loss of vision following a penetrating eye injury 5 days ago. Ocular movements are restricted and fundus view is not possible. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Panophthalmitis

Panophthalmitis = Suppurative inflammation involving:

• All coats of the eyeball
• Intraocular contents
• Tenon’s capsule
• Often spreads to orbit

The single discriminating idea:

• Endophthalmitis stops at the sclera. Panophthalmitis breaks through it.
• Both follow penetrating trauma. Both give pain, hypopyon, and vision loss.
• The orbital signs are what separate them:

| Finding in this stem | Meaning

| -------------------- | -------

| Proptosis | Inflammation has escaped the globe into orbital fat

| Restricted ocular movements | Extraocular muscles are now inflamed/oedematous

| Lid oedema + marked chemosis | Trans-scleral spread to Tenon's capsule and orbit

| Complete loss of vision (no PL) | Total intraocular destruction

| Severe boring pain | Scleral and orbital involvement
questions.learning: Panophthalmitis Panophthalmitis = Suppurative inflammation involving: • All coats of the eyeball • Intraocular contents • Tenon’s capsule • Often spreads to orbit The single discriminating idea: • Endophthalmitis stops at the sclera.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A woman presented with a BIRADS-5 breast lesion. Which of the following is a good prognostic factor for this lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ER positive

ER positivity is a good prognostic factor in breast cancer.

The ER and PR are two steroid hormone receptors present in breast cancer. The expression of these receptors indicates a favorable prognosis and response to hormonal therapy.

Other options:

Option A: The mutations in BRCA1 gene account for up to 40% of familial breast cancers. These tumors are high-grade, hormone receptor–negative, and aneuploid and do not have a good prognosis.

Option B: p53 is a tumor suppressor gene, which on mutation acts as an oncogene. p53 positivity is associated with highly malignant breast cancers and has poor survival.

Option D: Ki-67 is used to access the proliferative index (activity) of the tumor. High Ki-67 indicates a poor prognosis.
questions.learning: ER positive ER positivity is a good prognostic factor in breast cancer. The ER and PR are two steroid hormone receptors present in breast cancer.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is considered the treatment of choice for managing central diabetes insipidus?
questions.explanation: Central Diabetes Insipidus (DI) is caused by a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH/Vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary, leading to polyuria and polydipsia. Desmopressin (dDAVP) is the preferred treatment because it is a synthetic analog of vasopressin with high selectivity for V2 receptors in the collecting ducts of the kidney. It has a longer duration of action than natural ADH and can be administered intranasally, orally, or parenterally. Insulin (Option A) is used for Diabetes Mellitus, not DI. Diazoxide (Option C) is used for hypertensive emergencies or insulinomas. Chlorpropamide (Option D) is a sulfonylurea that can sensitize the kidney to ADH in partial central DI, but it is not the first-line "preferred" treatment due to the risk of hypoglycemia. Desmopressin provides effective control of water excretion with minimal V1-mediated vasoconstrictive side effects. Therefore, Desmopressin is the gold standard for hormone replacement therapy in patients with a confirmed diagnosis of central diabetes insipidus
questions.learning: Central Diabetes Insipidus (DI) is caused by a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH/Vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary, leading to polyuria and polydipsia.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: FBN gene mutation is seen in which of the following genetic disorders?
questions.explanation: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant multisystem connective tissue disorder caused by a mutation in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15q21. This gene encodes fibrillin-1, a protein essential for forming microfibrils that provide structural support to tissues. Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (Option A) is typically caused by defects in collagen synthesis, such as types III or V. Homocystinuria (Option C) results from a deficiency in cystathionine beta-synthase; while it mimics the Marfanoid appearance, its genetic basis is different . von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (Option D) is caused by the VHL gene on chromosome 3p. Classic Marfan clinical features include a tall, thin build, joint laxity, and ectopia lentis (lens dislocation). Therefore, the FBN1 mutation is the definitive genetic marker for Marfan syndrome
questions.learning: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant multisystem connective tissue disorder caused by a mutation in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15q21. This gene encodes fibrillin-1, a protein essential for forming microfibrils that provide structural support to tissues.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with obstetric score G2P1 at 14 weeks is advised uterine artery Doppler. What would it detect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Early-onset preeclampsia

Uterine Artery Doppler evaluates uteroplacental blood flow during pregnancy.

It is usually performed between 11–14 weeks or 18–24 weeks. The test detects impaired placental blood flow, which is associated with:

• Early Onset Preeclampsia
• Fetal Growth Restriction

However, uterine artery Doppler is primarily used to predict early-onset preeclampsia. Abnormal uterine artery Doppler predicts early-onset preeclampsia.

Normally in pregnancy:

Spiral arteries remodel

↓

Low resistance blood flow

↓

Adequate placental perfusion

In abnormal placentation:

Poor trophoblastic invasion

↓

High resistance uterine arteries

↓

Abnormal Doppler waveform

↓

Risk of early preeclampsia

| Finding | Significance

| ------- | ------------

| Increased pulsatility index (PI) | High resistance

| Early diastolic notch | Poor placental perfusion
questions.learning: Early-onset preeclampsia Uterine Artery Doppler evaluates uteroplacental blood flow during pregnancy. It is usually performed between 11–14 weeks or 18–24 weeks.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drug–class combinations is incorrectly matched?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Triptorelin — Aromatase inhibitor

Triptorelin is a GnRH agonist, not an aromatase inhibitor.

When administered continuously, GnRH agonists such as triptorelin initially produce a flare of gonadotropin secretion, followed by downregulation and desensitization of pituitary GnRH receptors. This ultimately decreases LH and FSH secretion and suppresses gonadal sex-hormone production.

Correct classifications:

• Raloxifene → SERM
• Fulvestrant → SERD
• Trastuzumab → Anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody
• Triptorelin → GnRH agonist

Examples of aromatase inhibitors include:

• Letrozole
• Anastrozole
• Exemestane

Educational Objective:

• Remember the distinction:

• GnRH agonists: Leuprolide, goserelin, triptorelin
• Aromatase inhibitors: Letrozole, anastrozole, exemestane
• Therefore, Triptorelin — Aromatase inhibitor is the incorrectly matched pair.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with GERD has no improvement after long-term medical therapy. He underwent surgical treatment for GERD. Identify the procedure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Nissen's fundoplication

The procedure in the given image shows a 360-degree wrap, which is known as Nissen's fundoplication; this procedure is done for GERD. Nissen's fundoplication is a complete fundoplication procedure.

Fundoplication is the procedure in which the fundus of the stomach is wrapped around the lower end of the esophagus. In the Nissen's fundoplication procedure, the fundus is wrapped the entire 360 degrees around the esophagus.

The most common complication of Nissen’s fundoplication is the gas-bloat syndrome. In this condition, patients are unable to belch gas from the stomach into the oesophagus. This causes increased gas in the stomach, resulting in a bloating sensation, abdominal discomfort, and flatulence.

Other options:

Option A: The toupet procedure is the re-creation of a sphincter around the EGJ done by wrapping the fundus around the oesophagus. A posterior 180-270-degree wrap is used.

Option B: The Dor procedure is fundoplication, most commonly used in the setting of the esophagal myotomy. It consists of an anterior 180-degree wrap.

Option C: Watson's fundoplication is a 90-degree anterior fundoplication. It is reported to achieve good reflux control while permitting burping and active vomiting and reducing gas bloat.
questions.learning: Nissen's fundoplication — The procedure in the given image shows a 360-degree wrap, which is known as Nissen's fundoplication; this procedure is done for GERD.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old child underwent adenoidectomy for adenoid hypertrophy. Postoperatively, the child develops a hypernasal voice and occasional regurgitation of fluids through the nose. What is the most likely cause?
options: Submucous cleft palate unmasked after surgery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Submucous cleft palate unmasked after surgery

Persistent hypernasal speech and nasal regurgitation following adenoidectomy suggest velopharyngeal insufficiency (VPI). The most common cause is an occult (submucous) cleft palate that was previously compensated for by enlarged adenoids. Removal of the adenoid pad unmasks the inability of the soft palate to achieve complete velopharyngeal closure during speech and swallowing.

Why not the other options?

• B. Choanal atresia unmasked after surgery: Causes nasal obstruction, not hypernasality or nasal regurgitation.
• C. Adhesions in the nasopharynx: May cause nasal blockage but do not typically produce velopharyngeal insufficiency.
• D. Uvular injury post surgery: Minor uvular trauma may cause sore throat or edema but is not a common cause of persistent hypernasal speech.
questions.learning: Submucous cleft palate unmasked after surgery Persistent hypernasal speech and nasal regurgitation following adenoidectomy suggest velopharyngeal insufficiency (VPI).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presented with a great toe infection. She had significant discoloration of the toenail with a subungual hyperkeratosis that caused color alteration and a rough surface area. She was suspected to have onychomycosis. Which topical drug is given for toenail onychomycosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tavaborole

Tavaborole is the topical drug given in toenail onychomycosis.

Tavaborole is a topical antifungal. It is an oxaborole antifungal that inhibits fungal protein synthesis by targeting leucyl-tRNA synthetase.

Onychomycosis is defined as the infection of the nail plate by fungus.

Most common cause is Trichophyton rubrum, but many fungi may be causative.

The clinical scenario of Tinea unguium presents with yellowish discolouration, which spreads proximally as a streak in the nail. Later, subungual hyperkeratosis becomes prominent and spreads until the entire nail is affected. Gradually, the entire nail becomes brittle and separated from its bed.

Diagnosis is made by KOH mount examination of dystrophic subungual debris.

Management of onychomycosis involves Oral terbinafine as the treatment of choice for Tinea unguium or onychomycosis. It acts as a non-competitive inhibitor of squalene epoxidase, which is essential in the synthesis of fungal ergosterol. Oral terbinafine at 250 mg/day is given for 6 weeks for fingernail infection and 3 months (12 weeks) for toenail infection. An oral Griseofulvin dose of 1 g/day for 4–8 months (longer for toenails) is used as a second-line treatment.

Other Options:

Option A: Caspofungin: Caspofungin is an echinocandin antifungal that works by inhibiting fungal cell wall synthesis. It is used in intravenous form for systemic fungal infections like candidiasis and aspergillosis.

Option B: Itraconazole: Itraconazole is an oral antifungal from the triazole class, used for onychomycosis due to its penetration into keratinised tissues.

Option C: Griseofulvin: Griseofulvin is an oral antifungal used for dermatophyte infections, including onychomycosis.
questions.learning: Tavaborole Tavaborole is the topical drug given in toenail onychomycosis. Tavaborole is a topical antifungal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structure marked in the image drains into:
options: Junction of superior vena cava and left brachiocephalic veins
Junction of left jugular and left subclavian veins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Junction of left jugular and left subclavian veins

The image shows the thoracic duct which drains into the junction of the left jugular and left subclavian veins.

Thoracic duct begins in the abdomen at T-12 vertebral level as the continuation of cisterna chyli.

* It is usually beaded due to its numerous valves.

* It drains the body below the diaphragm (lower limbs, pelvis, abdomen) and left half of the body above the diaphragm (thorax, upper limb, head and neck).

* Thoracic duct passes through the aortic hiatus in the diaphragm and ascends through the posterior mediastinum between the aorta and the azygous vein.

* At T-5 level, it deviates to the left side and ascends to pass the thoracic inlet.

Tributaries of the thoracic duct:

* Bilateral (right and left) descending thoracic lymph trunks which convey lymph from lower intercostal spaces (6 – 11).

* Left upper intercostal lymph trunks, which convey lymph from the upper intercostal spaces (1-5).

* Mediastinal lymph trunks

* Left subclavian lymph trunk

* Left jugular lymph trunk

* Left bronchomediastinal lymph trunk

The lymph passes through larger lymphatics and eventually collect into two large trunks, the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct, which in turn drain into the brachiocephalic veins.

* Thoracic duct- drains both lower limbs, left upper limb, abdomen, left halves of thorax, and left side of the head and neck regions (areas shaded green in the image).

* Right lymphatic duct- drains right upper limb, and right halves of thorax, and right side of the head and neck regions (areas shaded blue in the image).
questions.learning: Junction of left jugular and left subclavian veins — The image shows the thoracic duct which drains into the junction of the left jugular and left subclavian veins.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: In the Mental State Examination, (100-7=93) is done to examine which of the following mental function?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Concentration

(100-7=93) test in Mental Status Examination (MSE) is done to test concentration.

MSE is a structured way of observing and describing a patient's psychological functioning at a given point in time. It does not involve the scoring of a patient.

The main components of MSE are:

* Appearance and behavior

* Mood and affect

* Speech

* Thought process and content

* Perceptual disturbances

* Cognition

* Abstract reasoning

* Insight

* Judgment

The elements of cognitive functioning that are assessed are alertness, orientation, concentration, memory (both short and long-term), calculation, fund of knowledge, abstract reasoning, insight, and judgment.

Concentration is elicited in the following ways:

* Starting at 100, the patient can be asked to count backward by 7 - (100-7) test

* The patient can be asked to say the letters of the alphabet backward starting with Z.

* Can be asked to name the months of the year backward starting with December.

When conducting the MSE or interpreting MSE findings, it is important to consider the cultural background of both the clinician conducting the MSE and the interviewee because behavioral patterns vary significantly across cultures (e.g., nodding your head as a sign of approval in some countries might signify disagreement in others)

Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), also known as Folstein's test, is done out of a score out of 30 and is used to measure cognitive impairment.

Note: Mental Status Examination (MSE) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) are two different assessment tests.
questions.learning: Concentration (100-7=93) test in Mental Status Examination (MSE) is done to test concentration. MSE is a structured way of observing and describing a patient's psychological functioning at a given point in time.

questions.text: A patient presents with left-sided facial paralysis and weakness for the past 1 hour. Her blood pressure is 160/100 mmHg and CT is shown below. What would be your next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intravenous thrombolysis

NCCT shows a hyperdense MCA sign suggestive of acute thrombus in right MCA.

In acute ischemic stroke, if the patient presents within the therapeutic window (≤4.5 hours) and non-contrast CT shows no hemorrhage and BP <185/110 mmHg, the next step is intravenous thrombolysis (IV alteplase/tenecteplase).

Why not other options:

• CT angiogram: Done after initiating thrombolysis or if planning thrombectomy
• Aspirin + clopidogrel: Given after thrombolysis or if not eligible
• IV labetalol: Only if BP >185/110 before thrombolysis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with vaginal bleeding. A transvaginal ultrasound reveals an endometrial thickness of 8.0 mm. What should be the next step in management? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Histopathological examination of curettage

Postmenopausal bleeding must always be evaluated for endometrial carcinoma until proven otherwise. Transvaginal ultrasound is used to measure endometrial thickness:

• Endometrial thickness ≤4 mm → low risk of malignancy
• Endometrial thickness >4 mm → requires endometrial sampling

This patient has:

• Postmenopausal bleeding
• Endometrial thickness of 8 mm

Therefore, the next step is histopathological evaluation of the endometrium by endometrial biopsy or curettage.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Hysterectomy is not performed before tissue diagnosis
• Progesterone therapy should not be started without excluding malignancy
• Follow-up sonography alone is inappropriate in symptomatic women with thickened endometrium

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old female comes with a sudden onset of pain in the right eye. It is associated with colored halos, decreased visual acuity and a steamy cornea is seen, the pupil is mid-dilated and fixed. IOP is 60 mmHg. What is the diagnosis?
options: Secondary angle closure glaucoma by uveitis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute angle closure glaucoma

Acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) is an ophthalmic emergency caused by sudden closure of the anterior chamber angle, leading to a rapid rise in intraocular pressure.

Classical clinical features:

• Sudden severe eye pain
• Colored halos around lights (corneal edema)
• Decreased vision
• Steamy/hazy cornea
• Mid-dilated, fixed pupil
• Markedly raised IOP (often >50–60 mmHg)

Pupillary block → iris bows forward → trabecular meshwork obstruction → acute rise in IOP

Why not others:

• A. Neovascular glaucoma:

• Gradual onset, associated with diabetes/CRVO
• Iris neovascularization, not acute mid-dilated pupil

• C. Secondary angle closure glaucoma (uveitis):

• Associated with inflammation signs (cells, flare, posterior synechiae)
• Usually not such abrupt presentation with classic halos

• D. Phacomorphic glaucoma:

• Lens-induced angle closure (intumescent cataract)
• Typically with visible lens swelling and shallow anterior chamber, less classic mid-dilated fixed pupil picture
questions.learning: Acute angle closure glaucoma Acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) is an ophthalmic emergency caused by sudden closure of the anterior chamber angle, leading to a rapid rise in intraocular pressure.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presents with persistent tearing, ocular discharge, and swelling at the inner corner of her eye, and is diagnosed with chronic dacryocystitis. What is the treatment of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation: Chronic dacryocystitis in an adult is primarily caused by an irreversible obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct, leading to the accumulation of tears and subsequent infection within the lacrimal sac. The definitive treatment of choice is Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR). This surgical procedure creates a new, permanent bypass track between the lacrimal sac and the middle meatus of the nasal cavity, effectively restoring tear drainage. Lacrimal sac massage (Option A) and Probing (Option D) are first-line treatments for congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction in infants, but they have a very high failure rate in adults with established chronic inflammation. Syringing (Option C) is a diagnostic tool used to confirm the site of obstruction but is not a curative treatment. DCR can be performed via an external approach (with a skin incision) or endoscopically through the nose. Preoperative evaluation includes syringing and sometimes dacryocystography. Successful DCR provides immediate and long-term relief from epiphora and recurrent bouts of painful infection
questions.learning: Chronic dacryocystitis in an adult is primarily caused by an irreversible obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct, leading to the accumulation of tears and subsequent infection within the lacrimal sac.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department with an intense urge to urinate but is unable to void. He has a history of perineal trauma, and examination reveals blood at the external urethral meatus. Which anatomical structure is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation: In a young male with a history of perineal trauma (such as a straddle injury), the bulbar urethra is the most commonly injured segment of the anterior urethra. The classic clinical presentation includes an inability to void despite a full bladder and the presence of blood at the external urethral meatus. Regarding the distractors, a posterior urethral valve (Option B) is a congenital anomaly found in male infants, not healthy young adults. Intraperitoneal bladder rupture (Option C) occurs during blunt abdominal trauma and presents with peritonitis and urinary ascites rather than meatal blood. The membranous urethra (Option D) is part of the posterior urethra and is typically injured during pelvic fractures rather than isolated perineal trauma. Therefore, based on the mechanism of injury (perineal) and meatal bleeding, the bulbar urethra is the anatomical site of damage
questions.learning: In a young male with a history of perineal trauma (such as a straddle injury), the bulbar urethra is the most commonly injured segment of the anterior urethra.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a triage system, highest priority patients are respectively colour coded by
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Red

Highest priority patients are coded red in the triage system.

* Triage consists of rapidly classifying the injured on the basis of the severity of their injuries and the likelihood of their survival with prompt medical intervention.

* Triage is the only approach that can provide maximum benefit to the greatest number of injured in a major disaster situation.

Pearl PF1015: Triage Colour Coding

Triage system consists of four colour codes:

Color code
Priority
Type of patients

Red
High
Need for immediate resuscitation or surgery in the next 6 hours or transfer (Eg. massive hemorrhage, tension pneumothorax)

Yellow
Medium
Possible resuscitation or surgery in next 24 hours (Eg. Isolated simple fracture)

Green
Low
Ambulatory patients or minor illness (Eg. Isolated abrasions, contusions, sprains)

Black
Least
Dead or moribund patients (Eg. massive head injuries, 95% third degree burns)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with progressively worsening fatigue by the end of the day that improves with rest, along with drooping eyelids, and difficulty speaking and swallowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical hallmarks of fatigable weakness (worsening by the end of the day and improving with rest) and involvement of the ocular (drooping eyelids/ptosis) and bulbar (difficulty speaking/swallowing) muscles are pathognomonic for Myasthenia Gravis (Option A). MG is an autoimmune disorder where antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Lambert-Eaton syndrome (Option B) typically involves improving strength with repetitive movement and is often associated with malignancy. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (Option C) is a childhood-onset genetic condition causing progressive, permanent muscle wasting. Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option D) is an autoimmune disease with diverse organ involvement, but not this specific pattern of fatigable motor weakness. Diagnosis of MG is supported by positive antibody testing or the Tensilon test. Therefore, because the symptoms are strictly fatigable and bulbar in nature, Myasthenia Gravis is the definitive diagnosis. Treatment involves anticholinesterases and immunosuppression
questions.learning: The clinical hallmarks of fatigable weakness (worsening by the end of the day and improving with rest) and involvement of the ocular (drooping eyelids/ptosis) and bulbar (difficulty speaking/swallowing) muscles are pathognomonic for Myasthenia Gravis…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A 53-year-old male patient who is a known case of COPD developed breathlessness and is on mechanical ventilation. He suddenly developed hypoxia, and on examination, he has reduced/absent breath sounds on the left hemithorax with increased peak inspiratory pressure. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pneumothorax

Sudden hypoxia in a ventilated COPD patient with absent breath sounds on one side and increased peak inspiratory pressures is classic for acute pneumothorax, often tension pneumothorax.

COPD patients have fragile bullae that can rupture, especially under positive pressure ventilation.

Mechanical ventilation (positive pressure)

↓

Alveolar overdistension

↓

Alveolar rupture

↓

Air leaks into pleural space

↓

Lung collapse

↓

↓ Breath sounds + ↑ airway pressure

↓

Sudden hypoxia

Pulmonary embolism does not cause unilateral absent breath sounds or raised airway pressures.

| Finding | Likely Diagnosis

| ------- | ----------------

| ↑ Peak pressure + absent breath sounds |  Pneumothorax

| ↑ Peak pressure + wheeze | Bronchospasm

| Normal breath sounds + hypoxia | Pulmonary embolism

| Fever + crackles | Pneumonia
questions.learning: Pneumothorax Sudden hypoxia in a ventilated COPD patient with absent breath sounds on one side and increased peak inspiratory pressures is classic for acute pneumothorax, often tension pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presents with microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, and chorioretinitis. Which congenital (teratogenic) infection is most likely to have affected the mother during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of microcephaly, diffuse intracerebral calcifications, and chorioretinitis is highly characteristic of congenital toxoplasmosis, caused by maternal infection with Toxoplasma gondii. These calcifications are typically scattered throughout the brain parenchyma. Regarding the distractors, Cytomegalovirus (CMV) (Option B) also presents with intracranial calcifications and microcephaly, but its calcifications are characteristically periventricular (bordering the ventricles) rather than diffuse. Varicella (Option C) can cause microcephaly and chorioretinitis but is more commonly associated with limb hypoplasia and cutaneous scarring. Rubella (Option D) presents with a different classic triad: patent ductus arteriosus (heart defects), cataracts, and "salt and pepper" retinopathy, rather than chorioretinitis and heavy calcifications. Diagnosis of toxoplasmosis is confirmed via fetal ultrasound, PCR of amniotic fluid, or rising serological titers in the newborn. Therefore, the specific diffuse pattern of calcification and chorioretinitis points definitively to Toxoplasma
questions.learning: The classic triad of microcephaly, diffuse intracerebral calcifications, and chorioretinitis is highly characteristic of congenital toxoplasmosis, caused by maternal infection with Toxoplasma gondii.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Calculate the ECF volume in a volunteer in whom 10 gm of mannitol was injected in venous blood. At equilibrium urinary excretion of mannitol was found to be 10% and the plasma concentration of mannitol was 65 mg/100 ml.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 14L

ECF volume of the above volunteer is calculated to be 14 L.

The ECF volume can be calculated using the formula:

Where,

• V = ECF volume
• Amount injected = 10 gm
• Amount of mannitol excreted = 10% of 10 gm = 1gm
• Plasma concentration of mannitol = 65 mg/100mL = 0.65 gm/L

Calculation:

ECF Volume = (10-1)/0.65

= 13.8 L = approximately 14 L

Mannitol cannot cross cell membranes, hence, it will be distributed in ECF but not in ICF. Thus mannitol is a marker for ECF volume and therefore calculating the volume of distribution of mannitol gives the value of ECF volume.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer presents with fever, malaise, and diarrhea, with a history of close contact with livestock. Which organism is most likely responsible for this illness?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of fever, malaise, and diarrhea in a patient with significant livestock exposure (cattle, sheep, or goats) is characteristic of Q fever, a zoonosis caused by Coxiella burnetii. The bacteria are found in animal birth products, urine, and milk, and transmission occurs through inhaling aerosolized particles from animal waste or contaminated hay. Unlike many rickettsial diseases, Q fever typically lacks a rash. Rickettsia rickettsii (Option A) causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever and requires a tick bite and presents with a classic rash. Rickettsia typhi (Option B) causes murine typhus and is transmitted by fleas from rodents. Orientia tsutsugamushi (Option D) causes scrub typhus and is transmitted by chigger mites in forest/scrub areas. Thus, the specific link to livestock confirms Coxiella burnetii
questions.learning: The clinical triad of fever, malaise, and diarrhea in a patient with significant livestock exposure (cattle, sheep, or goats) is characteristic of Q fever, a zoonosis caused by Coxiella burnetii.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 39-year-old patient with HIV infection and a CD4 count of 139 cells/µL presents with altered mental status and impaired consciousness. Cerebrospinal fluid examination shows a positive finding. Which organism is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The patient’s HIV status with a low CD4 count (139 cells/µL), altered sensorium, and a positive CSF India ink preparation strongly indicates Cryptococcus neoformans. This encapsulated yeast is a leading cause of opportunistic meningitis in severely immunocompromised individuals. The India ink preparation highlights the thick polysaccharide capsule, which appears as a clear halo surrounding the budding yeast cells. Aspergillus (Option B) is a filamentous fungus that primarily causes pulmonary disease and is not typical for India ink-positive meningitis. Toxoplasma (Option C) and tuberculosis (Option D) are common HIV complications but do not produce the encapsulated yeast findings seen here. Symptoms of cryptococcal meningitis include headache, fever, memory loss, and cranial nerve paresis. Other diagnostic tools include mucicarmine staining and latex agglutination tests for capsular antigen. Treatment involves an induction phase with Liposomal Amphotericin B and Flucytosine, followed by long-term maintenance therapy with Fluconazole
questions.learning: The patient’s HIV status with a low CD4 count (139 cells/µL), altered sensorium, and a positive CSF India ink preparation strongly indicates Cryptococcus neoformans.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following vitamin deficiencies can cause laryngismus stridulus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin D

Laryngismus stridulus is primarily associated with a deficiency in vitamin D.

Laryngismus stridulus can be defined as laryngeal spasm caused by the sudden contraction of laryngeal muscles due to a reduced level of calcium. It is likely to be caused by vitamin D deficiency. Vitamin D, also known as cholecalciferol, plays a significant role in calcium and phosphate levels homeostasis. Its active form, calcitriol or  1,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol is produced by sequential hydroxylation in the liver and kidneys. It primarily increases the serum calcium and phosphate levels. Deficiency of vitamin D leads to rickets.

Causes of vitamin D deficiency  :

* Inadequate sunlight exposure.

* Poor dietary intake.

* Malabsorption disorders such as celiac disease.

* Liver or kidney disorders affecting vitamin D metabolism.

* Calcium Deficiency: Even with sufficient vitamin D, a diet low in calcium can lead to rickets.

* Phosphate Deficiency: Rarely, genetic disorders like hypophosphatemic rickets, which affect phosphate metabolism, can cause rickets.

Clinical features include bone pain and tenderness, delayed growth, skeletal deformities -bowed legs (genu varum) or knock knees (genu valgum), thickened wrists and ankles, and a protruding breastbone (pectus carinatum), dental problems muscle spasms, including those affecting the larynx, can occur due to hypocalcemia, and delay in motor milestones. There is increased risk of .

Radiological features show cupping at metaphyses, fraying, and widening of the growth plate.

Daily treatment with oral Vitamin D preparations is recommended, as daily supplementation is more physiological. The duration of treatment is at least 12 weeks. Vitamin D dosage is 2000 I.U in infants and 3000 I.U in children over one year of age. Stoss therapy was earlier used for treating Vitamin D deficiency. Here, 300,000-600,000 IU of vitamin D was administered orally or intramuscularly in 2 or 4 doses over 1 day.

Other options:

Option B: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone metabolism but is not typically associated with muscle spasms or laryngismus stridulus.
Option C: vitamin E deficiency is rare and primarily affects neurological and muscular systems, leading to symptoms like peripheral neuropathy and ataxia.
Option D: Vitamin A is important for vision, immune function, and skin health. Deficiency can lead to vision problems and increased susceptibility to infections.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As per the syndromic approach to sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and reproductive tract infections (RTIs), what is the treatment of choice of gonococcal and non-gonococcal urethritis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cefixime + Azithromycin

As per the syndromic approach to STIs/RTIs, the treatment of choice of for gonococcal and non-gonoccocal urethritis is azithromycin + cefixime.
questions.learning: Cefixime + Azithromycin As per the syndromic approach to STIs/RTIs, the treatment of choice of for gonococcal and non-gonoccocal urethritis is azithromycin + cefixime.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which intravenous fluid should be avoided when managing a hypotensive patient with a head injury?
questions.explanation: In the management of patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI), the priority is to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure while avoiding factors that worsen cerebral edema. 5% Dextrose (Option D) is essentially a hypotonic fluid once the glucose is metabolized. Hypotonic fluids allow water to shift from the intravascular space into the brain cells (cytotoxic edema), which dangerously increases intracranial pressure (ICP). Normal Saline (Option A) and Ringer's Lactate (Option C) are isotonic crystalloids and are the preferred choices for maintaining blood pressure without worsening brain swelling. 3% Saline (Option B) is hypertonic and is actually used as a therapeutic intervention to reduce ICP by drawing fluid out of the brain tissue. Therefore, dextrose-containing or hypotonic fluids must be strictly avoided in the resuscitation of head-injured patients. Maintaining an isotonic or slightly hypertonic state is crucial for neuroprotection
questions.learning: In the management of patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI), the priority is to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure while avoiding factors that worsen cerebral edema.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman presents with obstructed labor and is grossly dehydrated. Investigations reveal fetal demise. What will be the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cesarean section

The best management in the given clinical scenario is cesarean section.

Obstructive labor management involves administering intravenous fluids to correct dehydration, providing antibiotics to prevent infection, and promptly performing a cesarean section to relieve the obstruction. If the fetus is alive, an immediate cesarean section is typically performed. Management of obstructed labor never involves a wait-and-watch approach or augmenting with oxytocin.

Clinical features of obstructed labor include maternal exhaustion, dehydration, tachycardia, tachypnea, genital sepsis, postpartum hemorrhage, and shock.
On P/A examination the upper uterine segment is tender and tonically contracted. The lower uterine segment is thin and stretched. A groove/depression is felt between the upper uterine segment and the lower uterine segment. This is called a Bandls ring.

Complications of obstructed labor include rupture of the uterus and vesicovaginal fistula.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A child with loose stools for one day presented to your OPD. On examination, signs of dehydration were present and the child was given ORS. It facilitates glucose absorption through which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. SGLT1

ORS facilitates glucose absorption through SGLT 1 (Sodium-dependent glucose co-transporter - 1). In a child with diarrhea, when oral rehydration solution is given, there is coupled absorption of sodium and glucose through SGLT -1.

Glucose transport may be active or passive.

Active transport of glucose takes place through Sodium dependent glucose transporter (SGLT 1 and 2). SGLT 1 helps in glucose absorption in the small intestine and renal tubules. SGLT 2 primarily facilitates glucose absorption in the renal tubules.

Passive absorption of glucose occurs through facilitated diffusion. This is carried out by Glucose transporters (GLUT) 1 -7.
questions.learning: SGLT1 ORS facilitates glucose absorption through SGLT 1 (Sodium-dependent glucose co-transporter - 1). In a child with diarrhea, when oral rehydration solution is given, there is coupled absorption of sodium and glucose through SGLT -1.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the preferred pre-operative drug for the management of hypertension in a patient with pheochromocytoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phenoxybenzamine

Pheochromocytoma = Catecholamine storm

Tumor of adrenal medulla → excess:

• Epinephrine
• Norepinephrine

Tumor → ↑ catecholamines

↓

α1 stimulation → vasoconstriction

↓

Severe hypertension

Pheochromocytoma requires preoperative alpha blockade to prevent hypertensive crises. Phenoxybenzamine is an irreversible nonselective α-blocker that provides sustained control of catecholamine effects. It is started before surgery and followed by β-blockade if needed. Long-acting alpha blockade is the key preparation step.

| Drug | Type | Role in Pheochromocytoma

| ---- | ---- | ------------------------

| Phenoxybenzamine | Non-selective α-blocker | ✔ GOLD STANDARD

| Prazosin | α1 selective | Alternative

| Propranolol | β-blocker | Only after α-blockade

| CCBs | Vasodilators | Adjunct

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Va/Q = infinity means _________.
options: Partial pressure of O2 becomes zero
CO2 alone equilibrates with the venous blood
Partial pressure of both CO2 and O2 remain normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. No exchange of O2 & CO2

Va /Q = infinity means No exchange of O2 & CO2.

• Va represents the ventilation in alveoli.
• Q represents the blood flow through the alveolus.
• The ratio of Va and Q explains the respiratory exchange when there is an imbalance between alveolar ventilation and alveolar blood flow.
• Ventilation-perfusion ratio is considered normal if there is an equal amount of blood flow & ventilation through alveolus.
• When Va /Q ratio is infinity,

• There is adequate ventilation but no perfusion.
•  No exchange of gases through the respiratory membranes of corresponding alveoli.
• The alveolar air equilibrates the humidified inspired air
• No exchange of oxygen and carbon-di-oxide occurs.
• Partial pressures of the O2 and CO2 are 149 mmHg & 0 mm Hg respectively

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with the complaint of inability to close the eye, drooling of saliva, and deviation of the angle of the mouth. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Facial nerve

Facial nerve (CN VII) palsy causes ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial paralysis, leading to:

• Inability to close eye → orbicularis oculi paralysis
• Drooling of saliva → loss of buccinator tone
• Deviation of angle of mouth to opposite side → unopposed normal side
• Loss of forehead wrinkling (LMN lesion)

Functions of facial nerve:

• Motor: Muscles of facial expression
• Parasympathetic: Lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands
• Sensory: Taste from anterior 2/3 of tongue

Why not others:

• Trigeminal nerve (CN V): Mastication, facial sensation (not facial expression)
• Oculomotor nerve (CN III): Eye movements, ptosis
• Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX): Taste posterior 1/3, swallowing

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A married woman dies under unnatural or suspicious circumstances within three years of her marriage. Following this, her father lodges a complaint with the police. Under which legal provision will the inquiry into her death be conducted?
questions.explanation: Under Indian law, specifically Section 176 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrP(C) and the updated Section 196 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), a Magistrate-led inquiry is mandatory for the unnatural death of a married woman within seven years of her marriage. This legal provision ensures a thorough and impartial investigation by an Executive or Judicial Magistrate into potential dowry-related violence or foul play. Section 174 CrPC (or 194 BNSS) (Option A) refers to a standard Police Inquest, which is conducted for routine unnatural deaths but is insufficient for this specific high-priority category. Sections 106 and 116 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) (Options C and D) deal with substantive offenses like causing death by negligence or abetment, rather than the procedural rules for conducting an inquest. Therefore, the procedural inquiry must be initiated under the Magisterial mandate of Section 196 BNSS

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient presents with complaints of long-standing dacrocystitis. What is the treatment of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dacrocystorhinostomy

The treatment of choice for long-standing chronic dacryocystitis is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) surgery. it involves removal of the bone adjacent to the nasolacrimal sac and suturing the lacrimal sac with the lateral nasal mucosa. This allows tears to drain directly from the sac via a new low-resistance pathway into the middle meatus.

Chronic dacryocystitis is a multifactorial disease affecting the lacrimal sac.

Clinical features can be divided into 4 stages.

* Stage of chronic catarrhal dacryocystitis: inflammation of lacrimal sac and blockage of nasolacrimal duct

* Stage of lacrimal mucocele: chronic stagnation and distension of the lacrimal sac forming a swelling

* Stage of chronic suppurative dacryocystitis: purulent discharge from punctum

* Stage of chronic fibrotic sac: thickening of mucosa to form a fibrous sac

Treatment

Dacrocystorhinostomy (DCR) is the treatment of choice once local infection if present is controlled with topical antibiotics. it re-establishes the drainage

Dacrocystecomy is considered if DCR is contraindicated like in advanced age, TB or syphilitic infection of the sac
questions.learning: Dacrocystorhinostomy — The treatment of choice for long-standing chronic dacryocystitis is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) surgery. it involves removal of the bone adjacent to the nasolacrimal sac and suturing the lacrimal sac with the lateral nasal mucosa.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which receptor is primarily responsible for mediating glucose uptake in skeletal muscle?
questions.explanation: GLUT 4 is the primary glucose transporter found in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. It is uniquely characterized as the insulin-responsive transporter. Under resting conditions, GLUT 4 is sequestered in intracellular vesicles. When insulin binds to its receptor on the cell surface, or during physical exercise, these vesicles translocate to the plasma membrane, allowing for the rapid uptake of glucose from the blood into the muscle. GLUT 1 (Option A) provides basal glucose uptake in most tissues, including the blood-brain barrier. GLUT 2 (Option B) is a high-capacity, low-affinity transporter found in the liver, pancreas, and kidneys. GLUT 3 (Option C) is the primary transporter for neurons in the brain. The dysregulation of GLUT 4 translocation is a hallmark of insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes. Because exercise can stimulate GLUT 4 translocation independently of insulin, physical activity remains a cornerstone of managing blood sugar levels in diabetic patients
questions.learning: GLUT 4 is the primary glucose transporter found in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. It is uniquely characterized as the insulin-responsive transporter.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 54-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic heart disease and prosthetic valve replacement six months ago presents with fever, fatigue, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. Examination reveals a new heart murmur and splinter hemorrhages on the nail beds, suggestive of infective endocarditis. Considering her prosthetic valve and current presentation, which organism is most likely responsible for her infective endocarditis?
questions.explanation: Infective endocarditis (IE) following prosthetic valve replacement is categorized by timing. "Early" prosthetic valve endocarditis occurs within one year of surgery and is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis, a coagulase-negative staphylococcus (CoNS) that is part of the normal skin flora. This organism is highly adept at forming biofilms on foreign materials like prosthetic valves. While Option D (Coagulase-negative Staphylococci) is technically the broader group, standard medical examinations usually look for the specific species Staphylococcus epidermidis in this clinical context. Streptococcus viridans (Option B) is the most common cause of subacute IE on native, damaged valves, usually following dental procedures. Enterococcus faecalis (Option C) often causes endocarditis following gastrointestinal or genitourinary manipulations. Because this patient’s symptoms appeared within the 6-12 month post-operative window, S. epidermidis—introduced during the surgical procedure or through postoperative seeding—is the most statistically probable and classic answer for this board-style question
questions.learning: Infective endocarditis (IE) following prosthetic valve replacement is categorized by timing. "Early" prosthetic valve endocarditis occurs within one year of surgery and is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis, a coagulase-negative…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient presenting with severe pain during erection and progressive curvature of the penis over the past six months?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of progressive penile curvature and pain during erection are pathognomonic for Peyronie's Disease (Option A) . This condition is caused by the formation of fibrous plaques (scar tissue) within the tunica albuginea of the penis. The plaques are not elastic, so when the penis fills with blood during an erection, the affected side cannot expand, causing it to bend or curve toward the plaque. Priapism (Option B) is a prolonged, painful erection unrelated to sexual stimulation and is a medical emergency. Marion's disease (Option C) refers to congenital bladder neck obstruction. Erectile Dysfunction (Option D) is the inability to achieve or maintain an erection, whereas patients with Peyronie’s can usually achieve an erection, but it is deformed and painful. Diagnosis is clinical, sometimes supplemented by ultrasound to visualize the calcified plaques. Treatment options include oral medications, intralesional injections, or surgical straightening procedures in severe cases
questions.learning: The symptoms of progressive penile curvature and pain during erection are pathognomonic for Peyronie's Disease (Option A) . This condition is caused by the formation of fibrous plaques (scar tissue) within the tunica albuginea of the penis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient met with road traffic accident and complained of severe back ache. The X-ray is shown below. What fracture does the patient have?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chance fracture

The X-ray shows a vertebral fracture with a horizontal fracture line passing through the body of the vertebra. This indicates Chance fracture.

Chance fracture is also known as seat-belt injury or the jack-knife injury. This injury is typically located in the upper lumbar spine in people involved in motor vehicle collisions while wearing a lap seat belt without a shoulder harness. The sudden deceleration causes flexion and posterior distraction of the spine. This causes the mid-lumbar spine to bend like a jack-knife around an axis anterior to the vertebral column.

There is a tear in the vertebra that passes transversely through the bones (bony Chance fracture), or the ligamentous structures (soft Chance fracture), or both. There is little or no crushing of the vertebral body. However, it is an unstable injury as the posterior and middle columns are distracted. Neurological damage is uncommon. Associated intra-abdominal injuries are seen in 50% of these injuries.

X-rays may show a horizontal fracture with the split running through the vertebra. It may involve the spinous process, the transverse processes, pedicles and the vertebral body. There may be opening up of the disc space posteriorly.

Most Chance fractures can be managed conservatively with bed rest and bracing. If posterior fixation is done, it will allow early mobilization. Ligamentous Chance fractures require posterior instrumented fusion.

Other options:

Option B: Burst fracture results from severe axial compression that explodes the vertebral body. The lateral view CT image showing the L4 vertebra burst fracture is given below.

Option C: Spinal compression fractures occur as a result of injury, common fall onto the buttock or pressure from normal activities, to the weakened vertebrae due to osteoporosis. Compression causes a short oblique fracture. The image showing the L4 vertebra compression fracture is given below:

Option D: Fracture of the spinous process of C7(Clay Shoveller's Fracture) is an example of an avulsion injury which may occur with severe voluntary contraction of the muscles at the back of the neck.
questions.learning: Chance fracture — The X-ray shows a vertebral fracture with a horizontal fracture line passing through the body of the vertebra. Chance fracture is also known as seat-belt injury or the jack-knife injury.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the primary mechanism behind tissue damage in long-standing diabetes?
questions.explanation: Chronic hyperglycemia is the fundamental mechanism driving tissue damage in long-standing diabetes. Persistent high blood glucose levels lead to several destructive pathways, including the formation of Advanced Glycation End Products (AGEs), which cause inflammation and vascular injury. While sorbitol accumulation (Option B) contributes specifically to cataracts and neuropathy through the polyol pathway, it is just one of many mechanisms triggered by hyperglycemia. Insulin resistance (Option A) and decreased insulin secretion (Option D) are the underlying causes of the diabetic state, but the resulting hyperglycemia is what actually mediates chronic complications like retinopathy, nephropathy, and atherosclerosis. Other hyperglycemia-induced pathways include the activation of Protein Kinase C (PKC) and the hexosamine pathway, both of which increase vascular permeability and oxidative stress. Thus, managing blood glucose is central to preventing systemic diabetic complications

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child is brought to the pediatrician with short stature. On evaluation, growth hormone levels are found to be high and Insulin-like growth factor(IGF-1) levels are low. Which among the following could be the abnormality here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. GH receptor anomaly

The presence of high growth hormone levels and low Insulin-like growth factor(IGF-1) levels point towards Laron syndrome/dwarfism. It is caused by end-organ resistance to growth hormone(GH insensitivity) due to the mutation of the growth hormone receptor.

Here, growth hormones are produced, but not able to act on the target tissues as growth hormone receptors in the target tissue are not responding to growth hormones. So, the resting and stimulated growth hormone levels are high and insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) levels are low.

It is an autosomal-recessive disorder with clinical features that are the same as those seen in pituitary dwarfism. The primary clinical symptom associated with this condition is short stature.

Treatment is by subcutaneous injections of insulin-like growth factor 1 (a growth-promoting hormone), often called IGF-1.
questions.learning: GH receptor anomaly — The presence of high growth hormone levels and low Insulin-like growth factor(IGF-1) levels point towards Laron syndrome/dwarfism.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 7-year-old child is brought to the clinic with complaints of fatigue and poor concentration. The mother reports that the child has been eating non-food items such as soil and paint chips for the past few months. A peripheral blood smear image shows microcytic, hypochromatic red blood cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Iron deficiency anemia

Both iron deficiency anaemia and lead poisoning produce microcytic hypochromic anaemia, and this stem contains pull toward each:

| Stem element | Points to

| ------------ | ---------

| Fatigue, poor concentration | Both (non-discriminating)

| Eating soil (geophagia) | IDA — pica is a classic IDA feature

| Eating paint chips | Lead poisoning — the single most classic lead exposure vector in a child

| Microcytic, hypochromic RBCs | Both (non-discriminating)

| Age 7, few months' duration | Both

There's a second layer that makes this genuinely hard to key:

• Pica causes lead ingestion (child eats paint chips → lead poisoning)
• Iron deficiency causes pica (→ child eats paint chips)
• Iron deficiency increases lead absorption (both use DMT1 in the duodenum; low iron upregulates DMT1 → more lead uptake)
• Lead inhibits haem synthesis → worsens the anaemia

The smear is the only thing that can break the tie — and only if it shows one specific finding:

| Smear finding | Verdict

| ------------- | -------

| Coarse basophilic stippling | Lead poisoning

| Microcytosis, hypochromia, anisopoikilocytosis, pencil cells, ↑ RDW | IDA ✅
questions.learning: Iron deficiency anemia Both iron deficiency anaemia and lead poisoning produce microcytic hypochromic anaemia, and this stem contains pull toward each: | Stem element | Points to | ------------ | --------- | Fatigue, poor concentration | Both…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding the given image?
options: It is associated with facial angiofibroma
They are diagnostic of a neurocutaneous syndrome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is associated with facial angiofibroma

The given image shows discrete tan-colored nodules over the iris called Lisch nodules (pigmented melanocytic hamartomas). They are seen in neurofibromatosis-1 (NF-1). Facial angiofibroma (adenoma sebaceum) is a feature of tuberous sclerosis (TS) and not neurofibromatosis.

The image below shows facial angiofibroma seen in tuberous sclerosis (Bourneville disease).

Lisch nodules are specifically associated with NF-1 and are usually multiple and bilateral. They are best visualized with a slit lamp examination and don’t cause any visual disturbances.

Other important ocular manifestations in NF-1 include eyelid plexiform neurofibroma, which causes S-shaped deformity of the upper lid, with a 'bag of worms' like texture, optic nerve glioma, and spheno-orbital encephalocele due to dysplasia of greater wing of the sphenoid.

NF-1 (von Recklinghausen's disease) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a loss-of-function mutation of the NF-1 gene located on chromosome 17q11.2. NF-1 produces neurofibromin, which acts as a tumor suppressor and a negative regulator of RAS-MAP kinase signaling.

Clinical features of NF-1 include café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules,  neurofibromas, and optic gliomas.
NF-1 is more common than NF2 and typically diagnosed in childhood. NF-2 is rarer but often presents with bilateral acoustic neuroma, juvenile cataract and schwannoma.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A pregnant woman presents with urinary tract infection (UTI). Which of the following acts as a urinary antiseptic?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nitrofurantoin

A urinary antiseptic is a drug that achieves antibacterial concentrations only in urine, with negligible systemic (plasma/tissue) levels — hence it treats lower UTI/cystitis but never pyelonephritis or systemic infection.

Nitrofurantoin is the prototype: it is rapidly absorbed, concentrated by the kidney, and excreted into urine where it is reduced by bacterial nitroreductases into reactive intermediates that damage bacterial ribosomes, DNA and metabolic enzymes — a multi-target action, which explains its remarkably low resistance rate. It is safe in the first and second trimesters and is a preferred agent for asymptomatic bacteriuria/cystitis in pregnancy.

Other options:

• B. Ciprofloxacin → fluoroquinolone; contraindicated in pregnancy (cartilage/arthropathy risk); it is a systemic antibiotic, not an antiseptic.
• C. Doxycycline → contraindicated in pregnancy — teeth staining, enamel hypoplasia, bone growth inhibition, maternal hepatotoxicity.
• D. Cotrimoxazole → avoid in 1st trimester (folate antagonism → neural tube defects) and near term (kernicterus).

Pearl:

• Urinary antiseptics = Nitrofurantoin, Methenamine, Nalidixic acid.
• Avoid nitrofurantoin at term (38 wk onwards) → risk of neonatal hemolysis (G6PD deficiency).
questions.learning: Nitrofurantoin — A urinary antiseptic is a drug that achieves antibacterial concentrations only in urine, with negligible systemic (plasma/tissue) levels — hence it treats lower UTI/cystitis but never pyelonephritis or systemic infection.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with fatigue, pallor, and weakness. Laboratory tests show low hemoglobin levels with a normal reticulocyte count. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these findings?
questions.explanation: Anemia (low Hb) with a normal or low reticulocyte count indicates an "inadequate" response by the bone marrow; the marrow is failing to produce enough new red cells to compensate for the anemia. In Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA), there is a selective and severe decrease in erythroid precursors in the bone marrow, leading to anemia with a characteristically low reticulocyte count. Aplastic Anemia (Option A) also shows low reticulocytes, but it involves all three cell lines (pancytopenia), not just red cells. Iron Deficiency Anemia (Option C) is usually microcystic and would also show a low reticulocyte count until iron is replaced, but PRCA is a more specific "marrow failure" diagnosis for this clinical description. Hemolytic Anemia (Option D) would show a high reticulocyte count, as the marrow is healthy and frantically trying to replace the cells being destroyed in the periphery. PRCA is famously associated with thymomas and parvovirus B19 infection (especially in patients with sickle cell disease)
questions.learning: Anemia (low Hb) with a normal or low reticulocyte count indicates an "inadequate" response by the bone marrow; the marrow is failing to produce enough new red cells to compensate for the anemia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Voltage gated calcium channel present on T-tubule is?
questions.explanation: In skeletal muscle, the excitation-contraction coupling process relies on the transmission of action potentials down the T-tubules. The specific voltage-gated L-type calcium channel located on the T-tubule membrane is the Dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR). When an action potential reaches the DHPR, it undergoes a conformational change that mechanically triggers the opening of the Ryanodine receptor (RyR) (Option D), which is the calcium-release channel located on the adjacent terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The SERCA pump (Option A) is an ATP-dependent pump responsible for sequestering calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum to initiate relaxation. The troponin-myosin complex (Option B) represents the contractile proteins where calcium eventually binds to initiate cross-bridge cycling. Understanding the DHPR-RyR interaction is essential for comprehending muscle physiology and pathologies such as malignant hyperthermia, where defective RyR channels lead to uncontrolled calcium release and hypermetabolic crises when exposed to certain anesthetic agents
questions.learning: In skeletal muscle, the excitation-contraction coupling process relies on the transmission of action potentials down the T-tubules. The specific voltage-gated L-type calcium channel located on the T-tubule membrane is the Dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant patient, with a history of classical cesarean section in view of fetal growth retardation in the previous pregnancy, presents to you. She is currently at 35 weeks of gestation with breech presentation. What is the next step in management?
options: Advice USG and visit after 2 weeks
Internal podalic version followed by vaginal delivery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cesarean section at 37 weeks

The next step in the management of this pregnancy with breech presentation and a history of previous classical cesarean delivery is a cesarean section at 37 weeks.

A classical casarean section is done by a longitudinal uterine incision. A previous classical cesarean section is considered a high-risk factor for failure of VBAC (vaginal birth after previous cesarean). Hence, it is contraindicated. There is increased risk of uterine rupture (2-9%) in such cases. In some women, classical cesarean scar can even rupture several weeks before term.

Other contraindications for VBAC include:

• ≥2 previous lower segment cesarean section
• Contracted pelvis or cephalo-pelvic disproportion
• Other obstetric or medical complications
• Prior uterine rupture

If the fetal buttocks or legs enters the pelvis before the head, the presentation is known as breech. Vaginal delivery of a singleton breech fetus can be considered. It can be spontaneous breech delivery, partial breech extraction, or total breech extraction. However, cesarean delivery is considered in the presence of any associated obstetric (previous cesarean delivery) of medical complications.

Other options:

Option B: An ultrasound will not change the decision regarding mode of delivery.

Option C: Internal podalic version results in a breech presentation. It is done in case of transverse lie of second baby in twin pregnancy. It is not indicated in singleton pregnancy.

Option D: External cephalic version is a manipulation through the abdominal wall that results in cephalic presentation. It is usally done at 37 weeks as it can revert back to breech position if carried out before. However, it is contraindicated when vaginal delivery is not an option and in cases of previous cesarean delivery such as in this case.
questions.learning: Cesarean section at 37 weeks — The next step in the management of this pregnancy with breech presentation and a history of previous classical cesarean delivery is a cesarean section at 37 weeks.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after sustaining a fall onto an outstretched hand. The following cast was applied to the patient. What fracture did the patient suffer from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scaphoid fracture

The cast applied to a patient in the glass-holding position is known as the scaphoid cast/glass-holding cast. It is used to treat scaphoid fractures.

To apply a scaphoid cast, the wrist is held in slight dorsiflexion and the thumb is in abduction and slight flexion, as if a glass is being held between the index finger and thumb. It extends from just below the elbow to just proximal to the metacarpal necks of the digits. On the thumb, the cast extends to just proximal to the interphalangeal joint.

Scaphoid fracture presents with pain and swelling over the radial aspect of the wrist. A fall on an outstretched hand could result in such a fracture. The fracture can be confirmed (when an x-ray does not show a fracture) if there is pain elicited in the anatomical snuff box on the radial border of the wrist.

An oblique x-ray of the wrist should be able to show a scaphoid fracture.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not helpful for differentiating between necrosis and apoptosis?
options: Internal organelle disintegration with lipid change
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Altered cell shape

Both necrosis and apoptosis show altered cell shape (Necrosis-cell enlarges; apoptosis-cell shrinks), making it non-discriminatory.

| Option | Necrosis | Apoptosis | Discriminates?

| ------ | -------- | --------- | --------------

| A. Intact cell organelle | Organelles disintegrate | Organelles preserved (esp. early) | Yes → points to apoptosis

| B. Altered cell shape | Cell swelling (oncosis) | Cell shrinkage + apoptotic bodies | No — shape changes in both

| C. Caspase-mediated degradation | Lysosomal hydrolases (auto-/heterolysis) | Caspases + endonucleases | Yes → points to apoptosis

| D. Internal organelle disintegration with lipid change | Yes — myelin figures | No | Yes → points to necrosis

Why B is the answer: Both processes distort cell morphology — necrosis via swelling, apoptosis via shrinkage. The mere presence of an altered shape tells you a cell is dying but not by which mechanism, so it has no discriminatory value.

• Mnemonic — Apoptosis = "A SHRINK": ATP-dependent, Shrinkage, Hyperchromatic (chromatin condensation), Regulated (caspases), Intact membrane, No inflammation, Karyorrhexis into apoptotic bodies.
• Nucleus: pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis is the necrosis sequence; apoptosis stops at fragmentation into membrane-bound bodies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following antidiabetic drugs is recommended for weight loss in obese patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Liraglutide

Liraglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, promotes weight loss by increasing satiety, delaying gastric emptying, and reducing appetite. It is recommended for obese patients with type 2 diabetes, particularly those who would benefit from both glycemic control and weight reduction.

Why not the other options?

• A. Glimepiride: Sulfonylurea; causes weight gain due to increased insulin secretion.
• C. Sitagliptin: DPP-4 inhibitor; generally weight neutral.
• D. Insulin: Commonly associated with weight gain.
