questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Research is being conducted to find the association between aniline dye exposure and bladder cancer in workers who have worked in the industry for >20 years. Two groups were formed: one directly involved with dye handling and the other group consisting of office clerks not directly exposed to the dye. Years of occupation were noted from records. What type of study is being performed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retrospective cohort study

The study given here is a retrospective cohort study.

A retrospective cohort study is when both the exposure and outcome have occurred before the investigations and study is undertaken.

In this scenario, the workers in the industry were divided into two groups, viz those who are directly exposed and the clerical staff who are not directly exposed to the suspected carcinogen. The incidence of carcinogenesis among these two groups is studied going backward tracking their records.

An increased risk of bladder cancer was observed among long-term workers directly exposed to the chemical in aniline dye industries when compared with the other study group. It is also called a historical cohort study, a prospective study in retrospect, or a non-concurrent prospective study. The cohort is identified from past records and is assessed to date for the outcome. The same cohort is followed up prospectively in the future for further assessment of the outcome.

Other options:

Option B - Prospective cohort study: This type of study involves following a group of participants over time and monitoring their exposure to a risk factor and the development of an outcome. In this case, the outcome (bladder cancer) and exposure (aniline dye) have already occurred, making this a retrospective cohort study.

Option C - Case-control study: A case-control study involves comparing individuals with a specific outcome (cases) to those without the outcome (controls) and assessing their exposure history. This study design is not being used in the given scenario, as the workers are divided into two groups based on their exposure status and followed for the development of bladder cancer.

Option D - Intervention and response: This option is not a type of epidemiological study design. It could refer to an intervention study, in which an intervention is applied to a group of participants, and the response is measured. However, this is not applicable to the current scenario.
questions.learning: Retrospective cohort study — The study given here is a retrospective cohort study. A retrospective cohort study is when both the exposure and outcome have occurred before the investigations and study is undertaken.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A young female patient presents with ptosis which reportedly worsens in the evening and improves in the morning. What is the most probable cause?
options: Decreased calcium influx at presynaptic membrane
Increased sodium influx at postsynaptic membrane
Antibody against Ach receptor at postsynaptic membrane
Increased endplate potential at postsynaptic membrane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Antibody against Ach receptor at postsynaptic membrane

The most probable cause in the given case is myasthenia gravis, which is due to antibodies against the Ach receptor at the postsynaptic membrane.

Intermittent ptosis is considered one of the earliest signs of myasthenia gravis. Pyridostigmine is the preferred treatment for symptomatic patients at this stage of the disease.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that is characterised by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. It is due to the autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the postsynaptic membrane. This consequentially leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Failure of transmission results in muscle weakness. Hence, the goal is to increase the duration of action of acetylcholine by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase. The most commonly used anticholinesterase drug is pyridostigmine.

Females are more commonly affected than males. It occurs in individuals of all ages, but the highest incidence is seen in women during their twenties and thirties, and in men during their fifties and sixties.

Clinical features of myasthenia gravis:

* Muscle weakness and fatiguability increase with repeated use or late in the day and may improve following rest or sleep. Limb weakness is proximal and asymmetrical

* Cranial muscles, particularly the lids and extraocular muscles, are involved early in the course – diplopia, ptosis.

* Facial weakness – snarling expression when smiling

* Weakness in chewing

* Speech with nasal timbre due to the weakness of the palate and tongue

* Difficulty in swallowing

* Deep tendon reflexes are intact

* Myasthenic crisis – acute exacerbation of muscle weakness, especially intercostal and diaphragmatic muscles, resulting in ventilatory failure. It is most commonly due to infection and anticholinesterase medication overuse.

Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma and other autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, neuromyelitis optica, Systemic lupus erythematosus, etc.

Diagnosis:

* Ice-pack test – application of an ice pack over the eyes improves ptosis (decreases the activity of acetylcholinesterase; this increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and increases transmission).

* Antibodies associated with myasthenia gravis: Anti-AChR antibodies, Anti-MuSK antibodies, Anti-LRP4 antibodies

* A repetitive nerve stimulation test shows a decremental response.

* Edrophonium chloride or Tensilon test – improvement of symptoms occurs on injecting edrophonium. Edrophonium is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. This increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and improves transmission.

Treatment:

* Symptomatic treatment: Anticholinesterase agents – Pyridostigmine is the initial therapy of choice.

* Chronic immunomodulating therapy: Glucocorticoids (prednisone) and immunosuppressive drugs (azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine) are implemented in patients significantly symptomatic on pyridostigmine.

* Rapid immunomodulating treatment: IVIG and therapeutic plasma exchange —Used to tide over severe illness (myasthenic crisis) and as 'bridge' therapy before surgery or starting chronic immunomodulating treatment.

* Surgical approach: Thymectomy
questions.learning: Antibody against Ach receptor at postsynaptic membrane The most probable cause in the given case is myasthenia gravis, which is due to antibodies against the Ach receptor at the postsynaptic membrane.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 2-year-old child suddenly becomes unresponsive following a peanut ingestion. What is the next immediate step in management?
options: Intubate immediately with an endotracheal tube
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Start chest compressions

A suddenly unresponsive child with suspected FBAO is treated as cardiac arrest. When a child becomes unresponsive, you immediately start the CPR sequence, beginning with chest compressions, not back blows or abdominal thrusts. Airway maneuvers are done only during CPR cycles.
questions.learning: Start chest compressions — A suddenly unresponsive child with suspected FBAO is treated as cardiac arrest. When a child becomes unresponsive, you immediately start the CPR sequence, beginning with chest compressions, not back blows or abdominal thrusts.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 20 year old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. On examination breasts were found to be poorly developed, vagina was present. Ultrasound revealed normal uterus but gonads weren’t detected. Further evaluation done showed 46XY karyotype. The most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Swyer's syndrome

The given clinical scenario of a 46 XY individual with female internal & external genitalia and poorly developed breasts, presenting with primary amenorrhea points towards the diagnosis of sweyer’s syndrome.

Turner syndrome (option B) is a disorder of 45 XO individuals with short stature. The gonads in these individuals are streak ovaries.

Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (option A) is a disorder of 46 XY individuals with complete insensitivity to testosterone. These individuals have female external genitalia with an absent uterus. Secondary sexual characteristics like the development of breasts are adequate. However,pubic and axillary hairs are scanty.

True hermaphrodite (option C) can be a 46 XX or 46 XY individual with both ovaries and testis. These individuals have both male and female internal genitalia with ambiguous external genitalia.

Sweyer’s syndrome is a type of male pseudohermaphroditism where there is an inactivation of the SRY gene that leads to formation of dysgenetic testis.

Thus,in the absence of hormones; AMH & testosterone the mullerian duct grows and the wolffian duct regresses forming female internal genitalia such as uterus (infantile type).

These patients also lack the DHT hormone and hence present with poorly developed breasts ( tanner staging 1 or 2), scanty pubic,axillary hair and female external genitalia. These individuals are of normal stature with increased LH & FSH.

Management includes gonadectomy as soon as diagnosed and estrogen + progesterone for breast development.

AMH: Anti mullerian hormone
DHT: dihydro testosterone
questions.learning: Swyer's syndrome — The given clinical scenario of a 46 XY individual with female internal & external genitalia and poorly developed breasts, presenting with primary amenorrhea points towards the diagnosis of sweyer’s syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with grade 4 haemorrhoids underwent surgery. Identify the instruments used during the procedure from the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Haemorrhoids banding kit

The instruments depicted above are the components of a hemorrhoid banding kit.

Hemorrhoids are cushions of submucosal tissue containing venules, arterioles, and smooth muscle fibers that are located in the anal canal. They can be classified according to their location into 2 types:

* Internal hemorrhoids

* External hemorrhoids

External hemorrhoids are distal to the dentate line and are covered with anoderm; these may engorge causing pain. Thrombosis of these external hemorrhoids causes severe pain. Internal hemorrhoids are characterized by bright red, painless bleeding, or prolapse.

Internal hemorrhoids are stratified into four grades as follows:

GRADE

SYMPTOMS AND SIGNS

First degree

Bleeding; no prolapse

Second degree

Prolapse with spontaneous reduction

Third degree

Prolapse requiring manual reduction

Fourth degree

Prolapsed, cannot be reduced

Management of external hemorrhoids:

External hemorrhoids do not require treatment unless they become thrombosed. Acutely thrombosed external hemorrhoids cause intense pain and perianal mass during the first 24 to 72 hours. Patients who present within 72 hours of thrombosis are treated with elliptical excision performed under local anesthesia.

If the patient presents to the hospital after 72 hours, then it is treated conservatively with analgesics and a sitz bath. Once the symptoms come down, definitive surgery is performed.

Management of internal hemorrhoids:

Bleeding from grade 1 and grade 2 hemorrhoids often improves with the addition of dietary fiber, stool softeners, increased fluid intake, and avoidance of straining.

Grade 1, grade 2, and some grade 3 hemorrhoids with only an internal component can be treated with simple procedures like rubber band ligation, sclerotherapy, infrared and laser coagulation, and cryotherapy.

Rubber band ligation involves pulling mucosa located 1 to 2 cm proximal to the dentate line into a rubber band applier. The rubber band strangulates the underlying tissue, causing scarring and sloughing off of the mass in a few days.

Sclerotherapy involves injecting 1 to 3 mL of a sclerosing solution (phenol in olive oil, sodium morrhuate, or quinine urea) into the submucosa of internal hemorrhoids.

Surgery is indicated in:

* Internal grade 3 or grade 4 hemorrhoids

* Hemorrhoids with a significant external component

* Early-grade hemorrhoids not responding to simple procedures

Surgical procedures used in the removal of internal hemorrhoids are:

1) Doppler-guided hemorrhoidal artery ligation

2) Open hemorrhoidectomy- the artery forceps are applied to the skin-covered external components of the hemorrhoid and traction is given to reveal the internal components. Dissection of the lateral pedicle is performed and finally, the pedicles are transfixed. Mucocutaneous bridges are left intact in this technique. The image below shows the procedure.

3) Closed (Ferguson) hemorrhoidectomy- the hemorrhoid is excised with the overlying mucosa. The hemorrhoid is dissected from the underlying sphincter and the mucus defect is then closed. The image below describes the procedure.

4) Stapled hemorrhoidopexy (Longo operation)- the hemorrhoids are pulled up and a purse-string suture is placed a few centimeters above the dentate line. Then, a circumferential rectal mucosectomy is performed using a circular stapler. This technique is associated with higher chances of recurrence, however, it is quick to perform, less painful, and less traumatic. The image below shows stapled hemorrhoidopexy.
questions.learning: Haemorrhoids banding kit — The instruments depicted above are the components of a hemorrhoid banding kit. Hemorrhoids are cushions of submucosal tissue containing venules, arterioles, and smooth muscle fibers that are located in the anal canal.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient met with a road traffic accident and developed a cervical spine injury. The fracture fragment had pierced the lateral aspect of the dorsal column tract. Which of the following findings is seen in this patient?
options: Absence of ipsilateral lower limb proprioception
Absence of fine motor movement of fingers
Absence of contralateral lower limb proprioception
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Absence of ipsilateral arm proprioception

The above clinical scenario of transection of the spinal cord in the lateral aspect of the dorsal column would affect the fasciculus cuneatus. This lesion would result in absence of ipsilateral proprioception of the arm.

The fibers in the dorsal column are organized in such a way that the sacral segments are positioned most medially and those from the cervical segments are positioned most laterally.

These are called

• Fasciculus gracilis - carrying sensations from the ipsilateral lower limb
• Fasciculus cuneatus - carrying sensations from the ipsilateral upper limb.

This patient with an injury to the lateral part of the cervical cord's dorsal column tract will have damaged fasciculus cuneatus. This would result in loss of touch, vibration, and proprioception in the arm of the same side of the lesion.

The extent of neurological deficits resulting from a spinal cord injury depends on the level of the injury and the severity of the damage. Injuries may be classified as complete or incomplete, depending on whether there is a total or partial loss of sensory and motor function below the level of injury. The key to solving this question lies in recognizing that the question mentions that the damage is to the lateral aspect of the dorsal column tract.

Other options:

Option A: Absence of ipsilateral lower limb proprioception - This would be seen if the fasciculus gracilis was affected, which is responsible for carrying sensations from the ipsilateral lower limb. However, in this case, the injury is to the lateral part of the dorsal column, affecting the fasciculus cuneatus.

Option B: Absence of fine motor movement of fingers - This would be a result of damage to the corticospinal tract, which carries motor information. The question is specifically focused on the dorsal column tract, which is responsible for carrying sensory information.

Option D: Absence of contralateral lower limb proprioception - Proprioception is carried by the dorsal column pathway, and it is affected ipsilaterally. Damage to the lateral part of the dorsal column would not result in contralateral loss of proprioception.
questions.learning: Absence of ipsilateral arm proprioception — The above clinical scenario of transection of the spinal cord in the lateral aspect of the dorsal column would affect the fasciculus cuneatus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department (OPD) with wheezing and shortness of breath. On examination she is found to have low forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and low FEV1 : FVC ratio. Patients with which of the following other conditions present similarly?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Asthma

The condition that shares a similar presentation with wheezing, shortness of breath, and low FEV1 is Asthma. Asthma is characterized by reversible airflow obstruction and commonly presents with wheezing, making it the most appropriate option among the choices provided.

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by variable airflow obstruction, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and respiratory symptoms such as wheezing, shortness of breath, cough, and chest tightness. Low FEV1 is commonly observed during asthma exacerbations due to airflow limitation and bronchoconstriction. Wheezing is a classic symptom of asthma, and reduced FEV1 reflects airflow obstruction.

Low FEV1 and FVC with a low FEV1/FVC ratio are characteristics for obstructive lung disease (OLD).

Low FEV1 and FVC with a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio are characteristics for restrictive lung disease (RLD).

* Obstructive lung diseases (OLD)

* Asthma

* COPD

* Bronchiectasis

* Bronchiolitis

* Restrictive lung diseases (RLD)

* Intrinsic

* Interstitial lung disease

* Extrinsic

* Myasthenia gravis

* Kyphoscoliosis

* Pleural effusion

Other options:

A: Silicosis is a type of pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of silica dust. It typically presents with symptoms such as cough, shortness of breath, and chest pain. However, wheezing and low FEV1 are not typical features of silicosis. Instead, silicosis is characterized by restrictive lung function abnormalities on pulmonary function tests.

B: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive fibrotic lung disease characterized by scarring of the lung tissue. Common symptoms include progressive dyspnea (shortness of breath) and cough. While IPF can lead to reduced lung function and impaired gas exchange, wheezing is not a typical feature. Moreover, the pattern of lung function abnormalities in IPF typically demonstrates a restrictive pattern rather than airflow obstruction seen in asthma.

D: Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD) refers to a group of lung disorders characterized by inflammation and scarring (fibrosis) of the interstitium, the tissue that supports the air sacs of the lungs. ILD can present with symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, and crackles on auscultation. While ILD can lead to reduced lung volumes and impaired gas exchange, wheezing is not a typical feature. Additionally, ILD usually demonstrates a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function tests.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with drooping of the left eyelid and diplopia. On examination, the pupil of the affected eye is found to be dilated. Based on these clinical findings, which cranial nerve is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of ptosis (drooping eyelid), a "down and out" position of the eye, and a dilated pupil is diagnostic of a complete Oculomotor Nerve (CN III) palsy. The oculomotor nerve supplies the levator palpebrae superioris, medial rectus, superior rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique muscles. When these are paralyzed, the eye is pulled outward by the intact lateral rectus (CN VI) and downward by the superior oblique (CN IV). Dilation of the pupil is a critical "red flag" sign indicating compression of the parasympathetic fibers on the nerve surface. Option A (Optic nerve) palsy causes vision loss, not movement issues. Option B (Trochlear) palsy causes vertical diplopia. Option D (Abducens) palsy causes the eye to turn inward. A "surgical" CN III palsy with pupil involvement is a neurosurgical emergency, as it often results from an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery
questions.learning: The clinical triad of ptosis (drooping eyelid), a "down and out" position of the eye, and a dilated pupil is diagnostic of a complete Oculomotor Nerve (CN III) palsy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT typically associated with fibroids?
questions.explanation: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign smooth muscle tumors. The most common symptoms include a palpable pelvic mass (Option A), menstrual irregularities (Option D)—specifically heavy bleeding (menorrhagia) and prolonged periods—and infertility (Option C) due to cavity distortion . Amenorrhea (the absence of periods) (Option B) is not a feature of fibroids. In fact, fibroids are far more likely to cause excessive bleeding rather than no bleeding at all. Amenorrhea should prompt a clinician to investigate for pregnancy, PCOS, or hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis disorders. Fibroids grow in response to estrogen, so they typically regress after menopause. If a woman with known fibroids develops amenorrhea, it is usually due to a concurrent condition or the natural onset of menopause rather than the fibroids themselves. Therefore, amenorrhea is the correct "not" answer for typical fibroid presentations

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Cleft lip results from failure of fusion of ___
options: Lateral nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
Lateral nasal prominence and mandibular prominence
Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
Medial nasal prominence and mandibular prominence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence

Cleft lip is due to failure of fusion between the medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence.

Various defects of fusion of prominences in the face region are as follows:

* Cleft lip is due to the failure of the fusion of maxillary prominence with medial nasal prominence. It can be unilateral or bilateral. It can vary in severity from a small notch in the upper lip to a double cleft extending into both the nostrils. There is also associated underdevelopment of the part of the maxilla that bears the incisors.

* Median (midline) cleft lip is a rare defect occurring due to failure of fusion of the two medial nasal prominences in the midline.

* Oblique facial cleft is caused by the failure of the maxillary prominence to fuse with the lateral nasal prominence along the line of the nasolacrimal groove. The nasolacrimal duct is exposed to the surface in these cases.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Highest birth rate is seen in which stage of the demographic cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stage I

The highest birth rate is seen in stage I of the demographic cycle.

Demographic cycle of a country represents a population’s shift from high mortality and high fertility to low mortality and low fertility.

Pearl PF0983: Demographic Process and Cycle

* Demographic process

* Fertility

* Mortality

* Marriage

* Migration

* Social Mobility

* Demographic cycle

* Stage 1 : High stationary

* High birth rate and high death rate render the population stationary.

* Narrow demographic gap.

* Stage 2 : Early expanding

* Death rate declines and birth rate remains unchanged

* Demographic gap starts increasing and then becomes maximum

* Stage 3 : Late expanding

* Death rate decline further and birth rate falls

* India is in this stage, currently

* Demographic gap starts declining

* Stage 4 : Low stationary

* Low birth rate and low death rate renders the population stationary

* Narrow demographic gap

* Stage 5 : Declining

* Population begins to decline as birth rate is lower than death rate

* Demographic gap is negative
questions.learning: Stage I — The highest birth rate is seen in stage I of the demographic cycle. Demographic cycle of a country represents a population’s shift from high mortality and high fertility to low mortality and low fertility.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the gun that caused the wound and the range of the shot.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pistol, near shot

The given image showing a gunshot entry wound with powder burn around the wound is likely due to a near-shot injury by a pistol.

A near-shot injury is one when the range of flame is within 60 cm.

The features of a near-shot wound are a circular entry wound with the size same as that of the bullet. The edges are lacerated, inverted, and surrounded by a narrow zone of abrasion. There are no signs of burning or singeing. Powder tattooing around the entry wounds is another important feature.

Other options:

Option A: In an intermediate range which is up to 7 feet, the edge of the wound is abraded and the appearance is referred to as a rat hole. There is no burning and the tattooing is appreciable till 3-4 feet and then starts disappearing.

Option B: In shotgun injuries due to a close-range i.e between contact and 3 feet, the entry wound is circular or elliptical with features of the scorching, singing, and less dense tattooing.

Option D: In a close shot pistol injury,  the range of flame is within 5-8 cm with a circular entry wound. Other features such as burning, singeing, blackening and tattooing of skin are seen in and around the entry wound.
questions.learning: Pistol, near shot — The given image showing a gunshot entry wound with powder burn around the wound is likely due to a near-shot injury by a pistol. A near-shot injury is one when the range of flame is within 60 cm.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Peri-operative respiratory failure is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type III respiratory failure

Type III respiratory failure, also known as peri-operative respiratory failure, occurs due to reduced functional residual capacity (FRC) leading to alveolar collapse (atelectasis). It is commonly seen after major surgery, especially upper abdominal and thoracic procedures, because of anesthesia, pain, diaphragmatic dysfunction, and prolonged recumbency.

Why not the other options?

• A. Type I respiratory failure: Hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO₂ <60 mmHg with normal/low PaCO₂), seen in pneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary edema, and pulmonary embolism.
• B. Type II respiratory failure: Hypercapnic respiratory failure (PaCO₂ >50 mmHg), caused by alveolar hypoventilation (e.g., COPD, neuromuscular disorders, CNS depression).
• D. Type IV respiratory failure: Occurs in shock, where respiratory muscle hypoperfusion leads to ventilatory failure.
questions.learning: Type III respiratory failure Type III respiratory failure, also known as peri-operative respiratory failure, occurs due to reduced functional residual capacity (FRC) leading to alveolar collapse (atelectasis).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: How long does lochial discharge typically last in a woman after childbirth?
questions.explanation: Lochia is the physiological vaginal discharge following delivery, consisting of blood, mucus, and placental tissue. It progresses through three stages: lochia rubra, serosa, and alba. While the initial heavy red discharge (rubra) lasts only a few days, the entire process of uterine involution and shedding typically results in a discharge that persists for 24 to 36 days (roughly 4 to 5 weeks). Option A and B are too short, representing only the initial inflammatory stages. Option D (up to 42 days or 6 weeks) is the absolute upper limit of the puerperium, but most women find that the discharge tapers off before this point. Clinical monitoring of lochia is essential to identify secondary postpartum hemorrhage or endometritis (infection) if the discharge becomes foul-smelling or remains bright red after the first week. Therefore, the average clinical duration for standard lochial discharge is recognized as the 4-week window
questions.learning: Lochia is the physiological vaginal discharge following delivery, consisting of blood, mucus, and placental tissue. It progresses through three stages: lochia rubra, serosa, and alba.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While evaluating an influenza vaccine, it demonstrated an efficacy of 90% in randomized controlled trials, an effectiveness of 85%, and a protection rate of 85% in post-surveillance. Which of the following statements is incorrect? a. 90% chance that those who receive the vaccine will not be infected compared to those who were not vaccinated in a real-world scenario b. 85% chance that those who receive the vaccine will not be infected compared to those who were not vaccinated in the clinical trial c. Protection depends on the disease attack rate d. Vaccine effectiveness may be lower than efficacy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. a and b

Interpret vaccine efficacy, effectiveness, and protection rate correctly. Vaccine efficacy measures the percentage reduction in disease among vaccinated individuals under ideal conditions in randomized controlled trials (RCTs), whereas vaccine effectiveness measures the reduction in disease under real-world (field) conditions. Protection rate represents the proportion of vaccinated individuals protected from disease in the population and is influenced by the background attack rate.

Key Pearls:

• Vaccine efficacy → Assessed in randomized controlled trials (ideal conditions).
• Vaccine effectiveness → Assessed in real-world settings; may be lower than efficacy due to field conditions.
• Protection rate → Depends on the disease attack rate in the population.
• Efficacy ≠ Effectiveness: Trial results cannot be directly interpreted as real-world performance, and vice versa.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with xanthomas on the Achilles tendon. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Familial hypercholesterolemia

Tendon xanthomas (classically over the Achilles tendon) are a hallmark of familial hypercholesterolemia (Type II hyperlipoproteinemia). This condition is caused by a defect in LDL receptors, leading to markedly elevated LDL cholesterol levels and deposition of cholesterol in tendons and skin.

It is associated with premature atherosclerosis and early coronary artery disease.

Key differentiation:

• Familial hypercholesterolemia: Tendon xanthomas
• Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia: Palmar xanthomas
• Hyperchylomicronemia: Eruptive xanthomas
• Tangier disease: Low HDL, orange tonsils
questions.learning: Familial hypercholesterolemia Tendon xanthomas (classically over the Achilles tendon) are a hallmark of familial hypercholesterolemia (Type II hyperlipoproteinemia).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 20-year-old man presents with a 1-week history of jaundice without any other symptoms. He had a recent viral illness that resolved 10 days ago and reports a similar episode of jaundice 2 years earlier following strenuous basketball practice. Laboratory tests show total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL, with unconjugated bilirubin 2.1 mg/ dL and conjugated bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL, while AST and ALT levels are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (2.1 mg/dl) and normal liver enzymes (AST/ALT), which is the classic laboratory signature of Gilbert syndrome. This common, benign condition is caused by reduced activity of the enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase. Clinically, jaundice is intermittent and typically triggered by stressors such as viral infections, fasting, or vigorous physical exertion (like basketball practice). Dubin-Johnson (Option A) and Rotor (Option D) syndromes present with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and different gallbladder imaging or biopsy findings. Criggler-Najjar Type 1 (Option B) is a severe, life-threatening condition presenting in infancy with extremely high bilirubin levels (>20 mg/dl). Because the patient's jaundice is mild, isolated, unconjugated, and recurrent with clear physiological triggers, Gilbert syndrome is the definitive diagnosis. No specific treatment is required as the condition is asymptomatic and non-pathological
questions.learning: The patient presents with isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (2.1 mg/dl) and normal liver enzymes (AST/ALT), which is the classic laboratory signature of Gilbert syndrome.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: An elderly woman received a botox injection for the treatment of wrinkles. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of botulinum toxin?
options: Release of noradrenaline at synaptic cleft
Selectively and irreversibly inhibits nicotinic receptors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inhibits the release of acetylcholine

The botulinum toxin acts by inhibiting the release of acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft.

Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE protein, which is involved in the exocytosis of acetylcholine. Thus, it inhibits the release of acetylcholine.

The image given below shows the site of action of botulinum toxin:

This toxin causes a long-lasting loss of cholinergic transmission. Hence, it can be employed for the treatment of several spastic and neurological conditions caused by the overactivity of cholinergic nerves, such as age-related facial wrinkles, blepharospasm, spastic cerebral palsy, spasmodic torticollis, post-stroke spasticity, and axillary hyperhidrosis.

Adverse effects occur due to incorrect injection and overdose; they include ptosis, diplopia, facial swelling, dry mouth, muscle weakness, and respiratory paralysis.

Botulinum toxin is an exotoxin produced by the bacteria Clostridium botulinum. It is responsible for a type of food poisoning called botulism.
questions.learning: Inhibits the release of acetylcholine — The botulinum toxin acts by inhibiting the release of acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft. Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE protein, which is involved in the exocytosis of acetylcholine.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Medial lemniscus is a continuation of which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fasciculus gracilis

Medial lemniscus is a continuation of fasciculus gracilis.

Posterior column–medial lemniscal pathway:

First-order axons carrying discriminative touch and vibration sensations enter the dorsal horn and continue traveling upward in the posterior white column as the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus.

Fibers of these fasciculi synapse on the second-order neurons of the ipsilateral nuclei gracilis and cuneatus in the medulla oblongata, respectively.

Axons of these second-order neurons then cross over as the internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus in the contralateral medulla.

These second-order axons ascend through the brainstem to reach the third-order neuronal cell bodies in the ventral posterior lateral nucleus of the thalamus. Axons from the third-order neurons then project through the posterior limb of the internal capsule to reach the primary somatosensory cortex.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the formula for sensitivity?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity is a measure of a diagnostic test's ability to correctly identify individuals who truly have the disease (the true positive rate). It is calculated by dividing the number of true positives (TP) by the total number of diseased individuals, which includes true positives and false negatives (FN). Option A represents the Positive Predictive Value (PPV), which measures the probability that a person with a positive test actually has the disease. Option C is the formula for Specificity, measuring the ability to correctly identify healthy individuals (TN / [TN + FP]). Option D does not correspond to a standard epidemiologic measure. High sensitivity is vital for screening tests to ensure as many cases as possible are detected, minimizing the risk of missing diseased individuals due to false negatives

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The patient presents with miosis,anhidrosis and mild drooping of eyelids and a small pupil that remains small even in darkness. The likely diagnosis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Horner syndrome

The clinical scenario with a small sized pupil which does not dilate in response to darkness is due to sympathetic palsy  seen in Horner syndrome (miosis, anhydrosis, ptosis).

In a normal eye, the pupil dilates in response to dim light and constricts in response to bright light. Pupillary dilation is brought about by the contraction of dilator pupillae mediated by sympathetic innervation. Pupillary constriction is due to the contraction of sphincter pupillae mediated by parasympathetic innervation.

The difference in pupillary diameter is called anisocoria. A difference of up to 0.5 mm is common even in normal individuals.

Pearl PF0622: Horner's syndrome

Horner's Syndrome:

Horner's syndrome occurring due to occulo-sympathetic paresis is characterized by the classic triad of:

* Mild ptosis (due to paralysis of Muller's muscle).

* Miosis (due to paralysis of dilator pupillae).

* Reduced ipsilateral sweating (anhydrosis).

Other features include:

* Mild enophthalmos,

* Loss of cilio-spinal reflex,

* Heterochromia, i.e., the ipsilateral iris is lighter in colour,

* Pupil is slow to dilate, and there occurs slight elevation of lower eyelid.

Cocaine test (2% to 4%): Small pupils fail to dilate in Horner's syndrome.

In congenital Horner's syndrome, the additional features seen are heterochromia iridis and unilateral straight hair.

Pearl PF1404: Causes of small and dilated pupils

Causes of small pupils include

* Pontine hemorrhage

* Horner's syndrome

* Old age

* Argyll Robertson pupil

* Drugs and poisons (opiates, organophosphates)

Causes of dilated pupils include

* Holmes–Adie (myotonic) pupil

* Third nerve palsy

* Atropine

* Carbon monoxide

* Ethylene glycol
questions.learning: Horner syndrome — The clinical scenario with a small sized pupil which does not dilate in response to darkness is due to sympathetic palsy seen in Horner syndrome (miosis, anhydrosis, ptosis).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which cells, apart from natural killer (NK) cells, are capable of recognizing and destroying target cells bearing antibody-coated surface antigens through their effector functions?
questions.explanation: The process described is Antibody-Dependent Cellular Cytotoxicity (ADCC), an effector mechanism where immune cells actively lyse target cells that have been "tagged" by specific antibodies (usually IgG). While Natural Killer (NK) cells (Option A) are the most well-known mediators of ADCC, several other myeloid cells also possess the necessary Fc receptors to perform this task. Specifically, neutrophils, eosinophils, and macrophages (Option B and D) are all equipped to recognize antibody-bound targets and release cytotoxic granules to destroy them. Eosinophils are particularly famous for utilizing ADCC to kill large parasites like helminths. Because both neutrophils and eosinophils are listed together in Option C as additional cells capable of this function, it is the most complete and accurate choice. This mechanism bridges the innate and adaptive immune systems, allowing non-specific effector cells to target specific pathogens marked by antibodies
questions.learning: The process described is Antibody-Dependent Cellular Cytotoxicity (ADCC), an effector mechanism where immune cells actively lyse target cells that have been "tagged" by specific antibodies (usually IgG).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which one of the following conditions is a complication of bacterial pharyngitis involving extension of infection into the internal jugular veins leading to thrombosis and metastatic dispersal of the organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lemierre syndrome

Lemierre syndrome is a rare but life-threatening complication of bacterial pharyngitis or tonsillitis, most commonly caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum, an anaerobic Gram-negative bacillus.

The syndrome is characterized by:

• Recent pharyngitis/tonsillitis
• Internal jugular vein thrombosis
• Septic emboli, especially to the lungs, causing multiple cavitating pulmonary nodules or abscesses
• Isolation of Fusobacterium necrophorum

Why not the other options?

• A. Cystic fibrosis: An inherited autosomal recessive disorder causing chronic sinopulmonary infections and pancreatic insufficiency; unrelated to jugular vein thrombosis.
• B. Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis: Chronic fungal infection of the lungs, usually in patients with pre-existing lung cavities; not a complication of pharyngitis.
• D. Wegener’s granulomatosis (Granulomatosis with polyangiitis): ANCA-associated vasculitis involving the upper airway, lungs, and kidneys; not associated with internal jugular vein thrombophlebitis.
questions.learning: Lemierre syndrome Lemierre syndrome is a rare but life-threatening complication of bacterial pharyngitis or tonsillitis, most commonly caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum, an anaerobic Gram-negative bacillus.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient was diagnosed with bacterial vaginosis. Which of the following cannot be used to treat her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Erythromycin

Bacterial vaginosis cannot be treated with erythromycin.

Bacterial vaginosis is a polymicrobial condition caused by an increase in a number of organisms such as Gardnerella, Haemophilus vaginalis, Mobiluncus and Mycoplasma hominis.

This is due to the alteration in the normal vaginal flora which causes a decrease in the number of lactobacilli. It mainly reduces the pH and has antibacterial action by releasing hydrogen peroxide.

According to Amsel's criteria, the discharge has the following characteristics.

* White milky non-viscous discharge, adherent to the vaginal wall

* The pH of the discharge is more than 4.5

* Fishy odor when mixed with 10% KOH. This is called the Whiff test.

* Presence of clue cells-the epithelial cells has a fuzzy border due to the adherence of bacteria.

* Decrease in the number of lactobacilli and increase in the number of Gardnerella and other bacteria.

Treatment: Metronidazole orally or as gel, or clindamycin gel. Other drugs that can be used include tinidazole and secnidazole.

Pearl PF1362: Vaginal infections

Bacterial vaginosis
Trichomonas vaginalis

Candida albicans

Causative organism
Altered vaginal flora- increased concentration of Gardnerella vaginalis
Trichomas vaginalis-parasitic infection
Fungal infection

Etiology

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Identify the correct sequence regarding the family cycle?
options: Formation, extension, complete extension, contraction, complete contraction, dissolution, extinction
Formation, extension, complete extension, complete contraction, contraction, dissolution, extinction
Extension, Formation, complete extension, contraction, complete contraction, dissolution, extinction
Formation, extension, complete extension, con-traction, complete contraction, extinction, dissolution
questions.explanation: The family life cycle describes the standard developmental stages a family unit passes over time. The correct physiological and sociological sequence begins with Formation (marriage). This is followed by Extension, as the first child is born, and Complete Extension when the final child arrives. The Contraction phase begins as the first child leaves the home, progressing to Complete Contraction when all children have moved out (the "empty nest"). Dissolution occurs with the death of one spouse, and the cycle ends in Extinction when the remaining spouse passes away. Options B, C, and D present incorrect chronological orders of these events. Understanding these stages is essential for public health planning, as the health needs and socio-economic risks vary significantly between a family in the extension phase versus the complete contraction phase. For example, geriatric care becomes the priority during dissolution, while maternal and child health dominates the extension phases. This framework helps clinicians provide age-appropriate screening and support to families
questions.learning: The family life cycle describes the standard developmental stages a family unit passes over time. The correct physiological and sociological sequence begins with Formation (marriage).

questions.text: Which of these is the most common type of hernia in females?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Indirect inguinal

• Among inguinal types → indirect is most common
• Occurs due to patent processus vaginalis (canal of Nuck in females)

Option A : Direct inguinal: Occurs due to weakness in posterior wall. ; More common in older males

Option C : Femoral : More common in females than males; But still less common than inguinal hernias

Option D : Obturator : Seen in elderly thin females.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following does not indicate a syndromic approach treating sexually transmitted infection in males?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lower abdominal pain

The syndromic approach for STI management in males is based on presenting symptom complexes such as urethral discharge, genital ulcer disease, and inguinal swelling (bubo).

Lower abdominal pain is a syndrome used for females, not males. It usually indicates Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID).

Lower abdominal pain is a key syndrome in female STIs, often indicating pelvic inflammatory disease, and is not part of male STI syndromic management.

Syndromic management prioritizes immediate treatment without laboratory confirmation to prevent complications and transmission.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a child who has persistently poor mathematical abilities despite having a normal IQ and otherwise age- appropriate learning skills, and who shows no improvement even after one year of specialized mathematics tutoring?
questions.explanation: This child’s persistent difficulty with mathematics despite normal intelligence and adequate educational interventions is diagnostic of a Specific Learning Disorder (SLD). Under DSM-5, this term covers impairments in reading, writing, and mathematics (dyscalculia). ADHD (Option A) causes academic issues through inattention or impulsivity rather than a specific skill deficit. Mathematics Learning Disorder (Option B) is the specific description, but "Specific Learning Disorder" is the broader and clinically preferred diagnostic term in standardized examinations. Asperger’s Syndrome (Option C) involves social communication deficits; children with this condition often excel in mathematics. Given the persistence of the mathematical deficit despite tutoring, SLD is the most accurate over arching diagnosis. **************
questions.learning: This child’s persistent difficulty with mathematics despite normal intelligence and adequate educational interventions is diagnostic of a Specific Learning Disorder (SLD).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 30-year-old female patient with hearing loss underwent an audiogram, which is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Otosclerosis

The above Pure tone audiogram is characteristic of Otosclerosis.

In the above audiogram,

* An air-bone gap is present.

* BC > AC

This is suggestive of Conductive Hearing loss. In the above options, only Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss. Carhart’s notch is the characteristic dip in the BC curve at 2000 Hz seen in otosclerosis. It disappears after successful stapes surgery.

PTA in Sensorineural hearing loss :

* Shows no Air Bone gap.

* Both BC and AC are in hearing loss range (>25 DB)

Other options:

* Meniere’s disease shows a low-frequency loss in the SNHL curve.

* Noise-induced hearing loss is SNHL and PTA shows characteristic Acoustic dip at 4000 Hz.

* Ototoxicity causes SNHL and shows high-frequency hearing loss in the SNHL curve.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the earliest clinical sign of uterine rupture in a woman undergoing a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fetal bradycardia

Fetal bradycardia is the earliest and most consistent sign of uterine rupture during a trial of labor after cesarean.

Uterine rupture is defined as a disruption in the continuity of all the uterine layers (endometrium, myometrium, and serosa) after 20 weeks of pregnancy. It is a potentially life-threatening maternal complication, often associated with an unsuccessful Trial of Labour after Caesarean (TOLAC).

Clinical Features of Uterine Rupture:

Most consistent sign (seen in majority of cases):

* Fetal heart rate abnormalities in CTG – bradycardia, variable decelerations, or late decelerations.

Other maternal and fetal features:

* Persistent lower abdominal or suprapubic pain, especially if occurring between contractions.

* Sudden chest pain, shoulder tip pain, or shortness of breath (due to diaphragmatic irritation or hemoperitoneum).

* Scar tenderness on palpation.

* Vaginal bleeding or blood in urine.

* Contractions stop after being previously adequate.

* Signs of maternal compromise – tachycardia, hypotension, or shock.

* Loss of station of the presenting part felt on vaginal examination.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient develops numbness after taking a medication for migraine, and his hand appears as shown in the image. Which drug is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The image shows signs of Raynaud's phenomenon (numbness and digital discoloration), which is a classic side effect of ergot alkaloids like dihydroergotamine. These drugs act as partial agonists at 5-HT1B/1D receptors to cause vasoconstriction for treating acute migraine. However, their potent vasoconstrictive properties can extend to the peripheral arteries, leading to digital ischemia and, in severe cases, gangrene. Sumatriptan (Option B) is a more selective triptan that also causes vasoconstriction but is not typically associated with the peripheral vascular compromise and digital discoloration seen here. Butorphanol (Option C) is an opioid that does not cause vasoconstriction. Aspirin (Option D) is an NSAID that lacks significant vasoactive properties. Therefore, the specific development of hand ischemia following migraine therapy points to ergotamine-induced vasoconstriction
questions.learning: The image shows signs of Raynaud's phenomenon (numbness and digital discoloration), which is a classic side effect of ergot alkaloids like dihydroergotamine.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not related to disease progression?
questions.explanation: In the context of malignancies like Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), disease progression is defined by the aggressiveness and invasiveness of the tumor rather than simply how long it has been present. Depth (Option B) is a critical factor, as deeper invasion into muscle or bone indicates a more advanced and difficult-to-treat disease. The site (Option C) is also vital; tumors in high-risk areas like the central face or ears are more prone to recurrence and local spread. The stage of cancer (Option D) is the most comprehensive measure of progression, reflecting tumor size and metastasis. Duration (Option A) is often unrelated to the inherent aggressiveness of the cells; a tumor can exist for years with minimal progression, while others are highly invasive from the start. Therefore, biological and anatomical factors are the true predictors of disease severity
questions.learning: In the context of malignancies like Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), disease progression is defined by the aggressiveness and invasiveness of the tumor rather than simply how long it has been present.

Clearance (C) = U × V / P,

where

Renal clearance of a substance is the volume of plasma that is completely cleared of the substance by the kidneys per unit of time.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man is brought by his wife, as he calls other women, and achieves sexual gratification by talking obscenity and sharing obscene pictures. What does the patient most likely have?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Scatologia

Telephone and computer scatology- it involves obscene phone calling or sending of inappropriate videos/images to an unsuspecting person.

Paraphilias or perversions are sexual stimuli or acts that are deviations from normal sexual behaviors but are necessary for some people to experience arousal and orgasm.

Important paraphilic disorders are:

* Exhibitionism- Urge to expose genitals to a stranger or unsuspecting person.

* Fetishism- It is the use of objects for sexual gratification. Eg. shoes, gloves, pantyhose, and stockings. The objects can be used to attain gratification directly or the person may ask the partner to wear them during sexual intercourse.

* Frotteurism- is usually characterized by a man's rubbing his penis against the buttocks or other body parts of a fully clothed woman to achieve orgasm.

* Pedophilia- Defined as the presence of recurrent, intense sexual urges or fantasies involving children under 13 years of age, persisting for at least six months.

* Masochism- takes its name from the activities of Leopold von Sacher-Masoch, a novelist whose characters derived sexual pleasure from being abused and dominated by women.

* Sexual sadism- The person attains sexual arousal from the physical and psychosocial suffering of another person.

* Voyeurism- It is also called scoptophilia. The person has an urge to watch an unsuspecting person naked or in sexual activity.

* Transvestism- Fantasies and sexual urge to dress in opposite gender clothing.

* Telephone and computer scatology- it involves obscene phone calling or sending of video images to an unsuspecting partner.

* Necrophilia- it is an obsession with obtaining sexual gratification from dead bodies

* Zoophilia- having an urge to involve in sexual activity like intercourse, masturbation, or oral-genital contact with an animal.

* Coprophilia- Sexual pleasure associated with a desire to defecate on the partner or to be defected on.

* Urophilia- the sexual pleasure associated with the desire to urinate on a partner or to be urinated on.

* Hypoxyphilia- is the desire to achieve an altered state of consciousness secondary to hypoxia while experiencing orgasm. They may use volatile nitrite or nitrous oxide to produce hypoxia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about radiotherapy?
options: Intensity is inversely proportional to squared distance
Vomiting is a late adverse reaction
Rapidly proliferating cells are most radioresistant
Radiation-induced skin changes is a reversible adverse effect
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intensity is inversely proportional to squared distance

The intensity of radiation is inversely proportional to the squared distance from the source of radiation. This is known as the inverse square law in radiotherapy.

Inverse square law - the intensity of radiation is inversely proportional to the squared distance from the source of radiation. This principle is unsuitable for large tumors and has potential risks of radiation exposure to medical staff.

Other options:

Option B: Vomiting can be an acute (early) adverse reaction to radiation therapy, occurring shortly after treatment.

Option C: Permanent non-dividing cells are more radioresistant than rapidly proliferating cells.

Option D: Not all the adverse effects of radiation therapy are reversible. Some of the adverse effects of radiation therapy, such as fibrosis, radiation-induced skin changes, late radiation enteritis, etc are irreversible.
questions.learning: Intensity is inversely proportional to squared distance The intensity of radiation is inversely proportional to the squared distance from the source of radiation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The image below depicts which of the following types of cell-to-cell signaling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Paracrine

The given image shows the paracrine cell-to-cell signaling mechanism. In paracrine signaling, the signaling molecules released by a cell only affect target cells in close proximity to it.

An example of paracrine signaling is the release of endothelin-1, a potent vasoconstrictor released by the endothelial cells.

Synaptic signaling is a special case of paracrine signaling (for chemical synapses) between neurons and target cells.

Other options:

Option B: In the autocrine signaling mechanism, the cells respond to the signaling molecules that are released by themselves, which is the site of release and action within the same cell. Note that the signaling molecules are first secreted out of the cell and then act on the same cell through receptors. An example is the proliferation of activated T-cells by IL-2 released by the same cell after it interacts with antigen-presenting cells.

Option C: In endocrine signaling, a signaling molecule, a hormone (for example insulin, FSH, LH), is usually carried by the blood from its site of release to act on its target at a distance.

The below image shows the different types of extracellular cell-to-cell communication mechanisms.

Option D: Merocrine is a type of glandular secretion and not an extracellular signaling mechanism. In this, the secretions are poured out by exocytosis and the cell remains intact. An example of the merocrine gland is the goblet cell and eccrine sweat gland.

An illustration depicting this mechanism is given below.
questions.learning: Paracrine — The given image shows the paracrine cell-to-cell signaling mechanism. In paracrine signaling, the signaling molecules released by a cell only affect target cells in close proximity to it.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is not usually associated with the formation of a greyish-white membrane over the tonsils?
questions.explanation: "Ludwig’s angina" is a rapidly spreading cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces, typically arising from an infected lower molar. It is characterized by severe swelling of the neck and floor of the mouth, which can displace the tongue and obstruct the airway; however, it does "not typically" involve the formation of a membrane on the tonsils. Diphtheria (Option B) is the classic cause of a thick, grey-white pseudomembrane that bleeds when scraped. Streptococcal tonsillitis (Option A) frequently presents with a white or yellow exudate that can appear membranous. Infectious mononucleosis (Option D) characteristically features massive tonsillar enlargement with a thick, shaggy grey-white exudate. Diagnosis of the cause of a tonsillar membrane is essential, as management varies from antibiotics (Strep) to urgent antitoxin (Diphtheria) or supportive care (Mono). Ludwig’s angina is a surgical emergency requiring airway management and intravenous antibiotics

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following rules are used in case as tests of insanity?

1. Durham's rule
2. Curren's rule
3. Ashley's rule
4. Murphy's rule
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 only

Durham's rule and Curren's rule are used in cases as tests for insanity.

Durhams's rule states that an accused person is not criminally responsible if, his unlawful act is the product of mental disease or mental defect.

Curren’s rule states that an accused person is not criminally responsible if, at the time of committing the act, he did not have the capacity to regulate his conduct to the requirements of the law as a result of mental disease or defect.

In India, the law of Criminal responsibility is under Section 84 I.P.C. It states that "Nothing is an offense which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or what he is doing is either wrong or contrary to the law”. This is slightly different from McNaughten's rule followed in Britain.

McNaughten's rule states that every man is to be presumed to be sane, and possesses a sufficient degree of reason to be responsible for his crimes until the contrary is proved.

Other rules to assess the criminal responsibility of insane persons:

• The Irresistible Impulse
• Federal rule or American Law Institute test (ALT)
• The Brawner rule.

Note: Ashley's rule is used to differentiate males and females based on the combined length of the manubrium and sternum. It is considered to be male sternum when the combined length is >149mm, while if the combined length is <149mm, then it is considered female.
questions.learning: 1, 2 only Durham's rule and Curren's rule are used in cases as tests for insanity. Durhams's rule states that an accused person is not criminally responsible if, his unlawful act is the product of mental disease or mental defect.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The upper limit of age for attainment of visual fixation or following is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3 months

Visual fixation and following should be attained by 3 months of age. Although many infants begin to fix and follow faces or objects by 6–8 weeks, failure to achieve this by 3 months is abnormal and warrants evaluation for visual impairment or neurodevelopmental disorders.

Why not the other options?

• A. Birth: Newborns can briefly fix on faces but consistent fixation/following is not expected.
• B. 1 month: Visual tracking is still developing and may be inconsistent.
• C. 2 months: Many infants achieve fixation by this age, but the upper limit of normal is 3 months.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old female presented with dyspnea and chest pain. Which of the following proves that she has aortic stenosis rather than aortic regurgitation?
options: Increase in myocardial oxygen consumption is seen with increased pressure work than volume
Aortic stenosis causes reduced pressure at the aortic valve
Workload has nothing to do with myocardial oxygen consumption
Increased pressure - Increase in preload more than afterload
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase in myocardial oxygen consumption is seen with increased pressure work than volume

Valvular diseases affect the heart in two major ways:

| Type | Example | Cardiac Work

| ---- | ------- | ------------

| Pressure overload | Aortic stenosis | Pressure work

| Volume overload | Aortic regurgitation | Volume work

Pressure overload requires more myocardial oxygen consumption (MVO₂).

Thus, this helps differentiate AS from AR.

Aortic stenosis causes a pressure overload, requiring the left ventricle to generate high systolic pressures.

Myocardial oxygen consumption correlates more with pressure work than volume work, favoring a diagnosis of aortic stenosis.

In contrast, aortic regurgitation produces volume overload with relatively lower pressure work.

Thus, increased oxygen demand due to pressure overload distinguishes aortic stenosis.

B) Aortic stenosis causes reduced pressure at the aortic valve

Incorrect.

In AS: LV pressure increases, creating a pressure gradient across the valve.

C) Workload has nothing to do with oxygen consumption

Myocardial oxygen consumption is directly related to cardiac workload.

D) Increased pressure → increase in preload more than afterload

Pressure overload mainly increases afterload, not preload.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Xanthurenic aciduria is seen in which of the following vitamin deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin B6

Xanthurenic aciduria is seen in deficiency of vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate), a coenzyme required by kynureninase enzyme to convert 3-OH kynurenine to 3-OH anthranilic acid during tryptophan metabolism.

Other options-

Option A: Riboflavin or Vitamin B2 deficiency manifests as angular stomatitis, magenta tongue, seborrhea, corneal vascularization. It is seen in alcoholism, and individuals with a poor diet and decreased intake of dairy products.

Option B: A patient with thiamine or vitamin B1 deficiency presents either dry Beriberi with predominantly neurological symptoms like neuropathy, muscle weakness, and wasting or wet Beriberi with predominant cardiac symptoms like cardiomegaly, tachycardia, high output congestive cardiac failure.

Option C: Vitamin B12 or cobalamin deficiency presents as anemia, fatigue, and pallor symptoms. Other presenting complaints may include peripheral neuropathy, glossitis, diarrhea, headaches, neuropsychiatric disturbances like dementia, and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (SACD) leading to ataxia. A peripheral smear shows macrocytic anemia and hypersegmented neutrophils.
questions.learning: Vitamin B6 Xanthurenic aciduria is seen in deficiency of vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate), a coenzyme required by kynureninase enzyme to convert 3-OH kynurenine to 3-OH anthranilic acid during tryptophan metabolism.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: While observing anesthesia equipment in the operating theater, a specific vaporizer is in use. Which of the following gases is it most likely designed to contain?
questions.explanation: Anesthesia equipment uses a universal color-coding system to prevent medication errors. A vaporizer with a blue color-coded dial or housing is designed exclusively for Desflurane (Option A). Desflurane requires a specialized heated and pressurized vaporizer (like the Tec 6) due to its extremely high vapor pressure and boiling point near room temperature. Halothane (Option B) is color-coded red. Sevoflurane (Option C) is color-coded yellow. Isoflurane (Option D) is color-coded purple. Identifying these colors is a fundamental safety skill for anesthetists. Since the vaporizer in the image is marked with the blue distinctive color of Desflurane, that is the gas it comprises. This visual identification ensures that the correct agent is matched to its corresponding calibrated delivery device
questions.learning: Anesthesia equipment uses a universal color-coding system to prevent medication errors. A vaporizer with a blue color-coded dial or housing is designed exclusively for Desflurane (Option A).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: 1. It is a rare complication of chronic alcohol misuse characterised by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and delirium. 2. There is damage to the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial nuclei of thalamus. 3. The underlying cause is deficiency of Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin). 4. The syndrome can also arise due to malabsorption or protracted vomiting. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome is a neuropsychiatric disorder caused by thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, most commonly seen in chronic alcohol misuse, but it can also occur in malnutrition, malabsorption, hyperemesis, and prolonged vomiting. It consists of Wernicke encephalopathy (acute) and Korsakoff syndrome (chronic amnestic syndrome).

Why is B correct?

• 1. It is a rare complication of chronic alcohol misuse characterised by ophthalmoplegia\, ataxia and delirium✅: Wernicke encephalopathy classically presents with the triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion (delirium).
• 2. There is damage to the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial nuclei of thalamus✅: These are the characteristic pathological lesions responsible for memory impairment.
• 4. The syndrome can also arise due to malabsorption or protracted vomiting✅: Any condition causing thiamine deficiency can precipitate Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome.

Incorrect statement:

• 3. The underlying cause is deficiency of Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin)❌: The disorder is caused by Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) deficiency, not Vitamin B12.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome is a neuropsychiatric disorder caused by thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, most commonly seen in chronic alcohol misuse, but it can also occur in malnutrition, malabsorption, hyperemesis, and prolonged vomiting.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following are characteristics of health education, rather than propaganda? 1. Knowledge actively acquired, rather than instilled. 2. Appeals to emotion, rather than reason. 3. Behaviour centred, rather than information centred. 4. Arouses and stimulates primitive desires, rather than disciplines them. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 3

Health education is a planned learning process that helps individuals and communities voluntarily adopt healthy behaviors through understanding, motivation, and participation. Unlike propaganda, it emphasizes reason, active learning, and behavior change rather than emotional manipulation.

• 1. Knowledge actively acquired\, rather than instilled. ✓

• Health education encourages active participation, critical thinking, and self-learning.

• 2. Appeals to emotion\, rather than reason. ✗

• This is a feature of propaganda, which relies on emotional appeal rather than rational understanding.

• 3. Behaviour centred\, rather than information centred. ✓

• The ultimate goal of health education is behavior change, not merely providing information.

• 4. Arouses and stimulates primitive desires\, rather than disciplines them. ✗

• This is also a characteristic of propaganda, not health education.
questions.learning: 1 and 3 Health education is a planned learning process that helps individuals and communities voluntarily adopt healthy behaviors through understanding, motivation, and participation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In which of the following should a cotton swab with pus be discarded?
questions.explanation: According to Biomedical Waste Management rules, a cotton swab contaminated with pus is classified as soiled waste. Soiled waste, which includes items contaminated with blood or body fluids, must be disposed of in yellow category bags. These bags are made of non-chlorinated plastic because the contents are typically destined for incineration or plasma pyrolysis. Biodegradable materials like cotton and gauze are never chlorinated before incineration to prevent the release of toxic gases. The Red category (Options C and D) is strictly reserved for contaminated but recyclable plastic waste, such as tubing, catheters, and syringes without needles. Yellow chlorination bags (Option A) are not standard since yellow waste is already sterilized by high-heat methods. Therefore, the yellow non-chlorination bag is the only appropriate choice for pus-soaked cotton
questions.learning: According to Biomedical Waste Management rules, a cotton swab contaminated with pus is classified as soiled waste. Soiled waste, which includes items contaminated with blood or body fluids, must be disposed of in yellow category bags.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
What is the ideal maintenance fluid of choice in children?

N - normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5% dextrose and N saline

5% dextrose and N saline is the ideal maintenance fluid in children.

5% dextrose provides 17 calories/100 mL and nearly 20% of the daily caloric needs. This level is enough to prevent ketone production and helps minimise protein degradation. However, the child will lose weight on this regimen and therefore it is necessary to start enteral feeds sooner or if not possible, total parenteral nutrition is recommended.

Other options:

Hypotonic fluids like N/2 or N/4 saline can increase the risk of hyponatraemia and free water movement inside RBCs, leading to haemolysis. Hence, isotonic fluids with 5% dextrose are recommended as standard maintenance fluids in children.
questions.learning: 5% dextrose and N saline 5% dextrose and N saline is the ideal maintenance fluid in children. 5% dextrose provides 17 calories/100 mL and nearly 20% of the daily caloric needs.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Sample sizes of samples 1, 2 and 3 are 1000, 800, 600 respectively. The order of margin of error will be ____________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3 >2>1

Curve 1 has the least margin of error, followed by curve 2, and then curve 3. So the order is 3>2>1.

The image shows three normal distribution curves of different sample sizes, having the same mean but different standard deviations.

As the sample size is decreasing, the peak decreases and the curve becomes more flat, implying a wider confidence of interval for the given mean.

The width of the base of the curve is directly proportional to the margin of error.
questions.learning: 3 >2>1 Curve 1 has the least margin of error, followed by curve 2, and then curve 3. The image shows three normal distribution curves of different sample sizes, having the same mean but different standard deviations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with progressive shortness of breath for the last 6 months, accompanied by dry cough. Auscultation reveals bilateral basal end-inspiratory crepitations. There is no history of fever, joint pain, or occupational exposure. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

Correct answer is C because progressive exertional dyspnea with chronic dry cough and bilateral basal end-inspiratory “Velcro” crackles is classic for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Absence of fever, systemic symptoms, or exposure history argues against sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

Cor pulmonale is a consequence of chronic lung disease, not the primary diagnosis here.

| Option | Key Feature | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | ----------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Cor pulmonale | Right heart failure | Late complication |  Not primary disease | Secondary to lung disease

| B. Sarcoidosis | BHL + granulomas | Multisystem disease |  No lymphadenopathy or neuro signs | Non-caseating granulomas

| C. IPF ✅ |  Basal fibrosis + dry cough | ✔ Classic presentation | Correct |  Velcro crackles

| D. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis | Exposure-related ILD | Bird/mold exposure |  No exposure history | Immune-mediated
questions.learning: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis Correct answer is C because progressive exertional dyspnea with chronic dry cough and bilateral basal end-inspiratory “Velcro” crackles is classic for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The co-factor for glutathione peroxidase is __?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Selenium

Selenium act as a cofactor for glutathione peroxidase.

Glutathione peroxidases:

* Also known as selenoproteins

* Selenium-containing glutathione peroxidases help transform hydrogen peroxide to harmless water (anti–oxidant action)

* Selenium deficiency results in Impaired function of glutathione peroxidases. As a result, destructive hydrogen peroxide breaks down into even more dangerous hydroxyl radical which damages cell membranes and cell DNA leading to serious disease

Selenium:

Selenium is an important trace element that is a part of the 21st amino acid selenocysteine.

There are many selenium-containing enzymes such as :

* Glutathione peroxidase

* De-iodinase

* Thioredoxin reductase

Selenium is also an intracellular antioxidant that complements the role of Vitamin E. Dietary sources of selenium include seafood, muscle meat, and some cereals.

Note:

Keshan Disease: Endemic cardiomyopathy.
Population affected: Primarily children and young women.
Location: Occurs in areas of China with low dietary selenium intake.
Cause: Linked to selenium deficiency in the diet.
