questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During a seminar on cervical cancer epidemiology, high-risk HPV serotypes linked to malignancy are discussed. Which combination of HPV serotypes is most strongly associated with the development of cervical cancer?
questions.explanation: Cervical cancer is definitively caused by persistent infection with high-risk serotypes of the human papillomavirus (HPV). Globally, HPV 16 and 18 are the two most oncogenic types, responsible for approximately 70% of all cervical cancer cases. Other recognized high-risk types include 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58. Option D (16, 18, 31, 33) accurately identifies a grouping of the most significant high-risk serotypes . Options A, B, and C include serotypes 19 or 32, which are not standard members of the primary "high-risk" oncogenic group for cervical cancer. The integration of high-risk HPV DNA into the host genome leads to the overexpression of E6 and E7 oncoproteins, which disrupt tumor suppressor genes p53 and Rb, respectively. Therefore, this specific combination represents the most critical viral etiologies for cervical malignancy. Modern HPV vaccines target these types to effectively reduce the incidence of cervical cancer
questions.learning: Cervical cancer is definitively caused by persistent infection with high-risk serotypes of the human papillomavirus (HPV). Globally, HPV 16 and 18 are the two most oncogenic types, responsible for approximately 70% of all cervical cancer cases.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding oculocutaneous albinism: I. The disease results from genetic abnormalities leading to destruction of melanocytes. II. Type 1 albinism is due to a defect in the tyrosinase gene. III. Patients may present with poor vision, rotatory nystagmus and alternating strabismus. IV. Patients are at an increased risk of sunburn or developing skin cancer. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. II, III and IV

Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a group of autosomal recessive disorders characterized by reduced or absent melanin synthesis in the skin, hair, and eyes due to defects in enzymes involved in melanin production. Melanocytes are present in normal numbers, but they are unable to produce adequate melanin.

• I. The disease results from genetic abnormalities leading to destruction of melanocytes. ❌

• Incorrect. Melanocytes are normal in number; the defect is in melanin synthesis, not melanocyte destruction.
• Destruction of melanocytes occurs in vitiligo, not albinism.

• II. Type 1 albinism is due to a defect in the tyrosinase gene. ✅

• OCA Type 1 results from mutations in the TYR (tyrosinase) gene, leading to absent or markedly reduced tyrosinase activity. This is the most commonly tested subtype.

• III. Patients may present with poor vision, rotatory nystagmus and alternating strabismus. ✅

• Ocular features include:

• Reduced visual acuity
• Nystagmus
• Strabismus
• Photophobia
• Foveal hypoplasia
• Iris transillumination defects

• IV. Patients are at an increased risk of sunburn or developing skin cancer. ✅

• Reduced melanin predisposes patients to:

• Sunburn
• Actinic damage
• Squamous cell carcinoma
• Basal cell carcinoma
• Increased lifetime risk of skin malignancies
questions.learning: II, III and IV Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a group of autosomal recessive disorders characterized by reduced or absent melanin synthesis in the skin, hair, and eyes due to defects in enzymes involved in melanin production.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with black, foul-smelling nasal discharge and a black necrotic mass occupying the nasal cavity, causing erosion of the septum and hard palate. What is the main risk factor for this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation—black, necrotic nasal mass and discharge with severe bony erosion—is the hallmark of invasive Mucormycosis (specifically Rhino-cerebral Mucormycosis). This is a devastating fungal infection caused by angioinvasive molds of the order Mucorales. The absolute primary risk factor for this condition is uncontrolled Diabetes mellitus, especially when complicated by diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). The fungus thrives in high-glucose, acidic environments. Hypothyroidism (Option A) and Hypertension (Option C) are not recognized as primary predisposing factors for fungal invasion. While a foreign body (Option D) can cause foul discharge and localized necrosis, it would not lead to the rapid, life-threatening tissue destruction and systemic involvement typical of mucormycosis. Management of this condition is a medical and surgical emergency requiring aggressive debridement, intravenous Amphotericin B, and strict glycemic control. Without rapid intervention, the infection can spread into the orbit and brain with nearly 100% mortality
questions.learning: The clinical presentation—black, necrotic nasal mass and discharge with severe bony erosion—is the hallmark of invasive Mucormycosis (specifically Rhino-cerebral Mucormycosis).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents to OPD at 36 weeks of gestation and presents with complaints of breathlessness and excessive abdominal distension. On examination, fetal movements are normal, fetal parts not easily felt and muffled fetal heartbeat is heard. Symphysis fundal height came out to be 41weeks. Per abdomen examination reveals tense abdomen but not tender. What can be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Polyhydramnios

Polyhydramnios is diagnosed by ultrasound using:

| Parameter | Value

| --------- | -----

| Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI) | > 24 cm

| Deepest vertical pocket | > 8 cm

Causes of Polyhydramnios

Maternal causes

• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

Fetal causes

• Anencephaly
• Esophageal Atresia

Idiopathic

• Most common (\~60%).

Complications

| Maternal | Fetal

| -------- | -----

| Breathlessness | Preterm birth

| Preterm labor | Cord prolapse

| Postpartum hemorrhage | Malpresentation

Excessive distension, SFH far ahead of dates, difficulty feeling fetal parts and muffled FHR are classic of polyhydramnios. Abdomen is tense but non-tender with no bleeding or pain suggestive of abruption. Hydrocephalus alone doesn’t explain this degree of maternal breathlessness and distension.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is most effective for reducing uric acid levels to prevent renal injury in patients with tumor lysis syndrome?
questions.explanation: Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS) is an oncological emergency characterized by the massive release of intracellular contents, including nucleic acids which are metabolized into uric acid. Severe hyperuricemia can cause acute urate nephropathy and renal failure. Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase enzyme that directly converts uric acid into allantoin, a much more soluble metabolite that is easily excreted by the kidneys. It acts rapidly to lower existing high levels of uric acid. Febuxostat (Option D) and Allopurinol are xanthine oxidase inhibitors that prevent the formation of new uric acid but do not clear what is already in the blood. Furosemide (Option A) is a diuretic used to maintain urine flow but doesn't target uric acid. Corticosteroids (Option C) are part of chemotherapy but not a primary treatment for TLS hyperuricemia. Thus, Rasburicase is the most potent and direct agent for managing established hyperuricemia in TLS
questions.learning: Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS) is an oncological emergency characterized by the massive release of intracellular contents, including nucleic acids which are metabolized into uric acid.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old multigravida comes to the emergency at night with an inversion of the uterus following the delivery of the baby when the nurse waited till the delivery of the placenta. Her BP is 110/70 mmHg. Pulse rate 90 beats/min. What should be the management in this case?
options: Manually remove placenta and then reposition the uterus
Reposition the uterus without removing placenta
Shift the patient to OT and reposition the uterus under anaesthesia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Reposition the uterus without removing placenta

This patient with a uterine inversion with stable vitals should undergo manual reposition of the uterus without removing the placenta

Uterine inversion occurs when there is excessive traction leading to the loss of the uterine convexity and protrusion of the uterus outside the vaginal introitus.

Risk factors for uterine inversion:

• Fundal attachment of the placenta
• Uterine atony
• Attempts at cord traction before placental delivery
• Adherent placenta

There are 3 degrees of uterine inversion:

• First-degree - the fundus of the uterus inverts into the uterine cavity
• Second-degree - the uterine fundus protrudes through the cervix and lies in the vagina
• Third-degree - the whole of the uterus is inverted and protrudes through the introitus

Since uterine inversion presents with profuse bleeding and a severe degree of shock, it requires prompt diagnosis and management. It is managed by promptly repositioning the uterus by exerting a firm and constant pressure on the inverted uterine fundus. The placenta should not be removed until after the replacement of the uterus if it is still attached to the uterus.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: NARP syndrome is a?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mitochondrial function disorder

NARP syndrome - Neuropathy Ataxia Retinitis Pigmentosa syndrome is described as a mitochondrial function disorder.

NARP syndrome is due to a point mutation of the mitochondrial ATPase-6 gene. It has 2 phenotypes:

• NARP
• Maternally inherited Leigh syndrome (MILS)

It is characterized by moderate, diffuse cerebral and cerebellar atrophy and symmetric lesions of the basal ganglia on MRI. The severity of the syndrome corresponds to the mutant mitochondrial DNA load in the tissues.
questions.learning: Mitochondrial function disorder NARP syndrome - Neuropathy Ataxia Retinitis Pigmentosa syndrome is described as a mitochondrial function disorder. NARP syndrome is due to a point mutation of the mitochondrial ATPase-6 gene.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a major diagnostic criterion of neuromyelitis optica?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Focal epilepsy

Focal epilepsy is not considered a major diagnostic criterion of neuromyelitis optica (NMO).

Neuromyelitis optica (Devic’s disease) is an aggressive inflammatory demyelinating disorder characterized by recurrent attacks of optic neuritis and myelitis.

It is associated with a highly specific autoantibody directed against aquaporin-4(AQP-4). AQP-4 is localized to the foot processes of astrocytes in close proximity to endothelial surfaces.

The core clinical characteristics include optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome (unexplained hiccups/ nausea/ vomiting), acute brainstem syndrome, symptomatic narcolepsy or acute diencephalic clinical syndrome with Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD)-typical diencephalic MRI lesions, and symptomatic cerebral syndrome with NMSOD-typical brain lesions.

Attacks of optic neuritis are bilateral and severe in NMO, whereas in multiple sclerosis (MS) optic neuritis is usually unilateral. Progressive symptoms are not typical of NMO, unlike in MS. CSF findings in NMO show higher pleocytosis, with neutrophils and eosinophils in acute cases, and rare occurrence of oligoclonal bands, distinguishing it from MS.

Acute attacks of NMO are treated with high-dose glucocorticoids. Plasma exchange can be used in acute attacks that do not respond to glucocorticoids.

Drugs used for prophylaxis against relapses include mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, glucocorticoids, and azathioprine. Three monoclonal antibodies approved for attack prevention include eculizumab (terminal complement inhibitor), inebilizumab (B-cell depleter), and satralizumab (IL-6 receptor blocker).

NMO typically presents as a recurrent disease, with a monophasic course observed in less than 10% of patients. Untreated NMO can lead to disability, including respiratory failure, blindness, and limb paralysis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis for the given image?
questions.explanation: The laparoscopic image displays characteristic "beading" or nodules on the fallopian tubes, which are highly suggestive of female genital tuberculosis (FGTB). FGTB often presents with caseous nodules, tubercles, and the "Sharma’s python sign" (alternating constriction and dilation). Regarding the distractors, a normal fallopian tube (Option B) is thin-walled and smooth without any nodules. A hydrosalpinx (Option C) appears as a fluid-distended, thin-walled "sausage-shaped" tube but lacks the caseous nodules seen here. Endometriosis (Option D) typically shows "powder-burn" lesions or "chocolate cysts" on the ovaries rather than diffuse white nodules on the tubes. Because genital TB is a leading cause of infertility in endemic regions and presents with these specific laparoscopic features, it is the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The laparoscopic image displays characteristic "beading" or nodules on the fallopian tubes, which are highly suggestive of female genital tuberculosis (FGTB).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Reduced incidence of neural tube defects is observed with the use of ________ prior to conception.
questions.explanation: Extensive clinical research has definitively proven that the periconceptional supplementation of folic acid (Vitamin B9) significantly reduces the incidence of neural tube defects (NTDs) such as spina bifida and anencephaly (Option A). The recommended standard dose is 400 mcg daily for women with a low risk, started at least one month before conception and continued through the first trimester. For women with a prior history of an NTD-affected pregnancy, a higher dose of 4 mg is used. Iron (Option B) is essential for preventing maternal anemia but does not impact neural tube formation. Calcium (Option C) is vital for maternal bone health and preventing pre-eclampsia. Excess Vitamin A (Option D) can actually be teratogenic and is not used for NTD prevention. Therefore, folic acid is the only nutrient listed with a direct, preventative role in the embryological closure of the neural tube
questions.learning: Extensive clinical research has definitively proven that the periconceptional supplementation of folic acid (Vitamin B9) significantly reduces the incidence of neural tube defects (NTDs) such as spina bifida and anencephaly (Option A).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During a laryngeal surgical procedure, a patient develops loss of sensation above the vocal cords. Which nerve primarily supplies sensory innervation to this area?
questions.explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is the primary structure providing sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa situated above the level of the vocal folds (vocal cords). This nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane alongside the superior laryngeal artery to supply the vestibule of the larynx. In contrast, the recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option B) is responsible for sensory innervation below the level of the vocal cords and motor supply to all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid. The glossopharyngeal nerve (Option C) provides sensory supply to the oropharynx and the posterior third of the tongue, but not the internal larynx. The external laryngeal nerve (Option D) is a purely motor nerve that innervates the cricothyroid muscle. Injury to the internal laryngeal nerve typically results in a loss of the protective cough reflex, significantly increasing the risk of aspiration. Therefore, the specific anatomical boundary mentioned—above the vocal cords—definitively identifies the superior laryngeal nerve as the responsible sensory mediator
questions.learning: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is the primary structure providing sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa situated above the level of the vocal folds (vocal cords).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with difficulty responding to bright light. On examination, the pupillary light reflex is absent, while the near (accommodation) reflex is intact. Where is the lesion most likely located?
questions.explanation: The absence of the light reflex with the preservation of the near reflex is known as light-near dissociation. This phenomenon occurs when a lesion interrupts the pathway from the optic tract to the Edinger–Westphal nucleus but spares the fibers coming from the cortex for accommodation. This lesion is classically located in the pretectal area of the midbrain. Common causes include neurosyphilis (Argyll Robertson pupil) and Parinaud’s syndrome. Optic nerve lesions (Option A) cause an afferent defect, abolishing both light and near reflexes. Oculomotor nerve lesions (Option B) abolish reflexes and cause ptosis. The Edinger–Westphal nucleus (Option C) is the motor output for both reflexes; damage there would abolish both. Thus, the midbrain pretectal area is the only site where these reflexes can be dissociated

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In iron deficiency anemia, all of the following is increased except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transferrin saturation

Transferrin saturation is decreased in iron deficiency anemia.

Clinical presentation may include fatigue, pallor, reduced exercise capacity. Cheilosis (fissures at the corners of the mouth) and koilonychia (spooning of the fingernails) are signs of advanced tissue iron deficiency.

Laboratory findings are:

• Reduced hemoglobin and hematocrit values.
• hypochromia, microcytosis, and poikilocytosis.
• serum iron and ferritin levels are low.
• The total plasma iron-binding capacity that reflects the elevated transferrin levels is high.
• Low serum iron with increased iron-binding capacity results in a reduction of transferrin saturation to below 15%.
• RBC protoporphyrin levels are increased. Protoporphyrin is an intermediate in the heme synthesis pathway. Under conditions in which heme synthesis is impaired, protoporphyrin accumulates within the red cell.
• Bone marrow reveals a mild to moderate increase in erythroid progenitors. The absence of stainable iron in macrophages is a diagnostically significant finding.

Peripheral smear of microcytic hypochromic anemia:
questions.learning: Transferrin saturation Transferrin saturation is decreased in iron deficiency anemia. Clinical presentation may include fatigue, pallor, reduced exercise capacity.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A man falls onto his shoulder with his head forced to the opposite side and subsequently develops the shown deformity. Which cervical nerve root values are most likely to be involved in this injury?
questions.explanation: A traumatic separation of the head and shoulder causes a traction injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, specifically affecting the C5 and C6 nerve roots. This results in Erb's Palsy, which presents with a characteristic "waiter's tip" posture where the arm is held limp by the side, internally rotated at the shoulder, and pronated at the forearm. C6 and C7 (Option B) involve the middle trunk and do not produce this specific classic posture. C7 and C8 (Option C) affect lower plexus functions like wrist and finger movement rather than the shoulder. C8 and T1 (Option D) involve the lower trunk, typically injured by upward arm traction, resulting in Klumpke's palsy, which presents with intrinsic hand muscle weakness and sometimes Horner's syndrome. Because the mechanism involves downward shoulder traction and affects the upper limb's proximal segments, C5 and C6 are the damaged roots
questions.learning: A traumatic separation of the head and shoulder causes a traction injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, specifically affecting the C5 and C6 nerve roots.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presented to the hospital with cola-colored urine, hypertension, and puffiness of eyes. Laboratory investigations were done and creatinine was 2.5 mg/dL. Treatment was started, and despite treatment, the patient did not improve for the next 3 weeks. The creatinine value increased to 4.5 mg/dL. Which among the following electron microscopic findings will be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subepithelial deposits

The diagnosis based on the above clinical scenario is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Subepithelial deposits will be seen on electron microscopy.

The rapid decline in renal function and raise in creatinine value to 4.5 mg/dL within 3 weeks, is suggestive of PSGN progressing to RPGN (Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis). If the histopathology finding of the patient was asked then the answer would be crescent formation, which is characteristic of RPGN. Since the electron microscopy finding in the given patient is asked, the answer is subepithelial deposits, which is the characteristic finding of underlying pathology i.e. PSGN.

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is caused by Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infections. It is uncommon before the age of 3 years and most prevalent in kids between the ages of 5 and 12 years.

The patient typically develops an acute nephritic syndrome

• 1 to 2 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis or
• 3 to 6 weeks after streptococcal pyoderma

From asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with normal renal function to gross hematuria with acute renal failure, the severity of kidney involvement varies. Patients may experience different levels of edema, hypertension, and oliguria depending on the extent of the renal involvement.

Laboratory findings: More than 90% of patients see a considerable reduction in serum C3 levels during the acute phase, which lasts 6 to 8 weeks before returning to normal.
In order to confirm the diagnosis, evidence of preceding streptococcal infection is required. The antistreptolysin O titer frequently rises following pharyngeal infections. The anti-deoxyribonuclease B level is the most effective single antibody titer to demonstrate cutaneous streptococcal infection.

Microscopic Findings in PSGN:

• Light microscopy: Enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial and endothelial proliferation and leukocyte infiltration.
• Immunofluorescence: Granular deposits of IgG and complement C3 along the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and in the mesangium
• Electron microscopy: Primarily subepithelial humps are seen. Subendothelial deposits can be seen in early disease stages.

Below is the image showing light microscopy findings of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Other options:

Option A: Subendothelial deposits - These are characteristic of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) type I. MPGN typically presents with nephrotic or nephritic features but does not necessarily follow a streptococcal infection.

Option C: Crescentic glomerulonephritis, also known as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN)is a type of nephritic syndrome associated with severe glomerular injury with necrosis and formation of crescents. The disease progresses rapidly and leads to renal failure in weeks to months when not treated.

Option D: Mesangial deposits - These are characteristic of IgA nephropathy, which typically presents with recurrent episodes of gross hematuria following upper respiratory infections, rather than acute nephritic syndrome following streptococcal infection.
questions.learning: Subepithelial deposits — The diagnosis based on the above clinical scenario is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Subepithelial deposits will be seen on electron microscopy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a head injury opens their eyes in response to a loud voice, localizes pain, and is confused with disorientation. Based on these findings, what is the patient’s Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?
questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) assesses three components: Eye-opening (E), Motor response (M), and Verbal response (V). "Eye-opening in response to a loud voice" corresponds to an E3 score (normal spontaneous opening is E4). "Pain localization" (moving the hand to the site of a noxious stimulus) corresponds to an M5 score (obeying commands is M6). "Confusion with disorientation" corresponds to a V4 score (fully oriented is V5). Therefore, the total GCS is . Option B, C, and D are incorrect based on these specific clinical findings. A GCS of 12 is classified as a "moderate" head injury. Patients with a GCS of 8 or less are considered "comatose" and typically require airway protection via endotracheal intubation. Consistent monitoring of the GCS is vital to detect early neurological deterioration in trauma patients
questions.learning: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) assesses three components: Eye-opening (E), Motor response (M), and Verbal response (V). "Eye-opening in response to a loud voice" corresponds to an E3 score (normal spontaneous opening is E4).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An adult patient presents with fever and right- sided chest pain and is found to have a moderate right-sided pleural effusion. Diagnostic thoracocentesis reveals a straw-colored exudate with 50 mg% glucose and lymphocytic predominance. ADA levels are borderline. Which investigation is most likely to confirm a diagnosis of tuberculosis in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient has features suggestive of tuberculous pleural effusion—straw-colored exudate, lymphocytic predominance, and low glucose. Although ADA is borderline, TB still remains a strong possibility. The Pleural Fluid Xpert MTB/RIF assay is the most appropriate next investigation because it is a rapid molecular test (PCR-based) that detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA and also identifies rifampicin resistance. It has higher sensitivity and specificity than smear and provides quick results, making it clinically very useful. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Needle biopsy of pleura: More invasive; though diagnostic, it is not first-line and reserved if less invasive tests fail. (C) Pleural fluid AFB smear:Very low sensitivity due to low bacillary load. (D) Pleural fluid AFB culture: Gold standard but takes weeks, delaying diagnosis and treatment. Thus, the best confirmatory and practical test here is Xpert MTB/RIF assay

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the marked structure in the image:
questions.explanation: The provided sagittal MRI section of the head clearly delineates the components of the brainstem. The structure marked is the pons, which is the prominent, bulbous middle portion of the brainstem located between the midbrain and the medulla oblongata. Anatomically, the midbrain (Option A) is situated superior to the pons, forming the uppermost part of the brainstem. The medulla oblongata (Option C) lies inferior to the pons and is continuous with the spinal cord (Option D) at the level of the foramen magnum. The pons is easily identified on a sagittal view by its distinctive anterior protrusion, which contains transverse fibers connecting to the cerebellum. It serves as a vital bridge for neural signals and houses several cranial nerve nuclei, including the trigeminal, abducens, and facial nerves. Consequently, based on its anatomical position and shape, the marked structure is the pons

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient reports excessive consumption of bajra (pearl millet) roti and subsequently develops symptoms of drowsiness and giddiness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Consumption of Bajra (pearl millet) that has been contaminated with the fungus Claviceps purpurea leads to ergotism. The fungus produces ergot alkaloids which act as potent vasoconstrictors and CNS disruptors, causing symptoms such as giddiness, drowsiness, and tingling sensations. In severe cases, this can progress to gangrene or convulsions. Epidemic Dropsy (Option A) is caused by the adulteration of mustard oil with Argemone oil, presenting with cardiac failure and edema. Botulism (Option C) results from Clostridium botulinum toxin, typically found in improperly canned foods, and causes descending flaccid paralysis. Fusarium toxicity (Option D) is associated with alimentary toxic aleukia and pancytopenia but is not the classic link for Bajra-induced CNS symptoms. Ergotism is historically prevented by removing contaminated grains using a 20% salt solution flotation method

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Which among the following are appropriate techniques for chromosomal aneuploidy?

i.  In situ hybridization

ii. Conventional cytogenetics

iii. Sanger sequencing

iv. Polymerase chain reaction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. i,ii,iii,iv

In situ hybridization, Conventional cytogenetics, Sanger sequencing and Polymerase chain reaction are appropriate techniques for chromosomal aneuploidy.

Techniques to detect aneuploidy:

1. In situ hybridization: Fluorescent In Situ Hybridisation (FISH) helps in the detection of specific genetic information using fluorescent probes. FISH is used to detect chromosomal aneuploidy, subtle microdeletions and rearrangements, complex translocations, and gene amplification.
2. Conventional cytogenetics: This technique involves the study of chromosomes under a microscope, typically using methods like karyotyping, which arranges chromosomes by size, shape, and number. The analysis allows the identification of large chromosomal abnormalities, such as aneuploidy or structural changes.
3. Sanger sequencing: DNA sequencing that uses chain-termination to identify the exact sequence of nucleotides in a DNA molecule. Simple Senger sequencing can detect aneuploidy only with massive parallel sequencing.
4. Polymerase chain reaction: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a rapid automated method for the amplification of specific DNA sequences (or genes). It can accurately quantify the target nucleic acid sequence within a sample. It is useful for determining somatic mutation with low allele frequency. Quantitative Fluorescence (QF) PCR is a method of rapid aneuploidy detection. It is less expensive and allows simultaneous processing of large number of samples of FISH.
5. Array Comparitive Genomic Hybridization: microarray based technique which can reveal imbalances across the genome.
6. Multiplex Ligation Probe Amplification: to detect gene dosage.
questions.learning: i,ii,iii,iv In situ hybridization, Conventional cytogenetics, Sanger sequencing and Polymerase chain reaction are appropriate techniques for chromosomal aneuploidy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is calculated with the following information?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Maternal Mortality Rate

The given expression is used for calculating the maternal mortality rate. The maternal mortality rate is expressed as the "number of maternal deaths in a given period per 100,000 women in reproductive age during the same time period".

Other options:

Option B: The maternal mortality ratio is the "number of maternal deaths during a given period per 100,000 live births during the same time".

Option C: The death rate in reproductive women is expressed as the "number of deaths among women aged 15-49 years during a given period per 1,000 women of the same age group during the same time period.

Option D: The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is expressed as the "average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime if she were to experience the current age-specific fertility rates throughout her reproductive years (typically ages 15-49).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which drug is indicated for a 55-year-old premenopausal woman with early invasive breast cancer that is ER-positive, PR-positive on immunohistochemistry, and has lymph node involvement?
questions.explanation: In a 55-year-old premenopausal woman with ER-positive, PR-positive early invasive breast cancer with lymph node involvement, multimodal therapy is indicated. 1. Tamoxifen is the standard endocrine therapy in premenopausal women, acting as a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) to block estrogen effects on tumor cells. 2. Anastrozole (an aromatase inhibitor) is typically used in postmenopausal women, but may also be used in premenopausal patients with ovarian suppression. 3. Trastuzumab is indicated if the tumor is HER2-positive, which is often evaluated alongside ER/PR status in such cases. Thus, depending on receptor status (including HER2) and treatment plan, all three drugs may be part of therapy, making option (D) the best answer

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old child is brought to the OPD with a history of repeated fractures for the past 2 years. On examination, there is the presence of blue sclera and dental abnormalities. There is a positive family history. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteogenesis imperfecta

Positive family history and clinical features such as blue sclera with dental abnormalities are suggestive of Osteogenesis imperfecta.

Osteogenesis imperfecta occurs due to the abnormality in Type 1 collagen. It is characterized by increased fragility of bones, dental anomalies, and lax joints. Skin, sclera, and cornea are also involved.

It is classified into different types based on their characteristic features, severity, and mode of inheritance.

Type 1

* The most common and mildest form of the disease.

* Autosomal dominant inheritance.

* The presentation can be a young child with a history of recurrent fractures.

* Blue sclera and dental abnormalities are seen.

* The radiograph may show osteoporosis, cortical thinning with thin and gracile bones. Wormian bones are seen.

Type 2

* Most lethal variant

* Infants have deep blue sclera with short and deformed limbs due to multiple fractures.

* Pulmonary insufficiency is the usual cause of death due to rib fractures.

* Ribs having a beaded appearance may be seen in the radiograph.

* Intrasutural bones may be seen in the occipital and parietal regions.

Type 3

* Autosomal recessive inheritance

* Fractures of the long bones are present at birth.

* Deformity increases with the growth of the child.

* Progressive kyphoscoliosis is seen from childhood due to vertebral fractures.

* The radiograph shows abnormal epiphysis with islands of calcified cartilage.

Type 4

* Autosomal dominant inheritance

* Severity varies and hence can be confused with type 1 and type 3 disease.

* Short stature is seen and basilar invagination occurs in a large number of cases

Type 5

* It is similar to type 4 disease

* Autosomal dominant inheritance is seen but it can occur spontaneously.

* Hypertrophic callus formation at sites or fracture or surgical intervention is a typical finding.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In case of a child with an acute poisoning by ingestion, activated charcoal may be used in which one of the following situations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antiepileptic ingestion

Activated charcoal is useful in acute poisoning with drugs that are adsorbed by charcoal, provided the patient presents within 1 hour of ingestion (or later for sustained-release preparations) and has a protected airway. It is effective for many drugs, including antiepileptics (e.g., carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin).

Why not the other options?

• A. Iron ingestion: Activated charcoal does not adsorb iron.
• C. Corrosive ingestion: Contraindicated because it does not bind corrosives and may interfere with endoscopy or increase aspiration risk.
• D. Lithium ingestion: Activated charcoal does not adsorb lithium.
